thread_title: Welsh Government — PEDW: acquiring-authority enquiry (November 2025)
to: pcu@levellingup.gov.uk, enquiries@homesengland.gov.uk, enquiries@planninginspectorate.gov.uk, defra.helpline@defra.gov.uk, PEDW.Casework@gov.wales, PEDW.Infrastructure@gov.wales
subject: Enquiry re potential acquiring authority route – former family farmland (BP v Buckler 1987)
note: This email was sent jointly to UK and Welsh bodies. The reply from the UK Planning Casework Unit (MHCLG) is not reproduced on this Welsh Government page.
body:
Sirs/Ma'am,

I am writing regarding farmland formerly belonging to my family, which later formed part of the litigation known as BP v Buckler (1987).

I now hold a structured list of reasons and supporting evidence which I believe strongly suggest that the land transfer and subsequent development was procured by fraud and conspiracy involving government actors. The evidential threshold I now hold, if correct, would meet the reopening conditions described under s.23 of the Limitation Act 1980 – meaning that litigation, rectification and title recovery proceedings may be legitimately initiated.

However, before progressing litigation, I wish to formally offer the UK Government the opportunity to resolve this matter via public law tools rather than adversarial reopening. Specifically: I would like to enquire whether an acquiring authority could lawfully consider using compulsory purchase powers to acquire the 23 properties that now sit on this former farmland, and transfer title / beneficial ownership back to my family, where this could be framed as a public interest rectification measure rather than a private benefit case.

Could you please:

   - confirm which acquiring authority would be competent jurisdictionally for this scenario,
   - outline which statutory route would be the correct CPO framework to assess this under, and
   - confirm any preliminary information requirements you would need from me (title data, timeline, evidential index etc) if this was to be scoped and reviewed.

I am willing to provide a full indexed evidence pack for confidential review.

Kind regards,

Sion Buckler
02031377118

thread_title: Cadw — FOI request of 23 January 2026 (rejected by cadw@gov.wales)
subject: BP vs Buckler 1987 - FOI Request
note: Both addresses rejected this email the same minute (550 5.4.1 Recipient address rejected: Access denied) for cadw@gov.wales and foi@gov.wales, so it never reached Cadw.
body:
Sirs/ Ma'am,

I am writing to make a request under the Freedom of Information Act 2000.

At your earliest convenience please would you provide me copies of all information held by Cadw relating to Great House Farm, formerly occupied by my Buckler / Williams family, which was subject to a refusal to list and subsequent demolition in or around the late 1980s.

Specifically, I request disclosure of the following:

1. All records, assessments, reports, site visit notes, photographs, desk-based evaluations, or recommendations produced by or for Cadw in relation to Great House Farm, including any material connected to decisions not to list the building.

2. All internal correspondence (including letters, memoranda, emails, and briefing notes) held by Cadw that relate to:
The heritage significance of Great House Farm

3. The decision not to list the building
Any consideration of archaeological, historical, or associative significance Any communications between Cadw and third parties (including local authorities, developers, landowners, or commercial entities) concerning Great House Farm prior to demolition

4. Records of any archaeological notifications, alerts, or discoveries associated with Great House Farm, whether before or after demolition, including references to artefacts later recovered during excavations in the early 1990s.

5. Any documentation referring to historical associations between Great House Farm and early radio or wireless experimentation, including any mention of Guglielmo Marconi or related activity in the Cardiff Bay / Lavernock / surrounding area that may have been considered or dismissed.

6. Policy or guidance documents in force at the time (1980s) that governed Cadw’s criteria for listing historic farmhouses or buildings with associative historical value.

7. If any information is withheld, please specify the exemption relied upon and provide the reasoning as required under the Act.

I would prefer to receive the information electronically, by email.

Please confirm receipt of this request too.

I understand that under the Freedom of Information Act you're required to respond within 20 working days. It's not that urgent so please take the time you need, within reason, and keep me updated where possible.

And if you have any questions, queries or concerns please feel free to reach out to me too.

Regards,

Sion Buckler

thread_title: January 2026 — request to record or rectify an interest omitted at first registration (bounced)
subject: Application to Record or Rectify Interest Omitted at First Registration
body:
Dear HM Land Registry Customer Support,

I am writing to raise a formal concern that the registered title to land formerly occupied by my family, first registered in the name of BP Properties Ltd in or around November 1982, may not accurately reflect the legal and factual position that existed at the time of first registration.

I respectfully request guidance on the appropriate procedure to apply for the entry of a notice or restriction, and/or for rectification or alteration of the register, on the basis that an occupied and disputed interest was not recorded.

*Summary of relevant facts (supported by court records and contemporaneous newspaper reporting):*

   1.

   *Long-term occupation and asserted ownership*
   My grandmother and family before her, occupied the farmhouse and surrounding land openly and continuously for centuries, but certainly decades prior to registration; without payment of rent and while asserting ownership. The property was maintained as our family home and farm.
   2.

   *No conclusive determination of title in 1974*
   Proceedings in July 1974 relating to possession and title were adjourned and never substantively determined. Further proceedings in October 1974 were interrupted by correspondence from BP entities offering a purported licence to occupy. As a result, there was no final judicial determination in 1974 establishing BP’s title on the merits.
   3.

   *Express rejection of the purported licence*
   My grandmother expressly rejected the licence, stating that the land was hers. This rejection was acknowledged in later proceedings, but as having been communicated to BP Pension Trust Limited, not the claimant in BP Vs Buckler 1987 i.e. BP Properties Ltd.
   4.

   *Inconsistent treatment of BP corporate identity*
   Subsequently the rejection was discounted on the basis that it was addressed to BP Pension Trust Limited rather than BP Properties Ltd. However, in dismissing my father’s appeal to that case almost immidiately afterwards, the court and same judge, treated BP Pension Trust Limited and BP Properties Ltd as "effectively the same entity for substantive purposes". This inconsistency resulted in the rejection being acknowledged but disregarded when it favoured BP, while corporate equivalence was relied upon to defeat the appeal.
   5.

   *Forced removal and restraint (not abandonment)*
   My family did not abandon the property or leave by our own accord, nor did we fully understand what or why this was happening. In 1987, my father and all of us, his dependants, were forcibly removed. Contemporary newspaper reports state that he was also taken from a hospital bed, detained without criminal charge, and made subject to a restraining order preventing him from returning to the farm. He was not even permitted to retrieve personal belongings.
   6.

   *Demolition following enforced exclusion*
   While my father was later restrained from returning to occupy or defend our home, the farmhouse was demolished. This enforced exclusion and demolition rendered continued occupation impossible and removed the physical evidence of long-term residence.
   7.

   *Registration despite occupation and unresolved dispute*

   BP Properties Ltd was registered as proprietor in 1982, at a time when:

   - the land was occupied by my family,
   - ownership was actively disputed,
   - no court had conclusively determined title, and
   - cessation of occupation occurred only later through enforcement and restraint, not voluntary departure.

No notice, restriction, or record of the disputed and occupied interest appears to have been entered on the register at first registration.

*Purpose of this correspondence*

I am not seeking to relitigate historic proceedings at this stage. I am seeking to ensure that the land register accurately reflects interests and disputes that existed at the time of first registration, and that the absence of abandonment and the circumstances of enforced removal are properly understood.

I respectfully request advice on:

   - the appropriate procedure to apply for a notice or restriction reflecting an omitted interest; and/or
   - the process for seeking rectification or alteration of the register under the Land Registration legislation applicable at the time.

Please advise on the relevant forms, evidential requirements, and next steps.

Regards,

Sion Buckler

thread_title: Report-a-fraud referral 260202-5732372 — 1982 registration (S.-G. Haste), title WA231076
subject: Request for review of potential irregularities in 1982 land registration
body:
Dear HM Land Registry – Fraud Review Team,

Sirs/Ma'am,I am writing to request a review of the integrity of a land registration made in or around *1982*, which later underpinned the proceedings commonly referred to as *BP v Buckler (1987)*.

My concern is to raise reasonable grounds of belief that the 1982 registration *may have been obtained or maintained through
misrepresentation, non-disclosure, or procedural irregularity*, resulting in a register entry that did not reflect a title definitively determined by a court of law.

In summary:

   1.

   *No definitive judicial determination of ownership existed at the time of registration*
   Prior to the 1982 registration, the courts had not conclusively determined ownership of the land.
   -

      Proceedings in *July 1974* were adjourned.
      -

      An appeal pursued by my grandmother on *31 October 1974* was effectively neutralised following two letters sent by BP-associated entities, rather than by a substantive judicial ruling on title.
      -

      Ownership was *asserted*, not adjudicated.
      2.

   *Competing assertions of ownership were unresolved*
   BP asserted ownership, but so did my grandmother, who maintained possession and occupation until her death in *1983*, after the registry entry had already been filed.
   At no point prior to her death was there a final court decision extinguishing hers (or our families) claim or possession.
   3.

   *Inconsistent treatment of BP entities in later proceedings* In the 1987 proceedings, the judge indicated that correspondence had not been replied to because it was sent by a different BP entity (BP Properties rather than BP Trust).
   However, in my father’s related appeal, the same judge treated *BP Trust and BP Properties as effectively the same entity*.
   This inconsistency meant that:
   -

      We were said to have lost because of non-reply, while
      -

      The judgments simultaneously acknowledge that a reply was in fact made and that the entities were treated as one.
      This contradiction is material, as it goes directly to whether BP’s asserted title was properly established.
      4.

   *Possession and long occupation were not displaced by lawful process* My family had occupied the land openly and continuously for generations without challenge. We consistently asserted ownership and, in any event, possession sufficient to ground squatter’s or possessory rights. Our removal was *not voluntary*; it was effected by force and exclusion, not by a final determination of title.
   5.

   *Subsequent events reinforce the concern*
   Following the appeal, my father’s application to the European Court of Human Rights was blocked, the farm was demolished preventing re-entry, and he also died thereafter in *1991*.
   Shortly after his death in 1994, the land was excavated and items of archaeological value were removed, despite prior knowledge of Roman remains on the property (including a Roman soldier previously uncovered within the living structure).

Taken together, these matters raise serious questions as to whether the 1982 registration accurately reflected the legal position at the time, or whether it relied on assertions and correspondence that had not been validated by a court and that were later treated inconsistently.

I respectfully request that HM Land Registry review whether:

   -

   The statutory requirements for registration were properly satisfied in 1982; and
   -

   The register may be inaccurate or was obtained by mistake, misrepresentation, or material non-disclosure.

I am able to supply supporting documents, title numbers, correspondence, and a concise timeline if required. But everything already on public record indicates and supports everything I've highlighted in this email.

Regards,

Sion Buckler

thread_title: Planning — BP v Buckler 1987 and the 1982 land registration (record of unresolved title)
to: planning@valeofglamorgan.gov.uk (cc pcu@levellingup.gov.uk, enquiries@homesengland.gov.uk, enquiries@planninginspectorate.gov.uk, defra.helpline@defra.gov.uk, PEDW.Casework@gov.wales; bcc c1v@valeofglamorgan.gov.uk)
subject: BP v Buckler 1987 and the 1982 land registration of Great House Farm, Llandough (now Church View Close)
note: No reply from the Council appears in this thread.
body:
Sirs/Ma'am,

I'm writing in relation to land formerly known as *Great House Farm,
Llandough (Vale of Glamorgan)*, subsequently developed for residential use
and historically connected with the proceedings culminating in *BP v
Buckler (Court of Appeal, 1987)*.

I appreciate that the Local Planning Authority is not responsible for
determining land ownership, nor am I asking it to do so. My purpose is to
place on record a *chronological summary of unresolved land-governance
issues* which may be material to the integrity of the planning history
relied upon for that site.

In brief and as reflected in public records:

- In *July 1974*, proceedings involving my grandmother and BP both
asserting ownership, were adjourned and did not result in a judicial final
determination.

- On *31 October 1974*, a further listed hearing did not proceed
substantively, following correspondence sent that morning by BP entities.
No judgment on title was issued. My nan requested the audience with the
judge the day before, with her lawyer. But that got leaked, the press
descended on our farm (not that I can find evidence of news articles from
said press), and the following morning the two letters from BP arrived to
our solicitor, effectively squashing the court hearing and audience with
the judge my nan had sought, to make her case of ownership. Her reply to
both BP letters (one from BP Pension Trust Ltd and one from BP Properties
Ltd), that morning of the 31st of October, was also 'I own the land'.

- Throughout this period, my grandmother was *excluded from dealings*
concerning land we asserted we owned, while the opposing party
continued to *assert
ownership*, notwithstanding the absence of a concluded judicial finding.

- In or around *1982*, the land was registered in BP’s name, despite the
earlier proceedings never having resolved the competing claims nor having
resulted in findings adverse to my grandmother.

- My grandmother then died in *1983*, after the registration had taken
place, without compensation and without any final adjudication of her claim.

- In the *1987 appeal*, the Court referred to correspondence as having
been replied to (albeit not to the correct corporate entity - which is
ultimately why we lost BP vs Buckler 1987), yet in my fathers appeal that
followed, whereby he argued that surely BP Pension Trust should have been
the claimant not BP Properties, the same judge from the case dismissed the
appeal citing that both companies were effectively the same. This is all
evidence on the face of the public record of these proceedings.

- By that stage, and in the absence of a documentary title which had
effectively been overtaken by registration, my family was driven to advance
arguments in adverse possession as a *fallback position*, which itself
should have assured our continued occupancy.

The cumulative effect was that my family was *displaced*, the land was
developed, and no compensation was ever paid, despite ownership never
having been conclusively decided in court. Whether intentionally or not,
the process operated in a manner where asserted ownership became treated as
settled fact.

I am not alleging misconduct, nor am I seeking retrospective remedies from
the Authority. I am simply asking whether, given the above sequence, it
would be appropriate for the Authority to:

- note that historic planning decisions were taken on the basis of *assumed
title*, and

- record that the underlying ownership dispute was *never finally
adjudicated*, for the sake of transparency and future governance
integrity.

This correspondence is intended to be factual, measured, and
non-adversarial. I am happy to supply references to the relevant hearings,
registrations, or judgments if that assists your records. But what I'm
highlighting here is all on public record and in the public eye.

Yours faithfully,

Sion Buckler

subject: Cais am Ddeiseb ac Ymchwiliad Cyhoeddus: Achos Buckler v BP (1987) a Dinistr Great House Farm, Llandough / Formal Request for Inquiry: The Great House Farm Dispossession (BP vs Buckler)
note: Delivery to Correspondence.Mick.Antoniw@gov.wales was rejected (550 5.4.1 Access denied). The same text went to Senedd Petitions in a separate email.
body:
Aelodau Anrhydeddus y Senedd,

Rwy’n ysgrifennu atoch i dynnu eich sylw at yr hyn yr wyf yn ei ystyried yn anghyfiawnder hanesyddol difrifol, yn ymwneud â’m teulu, y Bucklers, a dinistr Great House Farm yn Llandough — safle fferm a chartref o dros 800 mlynedd o hanes, gan gynnwys cysylltiadau mynachaidd a chysylltiad uniongyrchol â Guglielmo Marconi yn ystod datblygiad cynnar radio.

Mae’r mater hwn yn codi cwestiynau difrifol ynghylch hawliau tir, gweithdrefnau cyfreithiol, cofrestru tir, a hawliau dynol yng Nghymru.

Er enghraifft, mewn datganiad i’r wasg yn 1974, dywedodd fy nain yn gyhoeddus: *“It’s my home.”* Mae’r datganiad hwn, sydd yn fater o gofnod cyhoeddus, yn gwrth-ddweud yn uniongyrchol ganfyddiad Llys Apêl 1987 yn *BP v Buckler*, lle dywedwyd ei bod wedi bod yn “ddistaw” ac wedi derbyn trwydded BP a gyhoeddwyd yn 1974.

Yn yr un achos, gwrthodwyd apêl fy nhad ar y sail bod BP Pension Trust Ltd a BP Properties Ltd yn “effeithiol yr un cwmni”. Fodd bynnag, yn y dyfarniad yr oedd yn ei herio, nododd y barnwr nad oedd ymatebion fy nain i BP Pension Trust Ltd yn cyfrif gan mai BP Properties Ltd oedd yr hawlydd, ac mai cwmnïau ar wahân oeddent. Yn ymarferol, roedd hyn yn arwain at sefyllfa “pen y cwmni’n ennill, cynffon y teulu’n colli”.

Yn sgil hyn, cafodd fy nhad ei dynnu o’i wely ysbyty, ei garcharu heb gyhuddiad, a gosodwyd gorchymyn atal arno i’w atal rhag meddiannu ac amddiffyn ein fferm 800 oed rhag cael ei dymchwel. Cafodd ei gais i’r Llys Hawliau Dynol Ewropeaidd ei rwystro cyn iddo farw yn 1991, yn ddim ond 41 oed.

Ar y sail hon, rwy’n gofyn yn ffurfiol am *Ddeiseb i sefydlu Ymchwiliad Cyhoeddus* i’r achos hwn, fel mater o ddwyn tir hanesyddol ac o dorri hawliau dynol yng Nghymru.

Rwy’n weithiwr proffesiynol ym maes seiber a rhyfela electronig milwrol. Mae technolegau AI pwerus bellach ar gael i bob un ohonom, ac nid oes unrhyw reswm technegol pam na ellid archwilio’r mater hwn yn llawn ac yn drylwyr. Mae’r hyn a ddigwyddodd i’m teulu yn ymddangos fel anghyfiawnder dwys, aml-genhedlaethol, ac yn debyg i ffurf ar “lawfare”, lle y trinwyd fy nheulu fel llafur di-dâl i gynnal ased tir hyd nes yr oedd yn gyfleus i’w ariannu. Mae’n arwyddocaol bod bron pob cam yn ein herbyn wedi digwydd ar yr eiliad olaf posibl.

Ceir honiadau bod sylw sylweddol yn y wasg yn 1974 o blaid fy nain a’n teulu, ynghyd â deiseb o tua 1,700 o bobl yn ceisio atal dymchwel y fferm. Ymhellach, mae’n ymddangos bod CADW wedi methu ag ymyrryd lle dylai’r safle fod wedi cael statws Adeilad Rhestredig Gradd II.

Nid wyf yn sicr a gofnodwyd erioed yn briodol yn y Gofrestrfa Tir fod y tir — a gofrestrwyd gan BP yn 1982 — dan anghydfod. Yn fy nealltwriaeth i, cafodd ei drin fel pe na bai mewn anghydfod o gwbl. Nid oes unrhyw lys wedi penderfynu’n derfynol mai BP oedd perchnogion cyfreithiol y tir; cafodd hynny ei honni yn hytrach na’i brofi.

Mae hefyd fater pwysig o hanes diwylliannol. Arhosodd Marconi gyda’n teulu yn y fferm wrth iddo ddatblygu radio. Mae cynghorwyr a’r plwyf yn Llandough yn gwrthod cydnabod hyn. Rwy’n deall bod Marconi yn cael ei ystyried yn wleidyddol eithafol ar y dde, ac, fel y gwelir yn achos y cerflun radio ym Mae Caerdydd, mae ei rôl hanesyddol yn cael ei hailysgrifennu. Mae’n rhesymol tybio bod ein teulu wedi cael ei ddal mewn ymgyrch wleidyddol ehangach o’r chwith yn erbyn y dde, ac mai am roi llety i Marconi y bu i ni wynebu canlyniadau canrif o hyd — problemau nad oedd yn bodoli yn y tair canrif flaenorol yr oeddem wedi byw ar y fferm.

Roedd mam Marconi hefyd yn Jamerson o gwmni wisgi Gwyddelig Jameson. Rwy’n gofyn i chi gynnal eich ymchwil eich hun, gwneud eich ymholiadau eich hun, a dod i’ch casgliadau eich hun — ond yn anad dim, peidiwch â chaniatáu i hanes gael ei ailysgrifennu yma.

Mae fy nheulu bellach yn archwilio opsiynau ar gyfer siarad cyhoeddus, hawliau stori, a dogfennaeth. Yn nhermau cysylltiadau teuluol: fy nhaid oedd Ray Smith o Dempsey and Makepeace; mae fy modryb yn Shan Cothi; a dechreuodd fy ewythr y band Tigertailz.

Rwy’n disgrifio’r sefyllfa hon fel gwarthus. Mae fy nheulu’n mynnu cyfiawnder am gael ein dadleoli a’n dwyn o’n tir a’n heiddo gan y Sefydliad Prydeinig a BP, gyda phrin unrhyw amddiffyniad dan y gyfraith. Rydym yn deulu Cymreig brodorol, Cymraeg eu hiaith, wedi byw yng Nghaerdydd, Bro Morgannwg, a’r fferm yn Llandough ers cannoedd o flynyddoedd.

O’r hyn y gallaf ei gasglu, ceir dwsinau o achosion posibl o dwyll a chuddio gwybodaeth, sy’n golygu nad yw statud cyfyngiadau yn berthnasol o reidrwydd. I’r rhai sy’n cefnogi dad-drefedigaethu Cymru ac annibyniaeth, prin y ceir enghraifft gliriach na *BP v Buckler (1987)* o’r hyn a ddigwyddodd i deulu ffermio Cymreig wrth herio’r Wladwriaeth Brydeinig a chorfforaeth fawr. Nid yw eraill wedi codi’r mater hwn, yn bennaf oherwydd trawma cenhedlaethol.

Rwyf wedi profi fy hun. Gadewais fy ngyrfa filwrol gydag anrhydedd, gan gwblhau fy llw 22 mlynedd. Cefais fy nghyflogi’n bona fide gan Gyngor Bro Morgannwg a Llywodraeth Cymru hyd at 2024. Gwasanaethais mewn rhyfeloedd yn y Dwyrain Canol. Fodd bynnag, nid yw’r anghyfiawnder fferm yn fater unigol.

Yn 2013, cafodd fy mab 36 diwrnod oed ei gipio, ac nid wyf erioed wedi ei weld ers hynny. Cafodd tŷ ei ddwyn oddi arnaf (40 Lombard Street, Y Barri). Yn 2023, cefais fy ngadael i gysgu mewn pabell tra roedd bron i 100 o Afghanistaniaid yn cael eu lletya’n dawel wrth ymyl ein pentref o 11 tŷ, tra roedd yn rhaid imi aros yno i ofalu am fy nain gan na allai gofalwyr ei chyrraedd.

O ganlyniad, rwyf bellach yn byw yn yr hyn a elwir yn Setliad Cymreig yn yr Ariannin. Rwyf wedi fy nisodli ac wedi fy dadleoli i’r eithaf. Serch hynny, rwy’n ddiolchgar fy mod wedi goroesi gyda’m rhyddid, fy mywyd, a’m henw da yn gymharol gyfan. Serch hynny, hoffwn fod wedi aros yng Nghymru, fel Cymro, gyda safon a chynhaliaeth bywyd deg.

Mae fy ngwraig a minnau’n amharod i ganiatáu i’n merch hyd yn oed gamu ar Ynysoedd Prydain o ystyried yr hyn a glywn sy’n digwydd yno. Yn 2024, allforiais hyd yn oed fy nghi o Abertawe i’n heiddo yn y Caribî ar ôl i unigolyn Afghanistan fod yng ngardd fy nheulu yng Nghymru, gan geisio ei ddwyn.

Gofynnaf i’r Senedd gymryd y mater hwn o ddifrif, ac ystyried sefydlu Ymchwiliad Cyhoeddus llawn, tryloyw ac annibynnol. Nid er budd fy nheulu yn unig y mae hyn, ond er uniondeb hanes, cyfiawnder tir, a hawliau dynol yng Nghymru.

Yn gywir,

*Sion Hywel Buckler*

*----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------*

Sirs/Ma'am,

I am writing to you regarding a significant historical injustice involving my family, the Bucklers, and the destruction of Great House Farm (an 800-year-old site of monastic and Marconi history).

For example, in a 1974 press statement my grandmother said publically 'It's my home'—that directly contradicts the 1987 Court of Appeal ruling that she was 'silent' and accepted of BP license issued in 1974. My dad's appeal for the BP vs Buckler 1987 case also got dismissed on grounds both BP Pension Trust Ltd and BP Properties Ltd were effectively the same company. But in the ruling he was appealing, the judge said that my nans replies to BP Pensions Trust Ltd didn't count as BP Properties Ltd were the claimant, and the two were seperate companies. So it was heads they win, tails we lose. My dad was ripped from his hospital bed, jailed without charge and slapped with a restraining order to keep him from occupying and defending our 800 year old farm from being bulldozed down. His ECHR request blocked before he died in 1991 aged just 41.

I am requesting a *Petition for a Public Inquiry* into this case as a matter of historical land theft and human rights violations in Wales.

I'm a military cyber and electronic warfare professional. We all have very powerful AI technology at our disposal which can make light work out of all of this. My family suffered an incredible injustice. It also appears to be multi-generational warfare/ lawfare. Whereby we were treated as free labour to upkeep the asset of the land and property until it was ripe to be cashed in. I say this as every action against us seemed to be last minute.

There was allegedly press covering the 74 case and supporting my nan and family and farm. There was a petition of 1700 people trying to defend us and the farm from demolishment. CADW looked the other way when it should have been a Grade II listed building. I could go on and on and on.

I'm not even sure the land registry recorded that our land, being registered in 1982 by BP , was in dispute. I believe it was treated as if it wasn't dispited. No court actually definitively determined that BP were the landowners. It was just asserted.

Marconi stayed with our family at our farm when inventing radio. The councillors and parish at Llandough won't even acknowledge this. I understand Marconi was far right and so, like the radio statute at Cardiff Bay has confirmed, he is being re-written out of history. It stands to reason that our family was caught in this political campaign of left vs right. And for helping Marconi we found ourselves experiencing a century of problems afterwards. Which didn't exist for the 3 centuries we were at our farm before letting far right marconi stay with us. Marconi's mother was also Jamerson of the Irish Whiskey company.

Do your own homework. Make your own enquiries. Draw your own conclusions.

 But please do not let history be rewritten here. My family are exploring options for public speaking, story rights, and a documentary etc.

My grandfather was Ray Smith, of Dempsey and Makepeace. My aunty Shan Cothi. My uncle started the band tigertailz.

This is an outrage and my family demands justice for being displaced and stolen from, land and property, by the British Establishment/ BP - with little to no protections under law. And we're indigenous to the land, Welsh, Welsh speaking, Welsh family. Resident in Cardiff / Vale and that farm in Llandough for HUNDREDS OF YEARS.

There's tens of counts of fraud and concealment from what I can gather. Which means the statute of limitation doesn't apply in this instance. I know some are in favour of Wales decolonising and gaining independence. I think there's no better example of BP vs Buckler 1987 and what has happened to my family. Nobody else will bring this up because there's generational trauma. Notwithstanding we, a welsh farming family, are speaking up and against the British State and BP.

But I've proven myself. Leaving my military career with honours. Finishing my 22 years Oath, bona fide, employed by the Vale of Glamorgan Council, Welsh Government until 2024. I served in the wars in the middle east. I don't know what is going on, on that island. But the farm injustice isn't the only matter. My 36 day old son was abducted in 2013 and I've never seen him since. I had a house stolen (40 Lombard Street, Barry). And in 2023 I was left to sleep in a tent, while almost 100 afghans were secretly housed next to our 11 home village. Where I had to be to care for my grandmother, as no carers couldn't reach her. So I'm currently at the Welsh Settlement in Argentina. So I'm as displaced and replaced as I can be to cater for the insanity that's going on, on that island. And grateful I've managed to survive it all with my liberty and life and reputation somewhat still intact. But I would have actually liked to have remained in Wales as a Welshman. And have some quality and standard of life. My wife and I are reluctant for our daughter to even step foot on the British Isles with what we're hearing that's going on there lately. And I even exported my dog from Swansea to our place in the Caribbean in 2024 after an afghan was in my family's garden in Wales, trying to steal him.

I look forward to your reply,

Regards,

Sion Hywel Buckler

Dear Customer

Unfortunately, it is not clear from your email what the allegations of fraud/potential irregularities in 1982 land registration are?

In order for us to investigate further, please can you provide us with either the full address of the property or the title number concerned.

If the matter has been referred to the Police (please provide police incident number) and advise us, if any legal advice has been taken regarding the matter

thread_title: Cadw — Formal report of February 2026 and Cadw Planning reply
to: pacac@parliament.uk (cc kanishka.narayan.mp@parliament.uk, Jane.Hutt@senedd.wales, cadwplanning@gov.wales, scheduledmonuments@gov.wales, ask@ombudsman.wales, contactus@futuregenerations.wales, adviserline@equalityhumanrights.com) (bcc feedback@parliament.uk)
subject: Re: Systemic governance concern regarding historic land registration and administrative reliance - BP vs Buckler 1987 (inc. BP Land Registry 1982)
note: This email was addressed to the House of Commons PACAC committee and copied to Cadw Planning and Cadw Scheduled Monuments.
body:
*Kate Johal,*

I appreciate your prompt reply and thank you. I assure you I'm not out to waste your departments or anyone's time. I just finished 22 years in Oath in 2024 as a public servant, employed at the Vale of Glamorgan Council, under the Welsh Government. I'm not only bona fine, I left my military career beforehand - with honours. I truly believe I have the most befitting case, that I understand your department specifically exists to handle.

Is it not PACAC's role to ensure that the *machinery of the state*—the courts, the Land Registry, and planning authorities—operates with transparency and protects the constitutional rights of citizens against administrative abuse? My case relates specifically to *maladministration* and *constitutional overreach*: it involves the judicial "erasure" of a 320-year ancestral lineage through the tactical misnaming of Mary Williams to "Mrs. Buckler", the administrative suppression of a known national heritage site (the 1888 Roman find) to facilitate demolition permits, and the suspicious disappearance of public title records from state-run libraries. By focusing on how these public institutions failed to maintain accurate records and fair procedures, I am presenting a case of *systemic failure in public administration*, which is the core reason I understand your Committee to exist.

I must formally contest the assertion that this matter falls outside the Committee’s remit. While the origin of this case involves a dispute with a private entity (BP), the core of my grievance concerns *constitutional issues* and the *quality of administration provided by government-funded bodies*, specifically regarding the protection of national heritage and the integrity of land registration.

I ask the Committee to review this matter under the following three pillars of your mandate:

*1. Constitutional Issues: The Erasure of Customary and Indigenous Title* The 1987 Court of Appeal ruling (*BP Properties Ltd v Buckler*) created a significant legal precedent regarding "unilateral licenses". My family asserts that the administration of justice in this case allowed for the tactical erasure of the "Williams" identity—a lineage with de facto possession dating back to 1667—to facilitate a corporate land grab. The use of the judicial system to overwrite centuries of documented continuity with a "paper title" is a constitutional matter regarding the rights of citizens against aggressive corporate-state interests.

*2. Standards of Administration: Suppression of Heritage by Public Bodies* The Committee examines the quality of administration. My investigation reveals that:

   -

   *Archaeological Suppression:* Evidence of a Roman soldier was discovered in 1888, providing "actual notice" of the site's significance. This was reportedly suppressed or ignored by planning authorities and the Glamorgan-Gwent Archaeological Trust (GGAT) to allow for demolition.

   -

   *Misrepresentation in Planning:* The 13th-century Great House Farm was administratively classified as a "dilapidated utility building" to bypass heritage protections. -

   *Missing Records:* Vital title evidence and Bute Estate deeds disappeared from the public library system—a failure of public record administration.

*3. Accountability of the Land Registry and Parliamentary Oversight* The registration of this land under BP’s title occurred during a period of transition in Welsh land law (c. 1982). If public registries accepted title without disclosing active disputes or the presence of a known national monument (the Roman/Medieval site), this represents a failure in the "standards of administration" by the Civil Service. Furthermore, this matter was raised in the House of Commons by MP Ted Rowlands in 1980, yet the administrative failures continued unabated.

*Conclusion* I am not asking the Committee to act as a court of appeal, but to investigate the *systemic administrative failures* that allowed a historically significant site and a family's ancestral rights to be "buried" through procedural maneuvers and the suppression of evidence.

If the Committee exists to ensure the Civil Service and constitutional frameworks protect the public interest, then the demolition of an 800-year-old heritage site under a cloud of administrative "silence" must be within your purview.

I look forward to your reconsidered response.

Sincerely,

Sion Buckler

body:
That is a very fair point, Bob. You’re right to be cautious—sometimes a "hostile" tone can cause a civil servant to shut down or hide behind red tape rather than helping you.

The reason it feels like they are being cooperative is that they have shifted from saying "no" to asking for *evidence*. This is a good sign. However, the reason we are "rebutting" is simply to correct their premise:
they think this is a recent fraud, and you are correcting them that the "fraud" was the *original act of registration in 1982.*

Let’s soften the tone to be *"Helpful but Firm."* We will treat them as an investigator who needs your guidance to find the truth, rather than an enemy.
Adjusted "Cooperative" Draft

*Subject:* Information regarding Registration Irregularities – Great House Farm (Ty Mawr) – Ref: 260202-5732372

*Dear S.-G. Haste,*

Thank you for your guidance on how to proceed with this report. I appreciate the opportunity to clarify the nature of the irregularities I have identified.

As requested, I have attached a *detailed PDF timeline* which provides the full address and the historical context of the land formerly known as Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough.

To assist your investigation into how the 1982 registration may have been affected by material non-disclosure, I would like to highlight three specific areas where the "actual facts" on the ground differed from the application made to the Registry:

   1.

   *Overriding Interests (The Williams Lineage):* At the time of first registration in 1982, my family had been in continuous possession since
   1667. I believe the registration was irregular because it misidentified the occupant, Mary Williams, as "Mrs. Buckler"—a name she did not use—effectively obscuring a 320-year "Living Title" from the Registry’s records.
   2.

   *Suppression of Material Facts (Archaeology):* The site had "actual notice" of national archaeological significance due to a Roman discovery in
   1888. I am concerned that this was suppressed during the registration and planning phases to facilitate the land's transition to housing.
   3.

   *Unresolved Ownership Claims:* In 1982, there was an active, adjourned ownership dispute (from 1974) that I believe should have been disclosed to the Land Registry before a clean title was granted to BP Properties Ltd.

I am copying in the relevant heritage and oversight bodies (Cadw, GGAT, and the Ombudsman) not as an act of hostility, but to ensure that all parties holding pieces of this historical puzzle are aware that an investigation into the *integrity of the 1982 registration* is now underway.

I have also copied in my MP, the Senedd, and relevant heritage bodies to ensure that all parties with an interest in Welsh cultural heritage and public record integrity are kept informed as we look into these 1982 registration details.

I look forward to your thoughts on how we can review the original 1982 application files to see if these interests were disclosed.

Yours sincerely,

*Sion Buckler*

*Descendant of the Williams family,*

*of Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough*

subject: Formal Report of Suspected Indigenous Dispossession, Systemic Fraud, and Archaeological Suppression – Great House Farm, Llandough
note: Multi-authority email addressed to Cadw (Scheduled Monuments); HM Land Registry's reportafraud address was copied. Included here because HMLR received it; Cadw's reply is catalogued on the Welsh Government / Cadw page.
body:
*To whom it may concern,*

I am writing to formally report a long-standing and systemic case of what I suspect may be dispossession, fraudulent misrepresentation, and archaeological suppression concerning my family’s ancestral land, Great House Farm (historically Tŷ Mawr/Cedfin), Llandough.

I am the descendant of the Williams/Buckler family, who held de facto possession and indigenous tenure of this land from 1667 until our forced displacement in 1988. I am currently the only member of my family who is not too traumatized to speak of these events. My mother (Mary Williams daughter in law), remains to this day too terrified to speak up about this multi-generational "lawfare" campaign waged against us. Our family have not seen justice or received reperations, nor have we sued or reopened this case under limitations act clauses of fraud and consealment. Yet. But this may not be just a grave injustice upon our family, but our nations archeological history and indigenous people on our ancestral birthland. We are Welsh Nationals, Welsh speaking, under Welsh flags. This is some British Colonisation-grade trespass I'm seeing and it's tandamount to a declaration of civil war on me, my family, community and people.

*The core of this report involves the following suspicions I have of concealment and fraud (see attached for my timeline and notes):*

   1.

   *Archaeological Suppression:* In 1888, my family discovered a Roman soldier in full armor beneath the living room floorboards. This discovery provided "actual notice" of the site's national significance a century before its demolition. We allege this notice was systematically suppressed by corporate and state actors to allow for commercial development.
   2.

Regards,

subject: Formal Notice for Record: Church View Close, Llandough / BP vs Buckler 1987
note: Multi-authority notice addressed to The National Archives; HM Land Registry's reportafraud address was copied and blind-copied, with the other bodies shown.
body:
*FORMAL NOTICE OF RECORD CHALLENGE, ASSERTION OF RIGHT, AND DEMAND FOR ENGAGEMENT*

Dear Sir/Madam,

This Notice is issued for placement on official record and for reliance. It is not informal correspondence. I urge you not to resort to silence, deflection, or delay, as doing so following receipt of this notice constitutes knowing reliance upon, and maintenance of, records alleged to be materially defective through fraud, concealment, denial of due process, and systemic erasure. Please report any suspicious activity and discrepancies identified.

This Notice is issued in pursuit of narrative justice at this stage; formal judicial remedies are expressly reserved. It serves to document our family's side of the story before it is completely erased and history rewritten, ensuring awareness among custodians of land, heritage, heraldry, archaeology, and public records.

My elder brother, Rhys Buckler, and I are the sons of the late William Buckler (d. 1991), defendant in the landmark legal case *BP Properties Ltd v Buckler* (1987), and the grandchildren of the late Mary Williams, whose dispossession, marginalisation, and exclusion from judicial determination remain unresolved matters of record. Mary Williams was repeatedly and materially falsely addressed/mislabeled in legal and administrative records as “Mrs Buckler,” a misidentification that was never judicially tested and which directly affected the handling, scope, and outcome of proceedings. The Williams/Buckler family held claim to the land title, having acquired and occupied Great House Farm continuously since 1667, based on family records, historical evidence, and centuries of resistance to adverse claims.

I place on record that I am the first member of my family able to speak publicly and formally on these matters. Other close family members remain too traumatised and intimidated by the historical conduct of these proceedings—including violent eviction, demolition, and loss of livelihood—to engage, despite the continuing consequences of dispossession. That silence must not be misread as consent, acquiescence, or abandonment of right. There is a material distinction between free silence and silence produced by fear, trauma, and coercive experience.

The story, as we have pieced it together, reveals a multi-generational pattern of lawfare and siege: from Norman/English conquests in 1100 granting lordships over ancient Welsh Christian landscapes, through monastic (1215–1539) and Crown seizures (1539 onward), to industrial encroachments (e.g., 1876 Limeworks severance without consent) and modern corporate possession actions. This culminated in the 1988 demolition of an 800-year-old farmhouse amid police standoffs, leaving the family homeless and the site scarred, now buried under Church View Close. Archaeological vindication came too late—1994 excavations revealed over 1,000 Roman and medieval burials, confirming family warnings (e.g., the 1870 Roman soldier discovery under the living room floor, suppressed by authorities)—yet heritage records celebrate the site while omitting our dispossession.

The following assertions of right are now formally placed on record. They have never been lawfully adjudicated or extinguished:

   1. Rhys Buckler may be the rightful Manorial Lord of the Manor of Llandough, by right of primogeniture and continuous hereditary connection arising from our family’s occupation of Great House Farm from 1667 until our narrative, legal, and physical dispossession.
   2. I assert a claim to act as Squire of the Manor of Llandough, as executive representative and guardian of the Buckler–Williams estate and matriarchal lineage, with a mandate to pursue correction of record, restitution, and restorative remedies.

These are assertions of right, not settled declarations, placed on record pending proper adjudication—which has been historically obstructed through procedural narrowing, missing documents, and avoidance of full hearings.

In 1974, Mary Williams was twice prevented from presenting her case and obtaining a judicial determination of superior ownership, despite claims grounded in long occupation, intent, and possession. The court confined inquiry to *animus possidendi* (intention to possess) and excluded *animus domini* (intention to own), reclassifying her from putative owner to mere occupier and foreclosing title adjudication. BP sought possession only, not ownership rulings—a choice unexplained and significant. Proceedings were adjourned or quashed without resolution.

This occurred despite evidence of ownership intent, including:

   - Centuries-long occupation and resistance (e.g., failed 1938 auction due to local support; post-1945 rent disputes).
   - Roman-era remains and historical significance (e.g., Guglielmo Marconi's 1897 residence during radio experiments, with family aid erased from records).
   - Unformalized deals like the 1895–1905 Daniel Thomas quarrying permission for promised title, undermined by vanished deeds.

Judicial ownership examination would have engaged archaeological/heritage protections, incompatible with redevelopment—consequences avoided, raising credibility concerns.

Serious unresolved anomalies persist, indicating something is still not right with the record:

   - Licence correspondence dated 31 October 1974 surfacing only on 4 November, potentially interrupting proceedings to prevent hearings.
   - Claims of 1974 benevolent withdrawal under press scrutiny unsupported by verifiable coverage.
   - Land registration before Mary Williams’s 1983 death without title determination; disputes possibly lodged/suppressed by Land Registry.
   - Inconsistent treatment of BP entities across proceedings to family detriment.
   - Procedural barriers preventing effective defense (e.g., interrupted essential services post-licence; 1960–1987 court rulings dismissing ancestral title as "notion" without evidence).
   - Knowing bypass of archaeological constraints (e.g., 1978 trenches ignored; no contemporaneous 1970s/1990s press on discoveries amid development).
   - Missing key documents (e.g., 1667 conveyance, 1811–1835 Lambert Williams agreements proving status, 1982–84 library deeds vanishing).
   - Risks of further erasure: Heritage databases celebrate "Llandough Roman villa cemetery" while omitting our saga; modern residents unaware of the "battleground" site.

These anomalies suggest systemic theft, from colonial English subjugation (e.g., 1543–1770 orbit shifts) to corporate siege, during Wales' cultural/economic transitions. Authority derived through such means is illegitimate under natural justice, customary Welsh principles, and moral-legal frameworks. The record's distortion secures advantage, but passage of time does not validate it.

Preliminary assessment indicates cumulative benefits from redevelopment (absent title extinguishment) exceed £100 million, forming a basis for reparations—covering lost land, artifacts, livelihood, and trauma.

I require relevant public servants, custodians, and office-holders (including Land Registry, heraldry bodies, museums, archaeologists, MPs, historians, and councillors) to cease delay, engage substantively, review/correct/annotate records where defective, and prevent further rewriting of history. Justice delayed is denied, especially with verifiable evidence available.

This Notice:

   - Challenges the record's accuracy, completeness, and legitimacy.
   - Place assertions of title/standing on record pending adjudication.
   - Reserves all rights without prejudice.
   - Puts officials/beneficiaries on notice that silence/reliance may aggravate responsibility.

For the avoidance of doubt, His Majesty the King was notified yesterday.

This serves as an invitation to engage constructively before reliance becomes untenable.

Regards, Sion Buckler On behalf of the Buckler–Williams family [redacted], Wales. https://bpvsbuckler.datro.xyz

*Postscript — Disability and Succession (Material Notice):* The heir-apparent to the asserted Manorial Lordship is Rhys Buckler’s son, a young man with Down syndrome. Any obstruction, marginalisation, or differential treatment affecting his inheritance would engage the Equality Act 2010 and UK international obligations on disability rights. Disability cannot bar succession or recognition. This is recorded to prevent claims of ignorance.

Any response about my request for a public enquiry of BP Vs Buckler 1987 and possible fraud & consealment, collusion, conspiracy and deception?

Fraud unravels all. And begins when the fraud is discovered, not occured. Yes?

Furthermore,

I am writing to invite interest in review of a potential coordinated action concerning historic adverse possession cases in England and Wales. As an indigenous Welshman. From Wales. Son of the late defendant, the possibly disspossed and victim of fraud; Mr. William Buckler.

Myself and my lawyers and team are investigating circumstances in which long-term occupiers were issued licence letters (often described as “rent-free life licences” or similar instruments) during or after limitation periods, and whether in certain instances such licences may not have constituted legally effective interruption of adverse possession.

Long-term occupation had exceeded 12 years;

Possession proceedings were either adjourned or unresolved;

A licence letter was issued and relied upon to defeat a possessory claim;

Questions may arise regarding identity, acceptance, or material disclosure.

A preliminary view as to whether a coordinated group litigation strategy (GLO or similar) could be viable;

Advice on limitation, concealment, and fraud thresholds;

Guidance on structured claimant intake if sufficient common issues are identified.

This enquiry is investigative only and no public allegations are being made.

We are seeking professional assessment before any formal steps are taken.

If this is of potential interest, I would welcome a confidential discussion at your convenience.

thread_title: Cllr George Carroll (Llandough ward member) — correspondence with no reply
subject: Title Fraud and Procedural Concealment – Church View Close, Llandough (formerly Great House Farm/ "Ty Mawr")
body:
Councillor Carroll & co,

I write regarding potential gaps in the Council's planning and
record-keeping processes relating to Great House Farm, Llandough, which was
demolished in 1988 following the 1987 Court of Appeal decision in BP
Properties Ltd v Buckler.

Recent evidence suggests the Council may wish to examine its own position
on this matter, as it raises questions about procedural compliance and
record integrity that could expose the authority to wider scrutiny.

CORE ISSUES

**1. Identity and Procedural Integrity**

The 1987 judgment turned on a 1974 licence addressed to "Mrs Buckler". My
grandmother, Mary Williams, did not use or accept this designation.
Contemporaneous evidence (1978 newspaper article attached) records her
asserting ownership under her correct name.

If the 1987 court was not presented with this evidence, the judgment may
rest on an incomplete factual record. This raises procedural fairness
concerns relevant to any future review of the decision.

**2. Heritage Information and Statutory Compliance**

The site's archaeological significance was documented by 1978 (Roman
burials, monastic associations). Yet professional excavations in 1994
revealed 1,026 early medieval burials and monastic structures—findings that
should have prompted evaluation under the Ancient Monuments and
Archaeological Areas Act 1979.

Critical question: Did the Council conduct or require prior archaeological
assessment before granting permissions to demolish? If not, this represents
a potential gap in statutory process that may affect the validity of the
permissions granted.

**3. Land Registry Disclosure**

BP registered title in 1982 based on the disputed licence. The Council
should establish:
- Whether any dispute notice or heritage caution was lodged;
- Whether the Council disclosed relevant heritage information to the Land
Registry;
- What planning records exist from 1978–1988 regarding the site's known
archaeological potential.

**4. Corporate Identity Inconsistency**

During my father's appeal, the court treated BP Properties Ltd and BP
Pension Trust Ltd inconsistently—as separate entities when convenient, then
as one when dismissing his claim. This raises questions about how
thoroughly the litigation was scrutinised and whether the Council's records
reflect this uncertainty.

WHY THIS MATTERS TO THE COUNCIL

These issues go beyond a single historical dispute. They touch on:

- **Planning record integrity**: Whether heritage information was
adequately documented and acted upon;
- **Procedural compliance**: Whether statutory protections (Ancient
Monuments Act) were properly applied;
- **Institutional liability**: Whether decisions were made on incomplete or
misleading information;
- **Precedent risk**: Whether similar vulnerabilities may exist in other
historical planning decisions.

REQUESTS

I ask the Council to:

1. **Commission a review** of the planning permissions granted between
1978–1988 for Great House Farm, specifically examining what heritage and
archaeological information was available to decision-makers and how it was
handled.

2. **Refer this matter to the Monitoring Officer** for examination of
procedural compliance and record integrity.

3. **Establish** what correspondence, cautions, or dispute notices exist in
relation to this site's title or heritage status.

4. **Clarify the Council's current protocol** for handling historical title
disputes, previously unknown heritage information, or allegations of
material non-disclosure in past planning processes—to prevent recurrence.

I am not asking the Council to reverse the 1987 judgment or disturb current
residents. I am asking it to ensure its own records are accurate and its
own processes are defensible.

I attach the 1978 article and supporting documents, and am available to
meet or provide further information.

Yours faithfully,

Sion Buckler, Sgt (Ret'd)
Executor for the Manor of Llandough
[redacted]

thread_title: Cadw — Formal report of February 2026 and Cadw Planning reply
subject: RE: Formal Report of Suspected Indigenous Dispossession, Systemic Fraud, and Archaeological Suppression – Great House Farm, Llandough
body:
Dear Sion,

Thank you for your email regarding Great House Farm, Llandough. However, I must inform you that much of the content in your correspondence falls outside the scope of Cadw’s work.

In relation to the claim of 'archaeological suppression' involving the discovery of a Roman soldier in full armour in 1888, any such find would typically have been reported in the antiquarian press at either the national or local level. It is possible that records of this nature may be held by local museums. It is worth noting that the first Ancient Monuments Act was passed in 1882, focusing solely on bringing threatened ancient monuments into guardianship. The legal recognition of nationally important archaeology did not come about until the Ancient Monuments Consolidation and Amendment Act of 1913.

Upon reviewing the Cof Cymru database, I found that there are no designated historic assets relevant to this topic. However, Archwilio contains two records that document the involvement of the Glamorgan-Gwent Archaeological Trust (GGAT):

1. Great House Farm HER site entry - GGAT03586s
2. Land at Great House Farm HER event entry - GGATE003872, which includes GGAT's 1990 archaeological assessment report commissioned by BP Properties Ltd.

Any advice or correspondence that Cadw may have provided should be preserved in the Royal Commission on the Ancient and Historical Monuments of Wales (RCAHMW) National Monuments Record of Wales (NMRW). I recommend you contact the NMRW to access any relevant documents. Additionally, you may want to reach out to Heneb and the Vale of Glamorgan Local Planning Authority (LPA) to explore what records they might hold concerning this matter.

Kind regards,

Jenna Arnold

Thank you for contacting HM Land Registry. This is an automated response to confirm that we have received your correspondence. We aim to formally provide an acknowledgement within three working days. If you have any special requirements that mean you would like us to communicate with you in a specific way, please let us know and we will make adjustments if we can.

If you are contacting us in respect of any matters relating to property registration or have a general customer enquiry – Our team are unable to respond to any general registration enquiries or provide updates on any property applications. Please redirect your customer enquiry to our Customer Support colleagues, using any of the methods below:

  * Online contact form: HM Land Registry Contact Us form<https://customerhelp.landregistry.gov.uk/guide-page-external/?stepid=2b31bc48-eb96-eb11-b1ac-002248413956>
  * Website - www.gov.uk/guidance/contact-hm-land-registry<http://www.gov.uk/guidance/contact-hm-land-registry>
  * Telephone
  * English language 0300 006 0411
  * Welsh language 0300 006 0422

Telephone lines are open between 08:00 and 17:00 Monday to Thursday. This does not include Bank Holidays.

  * Post

HM Land Registry Citizen Centre
PO Box 74
Gloucester
GL14 9BB

There is no direct contact e-mail address for Customer Support. Please use the online contact form and any responses will be issued via e-mail.

If you have made a request under the Freedom of Information Act or Environmental Information Regulations – the statutory timescale for response is 20 working days following receipt of your request.

If you have made a request in relation to your data rights, for example, a subject access request for personal data – the statutory timescale for response is one calendar month following receipt of your request.

Please note that where personal data is held on our register, it is exempt from the right of subject access under UK GDPR.

Where any personal data is held on record for a registered title, the exemption provided at Schedule 2, Part 1, Paragraph 5(1) of the Data Protection Act 2018 would be engaged.

This states:

“5(1) The listed GDPR provisions do not apply to personal data consisting of information that the controller is obliged by an enactment to make available to the public, to the extent that the application of those provisions would prevent the controller from complying with that obligation.”

Please see the section below titled 'Register information and your data protection rights' for further explanation.

If you have only copied your correspondence to us - we will not respond.

Yours sincerely

Information Rights Team
HM Land Registry

Accessing information held by HMLR on our register of title

To assist you in accessing information held by HMLR, please be aware most of the information held within our registers is open to public inspection and accessible via statutory routes of access. This means that we may be unable to provide access to this information via a Freedom of Information Act 2000 (FOIA) request.

Statutory Routes of Access to information held on Public Registers

The Land Registration Act 2002 is the principal legislation governing land registration in England and Wales. It sets out provisions for keeping a register of title to land and property, and in accordance with Section 66 & 67 of the Land Registration Act, it is a requirement that the Chief Land Registrar makes this information (including any documents held on the register of title) available for public inspection.

How to access information held on our Registers

The information you have requested is available to access under our statutory protocol under section 66 & 67 of the Land Registration Act 2002.

Search for Land and Property

Please visit our website for further information about our registers:

www.gov.uk/get-information-about-property-and-land<http://www.gov.uk/get-information-about-property-and-land>

Official Copies

For information about how to apply for official copies of documents held in relation to registered titles, and information about the types of documents available, please refer to practice guide 11:

www.gov.uk/government/publications/inspection-and-application-for-official-copies/practice-guide-11-inspection-and-application-for-official-copies<http://www.gov.uk/government/publications/inspection-and-application-for-official-copies/practice-guide-11-inspection-and-application-for-official-copies>

Index of proprietors’ names

Under rule 11 of the Land Registration Rules 2003 the registrar is required to keep an index of proprietors’ names which shows for each individual register the proprietor of the registered estate and the proprietor of any registered charge together with the title number. When you search the index of proprietors’ names, you will receive a list of titles that are owned by, or mortgaged to, the name that you have searched against.

For further information about this please refer to practice guide 74:

www.gov.uk/government/publications/searches-of-the-index-of-proprietors-names/practice-guide-74-searches-of-the-index-of-proprietors-names<http://www.gov.uk/government/publications/searches-of-the-index-of-proprietors-names/practice-guide-74-searches-of-the-index-of-proprietors-names>

Section 21 FOIA exemption: Information accessible to the applicant by other means

Where information held on the register of title is available for inspection through these statutory routes of access it is exempt from disclosure under section 21(2)(b) of FOIA.

Section 21 states:

“21 Information accessible to applicant by other means.

(1) Information which is reasonably accessible to the applicant otherwise than under section 1 is exempt information.

(2) For the purposes of subsection (1)—

(a) information may be reasonably accessible to the applicant even though it is accessible only on payment, and

(b) information is to be taken to be reasonably accessible to the applicant if it is information which the public authority or any other person is obliged by or under any enactment to communicate (otherwise than by making the information available for inspection) to members of the public on request, whether free of charge or on payment.”

Therefore, we are unable to provide information held on our register through FOIA, as it covered by this exemption.

Advice and assistance

Under Section 16 of FOIA and in accordance with the Section 45 FOIA code of practice, we have a duty to provide you with reasonable advice and assistance.

Please note that the ICO has previously reviewed HM Land Registry’s use of the section 21 exemption. Relevant decision notices can be accessed here<https://icosearch.ico.org.uk/s/search.html?collection=ico-meta&profile=decisions&query&query=&f.By+authority%7CpublicAuthority=HM%20Land%20Registry&f.By+section%7CsectionOfLegislation=FOI%2021> including IC-173302-N4J1<https://ico.org.uk/media/action-weve-taken/decision-notices/2022/4022883/ic-173302-n4j1.pdf>, FS50685812<https://ico.org.uk/media/action-weve-taken/decision-notices/2017/2172810/fs50685812.pdf> and FER0454056<https://ico.org.uk/media/action-weve-taken/decision-notices/2012/780474/fer_0454056.pdf>.

The ICO has agreed that this position is long established, and the Commissioner is satisfied that section 21 would be engaged for this type of request.

For assistance on how to obtain official copies of documents you can contact our Customer Support Centre by telephone between 8am and 5pm, Monday to Thursday on 0300 006 0411 or online through our Contact Us<https://customerhelp.landregistry.gov.uk/guide-page-external/?stepid=2b31bc48-eb96-eb11-b1ac-002248413956> form.

Our Customer Support colleagues are trained to handle queries which relate to information that is held on the register of title.

Register information and your data protection rights

Data protection law permits HM Land Registry to use personal data for our official purposes.

The lawful basis for HM Land Registry processing personal data under the United Kingdom (UK) General Data Protection Regulation (UK GDPR) is that it is necessary to enable us to perform our public task of the registration of land and property (Article 6(1)(e) of UK GDPR). This is defined in the Land Registration Act 2002.

Paragraph 5 of Schedule 2 Part 1 of the Data Protection Act 2018 provides the following exemption from the specified UK GDPR provisions:

“The listed UK GDPR provisions do not apply to personal data consisting of information that the controller is obliged by an enactment to make available to the public, to the extent that the application of those provisions would prevent the controller from complying with that obligation.”

The Land Registration Act 2002 is the principal legislation governing land registration in England and Wales. It sets out provisions for the keeping of a register of title to land and requirements for its administration by HM Land Registry under a Chief Land Registrar.

The Chief Land Registrar is required by the Land Registration Act 2002 and to make register information (including any documents held on the register of title) available to the public, therefore the following data protection provisions do not apply:

  * the requirement to provide ‘privacy notices’ to individuals
  * the requirement to provide personal data in response to subject access requests
  * the requirement to rectification
  * the requirement to comply with requests to erasure (right to be ‘forgotten’)
  * most of the principles of UK GDPR

subject: Re: Your Ref: EDD Our Ref: WA231076/A/216/LG
body:
Ms Griffiths,

Thanks for your letter of 23 March 2026 regarding the historic registration of Ty Mawr Farm, title WA231076. I note your explanation of HM Land Registry’s administrative role and that you say there is no evidence of a “mistake” on the basis of the file you have reviewed.

My family’s concern, however, is that the first registration was procured by misrepresentation and identity fraud by BP, rather than by a simple clerical error. The occupier was my grandmother, Mrs Williams, from a family that had occupied the property and land since at least 1667, not the fictitious “Mrs Buckler” BP fabricated in 1974 for their unilateral licence, which was the basis of the BP Properties Ltd v Buckler (1987) case. BP also appears to have failed to disclose the long‑running ownership dispute. In a 1978 suppressed newspaper article, my grandmother publicly asserted her ownership and stated that BP could not prove ownership and had never obtained a court ruling that it was the owner, only possession orders.

How was BP able to register our land in its name? Did HM Land Registry enquire whether there was any dispute over the land, given that the dispute appears in court records from 1974? Twice that year BP obstructed my grandmother from making her case that she owned the land: first, the hearing was adjourned without a ruling; then the licence letters, using identity fraud, prevented the second hearing from taking place. These were opportunities to dispossess a widowed, disabled woman.
Had HM Land Registry recorded or investigated the existence of this dispute, BP’s inability to prove ownership, the archaeological and historic significance of the site, or sought a copy of my grandmother’s death certificate to see that the name on the licence and narrative were completely different, we believe BP would not have been able to achieve first registration on the basis presented. Instead, the use of the wrong name (“Mrs Buckler” instead of my married grandmother, Mrs Williams) and the non‑disclosure of the dispute and family claim enabled dispossession through what we say was identity fraud, which my grandmother was unable to contest as she also died in the same year as registration.

I wish to append to this land parcel our maintained position of dispute. We never surrendered. We were removed by around 30 police officers and information was suppressed. My family being paralysed by fear and silence is not the same as surrender from sound mind and agency.
Further background is set out at bpvsbuckler.datro.xyz. My family wants narrative justice as the possibly rightful, dispossessed via fraud, executors of the Manor of Llandough.

I am aware that HM Land Registry operates a statutory indemnity and redress scheme under the Land Registration Act 2002, and that substantial payments (including around £8 million in a single year) have been made where people suffer loss because of mistakes or fraud in the register. I therefore wish to explore, formally, whether our family’s loss of Ty Mawr Farm, in circumstances where BP’s misrepresentations and the suppression of an active dispute were not reflected on the register, can be considered within that indemnity/redress framework.

In light of the above, I ask HM Land Registry to state clearly whether you accept or deny that:
BP was able to obtain first registration of Ty Mawr Farm even though there was no court ruling that BP owned the land and BP had been unable to prove ownership in proceedings, which were confined to possession.

The land was registered while there was an active and public dispute over ownership (including my grandmother’s 1978 public assertion of ownership and the BP v Buckler litigation), and while the long‑term occupier, my grandmother, had died and was therefore unable to challenge the application.

My grandmother’s identity and superior family title and land claim associated with that name were mis‑described in the material on which you relied, as BP used “Mrs Buckler” instead of my married grandmother’s actual name, Mrs Williams, and that this misdescription and the concealment of the dispute were not detected or queried by HM Land Registry before completing first registration.�
If these matters are admitted, I consider they amount to negligence and maladministration by HM Land Registry in allowing BP to register our family land in its name in those circumstances. If you do not accept that, please explain precisely which of the above points you dispute and on what basis, so that I can take appropriate legal advice and pursue an indemnity/redress claim if available.
Separately from that, please also:
Provide official copies of the 23 May 1975 and 19 November 1982 conveyances, and of the first registration applications and all supporting documents for WA231076 and WA240304, so I can obtain specialist advice on the extent of any misrepresentation in what was lodged.

Confirm the correct procedure and forms to make a claim under your indemnity/redress scheme in a historic case of alleged fraud and misrepresentation in first registration, and whether you consider this matter potentially falls within that scheme, subject to evidence.

I appreciate that you cannot determine the underlying ownership dispute, but it is important that HM Land Registry notes that the Buckler/Williams family contests the integrity of the original registration of Ty Mawr Farm on the basis of identity fraud, non‑disclosure of a live dispute, and the absence of any judicial determination that BP owned the land.

Regards,

Sion Buckler
