to: Amy.Longford@gov.wales (cc cadwplanning@gov.wales, planning@valeofglamorgan.gov.uk, stephen.doughty.mp@parliament.uk) (bcc cadw@gov.wales, cadw@tfw.wales, cadwplanning@gov.wales, scheduledmonuments@gov.wales, customerhelp@gov.wales, Freedom.ofinformation@gov.wales, planning@valeofglamorgan.gov.uk, contactonevale@valeofglamorgan.gov.uk, c1v@valeofglamorgan.gov.uk, press@valeofglamorgan.gov.uk, democratic@valeofglamorgan.gov.uk, SeneddCulture@senedd.wales, nmr.wales@rcahmw.gov.uk, her@heneb.org.uk, info@heneb.co.uk)
subject: Re: CADW failures
note: A copy sent to cadw@gov.wales was rejected on delivery. The RCAHMW acknowledgement of 14 August in this thread is catalogued on the Royal Commission page.
body:
Sirs/Ma'ams,

I write on behalf of my household; the Williams / Buckler Family of what once was Great House in Llandough, Cardiff. I formally submit the attached forensic review dated 9 August 2026 concerning Cadw’s 1988 assessment of Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough, the subsequent demolition, and the near-total absence of contemporary decision records confirmed in ATISN 27021.

The report sets out the surviving documentary evidence, the compressed emergency process of December 1988, the independent professional record (including the H.J. Thomas RCAHMW survey and post-demolition notes), and twenty specific questions arising from Cadw’s own disclosures. It does not assert criminal wrongdoing; it identifies material evidential gaps and requests administrative accountability.

I respectfully request that the addressed bodies:

Provide a full account of the 1988 processes, answering the questions in Section 8 of the report so far as records and institutional knowledge permit.

Confirm whether the H.J. Thomas RCAHMW survey was held, accessed or considered.

Issue a public statement acknowledging the record-keeping gap for an irreversible heritage decision.

Consider formal administrative acknowledgement of process deficiencies and appropriate annotation of the National Heritage List / Coflein / HER entries.

Preserve and accession remaining material, including the two July 1988 photographs.

I ask Vale of Glamorgan Council to disclose any surviving records relating to Building Preservation Notice consideration in November–December 1988, and RCAHMW / HER custodians to update the relevant entries to reflect the independent professional evidence and the missing Cadw assessment record.

I look forward to your substantive response within a reasonable timeframe. Please cooperate in this matter. Our family have been heavily displaced, dispossessed and justice delayed/ denied for decades. Having already taken it to ECHR all avenues for recourse appeared to have expired. That was until I discovered, what I believe to be, fraud and consealment. Which is why I am calling for this case to be reopened, revisted and investigated by local authorities as a matter of public interest.

As it stands with this case the law has become a monument to injustice, as the practical application of property law resulted in the inhumane treatment of my family. And for authority to be authority, legitimacy is paramount. And I question a lot of the legitimacy in the decisions and actions of the authorities in this matter. I seek in good faith to remedy this entire matter so that it can be put behind us all. And so that the account of what happened at that location, is accurate and no longer remains so inaccuracte, fragmented and concealsed.

Regards,

Sion Buckler (Ret’d Sgt)
Royal Signals
Cyber and Electronic Warfare Professional and Life Member

subject: Re: CADW failures – Revised Report (10 August 2026)
note: A copy sent to cadw@gov.wales was rejected on delivery.
body:
Sirs/Ma'ams,

I write further to my email of 9 August 2026 submitting a review concerning Cadw’s 1988 assessment of Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough.

Please find attached (and linked below) a revised edition of the report, dated 10 August 2026. This version has been carefully restructured to present the same evidence in a more measured and administratively focused form. It is offered as a request for historical record correction, archival explanation, and administrative acknowledgement rather than as a forensic challenge.

The revised document:

• Clearly states what it is and is not;
• Sets out the surviving independent evidence (principally the H.J. Thomas RCAHMW survey of 1974);
• Notes the near-total absence of Cadw’s 1988 working papers confirmed in ATISN 27021;
• Asks only for realistic, achievable administrative steps: explanation of the archival position, reflection of the surviving evidence in the Historic Environment Record, acknowledgement of the records gap, and consideration of a local heritage marker.

It does not claim unlawfulness, seek compensation from Cadw, or demand a public inquiry.

I hope this revised presentation is more palatable and will assist the relevant bodies in providing a constructive response.

I look forward to your substantive response.

Regards,

subject: Clarification of surviving first-registration documents — N610CGV / WA231076 & WA240304
body:
Dear Mr Haste,

Thank you for your letter of *30 July 2026* concerning reference *N610CGV* and the surviving records relating to the first registration of titles *WA231076
and WA240304* at Great House Farm, Llandough.

I am writing to clarify the factual contents of the surviving first-registration records and to identify the appropriate documents for inspection/copying. *This is not a request to reopen my previous complaint, nor am I asking HM Land Registry to determine the historical ownership dispute.*

I would be grateful if you could clarify the following.
1. The 1971 Abstract of Title

You previously confirmed that a *1971 Abstract of Title* was seen in connection with this matter.

Please confirm:

   - whether it still survives;
   - which title/file it relates to;
   - its item or document reference within the surviving records; and
   - whether it is available for inspection or copying.

2. The “question or doubt” certificate

Please confirm where in the surviving first-registration material the certificate/declaration appears in which the applicant's solicitors stated that they were *“not aware of any question or doubt affecting the title.”*

In particular, please confirm whether this forms part of the *Form 1E dated 30 November 1982*, or is a separate surviving document.
3. What the first-registration file records about other interests

Please confirm whether any of the surviving first-registration documents contain any reference to:

   - *Mary Williams*;
   - *Fred Buckler*;
   - *William (Billy) Buckler*;
   - *Great House Farm / Ty Mawr* and its farmhouse, garden or curtilage;
   - any person other than the applicant asserting ownership or another interest in the land;
   - possession proceedings concerning the farmhouse or land; or
   - any objection, dispute, question or doubt concerning title.

I am asking this *solely as a factual question about the contents of the surviving records*.

If no such reference appears in the surviving first-registration material, confirmation of that fact would be sufficient.
4. Identification of the surviving documents

Your 30 July letter identifies, amongst other things, the *Form 1E, A13-DL list of documents lodged and correspondence from Linklaters & Paines*.

Please identify the specific item numbers I should request by *Form OC2* to obtain the fullest available surviving first-registration record, particularly:

   - the title evidence submitted by the applicant;
   - the 1971 Abstract of Title, if it survives;
   - the A13-DL list of documents lodged;
   - correspondence with Linklaters & Paines;
   - examiner's notes, requisitions, memoranda or file notes, if any survive; and
   - any document recording the basis upon which the Registrar accepted the applicant's title.

If any of these categories do not survive, please identify which ones do not.
5. Historic records relevant to identifying the land

I also wish to ensure that the correct physical parcel is being compared with the land registered in 1982–83.

During recent research at the Glamorgan Archives, I have located historic material concerning Great House Farm/Ty Mawr, including:

   - the *6 November 1877 Bute Estate counterpart lease to John Williams*;
   - the *1872 Llandough Rate Book*;
   - the *1924 and 1938 Great House Farm sale particulars and associated OS parcel references*; and
   - historic plans and notes concerning the farmhouse, gardens and associated boundaries.

These records appear potentially relevant to identifying the historic extent and boundaries of the farmhouse and curtilage.

I am *not asking HM Land Registry to determine the legal effect of those documents*. I simply wish to establish whether the documents submitted during the 1982/83 first-registration process identify the same physical parcel and, if so, what documentary evidence was relied upon to establish that identity.
6. Subsequent planning record

For completeness, the later planning record also contains a significant contemporaneous document: *BP Properties Ltd's Certificate A dated 16 October 1989 in respect of outline application 89/01396/OUT*, in which BP certified its position concerning ownership of the application land.

Again, I am not asking HM Land Registry to determine the effect of that document. I mention it only because it makes it particularly important for my research to establish precisely *what documentary evidence was actually before the Registrar in 1982–83*, several years before that planning certification.
7. Form OC2

I am particularly keen to avoid submitting an unnecessarily broad OC2 request.

If you could therefore identify the *specific item numbers* from your 30 July schedule which would provide the fullest surviving first-registration record, I can request those documents directly.

In particular, I would appreciate confirmation of the items corresponding to the *Form 1E, A13-DL list, title evidence, Linklaters & Paines correspondence, the 1971 Abstract of Title, and any examiner/requisition material that survives*.

Thank you for your assistance. I would be grateful for a substantive clarification of the above points so that I can proceed with a properly targeted inspection/copy request.

Regards,

*Sion Buckler*
*Sgt (Ret’d)*

thread_title: Complaint about Cllr George Carroll (Llandough) — Monitoring Officer determination
from: Victoria Davidson, Monitoring Officer/Head of Legal and Democratic Services (VDavidson@valeofglamorgan.gov.uk)
subject: RE: Complaint – Failure to Respond / Failure to Deal Properly with Case – Cllr George Carroll (Llandough) – Great House Farm / Church View Close
body:
Dear Mr Buckler,
Thank you for your email regarding Councillor George Carroll and for setting out the background to your concerns relating to Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough, now Church View Close.
I acknowledge receipt of your correspondence and have carefully considered the matters you have raised.
Having reviewed your complaint, I do not consider that it falls within the scope of the Vale of Glamorgan Council's Corporate Concerns and Complaints Policy. The substance of your correspondence relates to historic planning, enforcement, land ownership, heritage and record keeping matters dating back several decades, together with requests for review, explanation and further investigation of those matters.
The Corporate Concerns and Complaints Policy is not intended to provide a mechanism for challenging or revisiting decisions where there is a separate statutory process or right of appeal; seeking changes to properly made decisions, policies or legislation; pursuing matters which are not the responsibility of the Council; promoting a particular cause or campaign; or addressing matters for which alternative legal or regulatory processes exist.
You have also requested that the matter be considered by me as the Monitoring Officer as a potential breach of the Member’s Code of Conduct by Councillor Carroll.
The role of the Monitoring Officer in this context is limited to considering whether there is evidence that a member has failed to comply with the statutory Members’s Code of Conduct. Having reviewed the information you have provided, I have not identified evidence which would indicate a breach of the Members Code of Conduct.
Accordingly, the issues raised will not be progressed under the Council's Corporate Concerns and Complaints Policy as they fall outside the scope of that procedure. I do not consider there is sufficient evidence to justify referral of the matter for consideration under the Members’s Code of Conduct. No further action will therefore be taken by me in my capacity as the Council’s Monitoring Officer in relation to this complaint.
I appreciate that this response may be disappointing. However, I trust it clarifies the Council's position and the limits of the Corporate Complaints Procedure and the Monitoring Officer's role in the context of the matters you raise.
Yours sincerely,

thread_title: Complaint about Cllr George Carroll (Llandough) — Monitoring Officer determination
subject: Re: Complaint – Failure to Respond / Failure to Deal Properly with Case – Cllr George Carroll (Llandough) – Great House Farm / Church View Close
body:
Ms Davidson,

Thank you for your response.

I accept the distinction you draw between the Council's Corporate Concerns
and Complaints Policy and the separate statutory framework governing the
conduct of elected members. I am not seeking to use the corporate
complaints procedure as an appeal against historic planning, enforcement,
land or judicial decisions.

However, I do wish to clarify one important point concerning your decision
in your capacity as Monitoring Officer.

My complaint about Councillor George Carroll was not simply that the
Council should revisit historic decisions concerning Great House Farm. The
specific concern was his repeated failure to provide any substantive
response to correspondence sent to him in his capacity as the elected
councillor for Llandough, despite repeated approaches over a period of
approximately five months and despite the correspondence setting out
specific matters concerning his ward.

The chronology supplied with my complaint records correspondence on:

   - 16 February 2026;
   - 4 May 2026;
   - 7 June 2026;
   - 25 June 2026; and
   - 13 July 2026.

My complaint therefore concerned the conduct and handling of that
correspondence by an elected member, rather than asking the Monitoring
Officer to determine the underlying historical ownership or planning
dispute.

You state:

“Having reviewed the information you have provided, I have not identified
evidence which would indicate a breach of the Members Code of Conduct.”

I would therefore be grateful for clarification of the basis upon which
that conclusion was reached.

In particular, please confirm:

   1.

   *Which specific provisions of the Members' Code of Conduct were
   considered* in assessing my complaint.
   2.

   *Whether the complete correspondence chronology and the underlying
   emails and attachments were considered*, rather than merely my summary
   of them.
   3.

   *Whether Councillor Carroll was invited to provide an explanation or
   response* concerning the repeated absence of any substantive response to
   the correspondence.
   4.

   If so, whether his response was taken into account in reaching your
   conclusion.
   5.

   If not, please explain how the Monitoring Officer was able to determine
   that there was no evidence indicating a possible breach without obtaining
   the member's account of the conduct complained of.
   6.

   Please explain, in sufficient detail to enable me to understand the
   decision, *why the documented pattern of conduct was considered
   incapable of engaging any provision of the Members' Code of Conduct*.

I appreciate that failure to answer correspondence does not, by itself,
necessarily constitute a breach of the Code. I am not asserting that
proposition. My concern is that the Monitoring Officer appears to have
reached a definitive conclusion without identifying the relevant Code
provisions, the evidence considered, or the reasoning by which that
evidence was found insufficient.

I would also ask you to clarify whether you consider that the matter should
instead be referred to the *Public Services Ombudsman for Wales* for
consideration under its jurisdiction concerning complaints about the
conduct of elected members.

I note that your response states that no further action will be taken by
you as Monitoring Officer. I will therefore retain your letter, together
with my original complaint and the complete correspondence record, for
consideration of whether a complaint should be submitted to the Public
Services Ombudsman for Wales.

For the avoidance of doubt, I am not asking you to determine the historical
merits of the Great House Farm dispute through the corporate complaints
procedure. I am asking for the reasoning and evidential basis for the
separate determination you have made concerning the conduct of an elected
member.

I would be grateful if you could therefore provide the above clarification
and confirm the relevant Code provisions considered.

Regards,

Sion Hywel Buckler
(Ret’d Sergeant)
Royal Signals Cyber & Electronic Warfare Professional and Life Member

thread_title: Cardiff Castle furniture / movable property (became FOI 2026-020)
subject: RE: FOI 2026-020 - Great House Farm, Llandough | Cardiff Castle Furniture
body:
Dear Sion

Thank you for your email.

Following receipt of your query, Amgueddfa Cymru undertook further enquiries to satisfy itself that no information had been overlooked when responding to your request.

These enquiries included a review of records held across the Museum's collections and a review of archived electronic systems and records by the Museum's Information Technology team. The review considered all collections management systems used by the Museum, including those most likely to contain information falling within the scope of your request.

For the History collections, searches were undertaken of the Collections Management System (CMS), accession files, donor indexes, location indexes and associated collection documentation. Searches were carried out using terms including "Great House Farm", "Ty Mawr", "Llandough", "Buckler" and "Bute". Additional consideration was given to acquisition records, provenance information and associated administrative records.

For the Art collections, searches were undertaken within the collections management system across description, comments, acquisition notes and place fields using the terms "Ty Mawr", "Great House Farm", "Great House", "Williams", "Buckler", "Llandough" and combinations of those terms. No additional paper archives relating to Great House Farm, Ty Mawr, Great House or Buckler were identified.

The Museum's Information Technology team also reviewed archived electronic systems and records retained by the Museum.

These enquiries identified some information relating generally to Great House Farm and the surrounding area. However, no information was identified concerning furniture, furnishings, antiques, fixtures, heirlooms or other movable property originating from Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough. We did not identify any inventories, catalogues, acquisition records, disposal records, loan records, provenance files, ownership records, photographs, correspondence or other records falling within categories 1 to 9 of your request.

We are also not aware of any relevant collection records relating to such material having been transferred to another institution or destroyed.

Accordingly, having completed these additional enquiries, Amgueddfa Cymru remains satisfied that it does not hold recorded information within the scope of your request and our response under section 1(1)(a) of the Freedom of Information Act 2000 remains unchanged.
In relation to your request for advice and assistance, Cardiff Council and Cardiff Castle would appear to be the organisations most likely to hold records relating to furniture, furnishings or other movable property associated with Great House Farm.

If you remain dissatisfied with this response, you may request an internal review within 40 working days of the date of this email.

Cofion cynnes,

FOI Team
Amgueddfa Cymru

thread_title: Cardiff Castle furniture / movable property (became FOI 2026-020)
subject: Re: FOI 2026-020 - Great House Farm, Llandough | Cardiff Castle Furniture — internal review request
body:
FOI Team,

Thank you for your detailed response and for undertaking the additional enquiries.

I appreciate the further information you have provided concerning the searches undertaken. However, I would like to request an internal review under the Freedom of Information Act 2000.

My concern is not simply that no objects have been identified. It is whether the searches undertaken have fully addressed the scope of my original request, particularly the documentary evidence concerning the provenance, acquisition, transfer, ownership, identification and dispersal of material originating from Great House Farm (Ty Mawr).

I would be grateful if the internal review could consider the following points.

1. Information identified concerning Great House Farm

Your response states that the additional enquiries identified "some information relating generally to Great House Farm and the surrounding area".

Please could you identify what categories of information this refers to and, where it is not exempt, provide the relevant recorded information or explain where it can be accessed?

This appears potentially relevant to the original request even if it does not itself identify furniture or household objects.

2. Scope of the archived electronic search

You state that the Information Technology team reviewed "archived electronic systems and records retained by the Museum".

Please could the review clarify:

- which archived systems were searched;
- the approximate date ranges covered;
- whether historical email or correspondence archives were searched;
- whether legacy collections-management databases were searched;
- whether databases or systems preceding the current CMS were searched; and
- whether any archived systems were unavailable, incomplete or incapable of being searched.

3. Correspondence and administrative records

My original request expressly sought correspondence concerning the identification, recovery, ownership or location of objects, as well as correspondence with the Bute Estate, Cardiff Council, Cardiff Castle and other public authorities.

Your response refers generally to "associated collection documentation" and "administrative records", but does not make clear whether historical correspondence files were specifically searched.

Please could the internal review establish whether searches were made of:

- curator correspondence;
- departmental correspondence files;
- donor correspondence;
- acquisition correspondence;
- disposal correspondence;
- loan correspondence;
- provenance correspondence;
- correspondence with Cardiff Council;
- correspondence with Cardiff Castle;
- correspondence with the Bute Estate;
- correspondence with other museums or public authorities; and
- any relevant institutional or external correspondence indexes.

4. Search terms

Thank you for identifying many of the search terms used.

Please could the internal review confirm whether the search also included combinations and variants involving: "Bute Estate", "Bute", "Cardiff Castle", "Cardiff Council", "Great House Farm", "Ty Mawr", "Great House", "Llandough", "Buckler", "Williams", "Mary Williams", "Mary Doreen Williams", "household effects", "contents", "furniture", "furnishings", "heirlooms", "fixtures", "estate", "dispersal", "recovery", "provenance", "ownership", "transfer", "demolition".

I appreciate that historical records may not have been consistently indexed, which is why I would be grateful for confirmation of the methodology used.

5. Transfer, disposal and destruction

Your response states:

"We are also not aware of any relevant collection records relating to such material having been transferred to another institution or destroyed."

Please could the internal review clarify whether this conclusion is based upon:

a. a search of transfer/accession-out records;
b. a review of retention and disposal records;
c. enquiries with relevant collections staff;
d. review of archival transfer documentation; or
e. institutional knowledge rather than a documentary search.

I am particularly interested in distinguishing between "no record exists" and "no record was identified in the systems searched".

6. The original request concerning external institutions

The original request was deliberately framed broadly because the question concerns possible dispersal of the contents of a demolished historic property.

It expressly included records concerning Cardiff Council, Cardiff Castle, the Bute Estate, museums, Arts Council England, DCMS, RCEWA and other public authorities.

I would therefore be grateful if the review could confirm whether records of communications or transactions involving those bodies were searched within Amgueddfa Cymru's records, rather than simply searching the Museum's object catalogue for Great House Farm objects.

7. Advice and assistance

You have stated that Cardiff Council and Cardiff Castle "would appear to be the organisations most likely to hold records relating to furniture, furnishings or other movable property associated with Great House Farm".

I appreciate that you cannot transfer another authority's records to me. However, could you please provide any further information available to the Museum as to which particular department, collection, archive or record series at Cardiff Council or Cardiff Castle is most likely to contain such material?

That would materially assist me in directing subsequent FOI and archival enquiries.

I am grateful for the additional work already undertaken. I am requesting the internal review because I would like the record to be clear as to precisely what was searched, what information was identified, and what the negative result does and does not establish.

I am not asking Amgueddfa Cymru to determine any allegation concerning the historical ownership of Great House Farm. The purpose of the review is simply to ensure that the documentary search corresponds fully with the scope of the original FOI request.

Please treat this email as my formal request for an internal review of FOI 2026-020.

Regards,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)
Royal Signals Cyber and Electronic Warfare Professional and Life Member
Williams / Buckler Family Estate

subject: Re: Great House Farm, Llandough  Request 00210772
body:
Information Governance Team,

I refer to the internal review of Case Ref 00210772 (Great House Farm / Ty
Mawr, Llandough) which I requested on 7 July 2026.

On 5 August 2026 you acknowledged that the matter remained outstanding
beyond the 20-working-day statutory period and stated that further
enquiries with service areas were ongoing. You indicated a further update
or decision would be provided.

As of the close of business on Friday 14 August 2026 no substantive
response or decision has been received.

This is a formal chase. The Environmental Information Regulations 2004
require that internal reviews be completed promptly and, in any event,
within a reasonable time. The delay is now significant.

Please provide the completed internal review decision within 5 working days
of this email (i.e. by close of business on Monday 24 August 2026).

If a full response is not received by that date I may escalate the matter
to the Information Commissioner’s Office for non-compliance with the
statutory timescales under the EIR, which I do not care to do.

Please also confirm, as part of the outstanding review or by way of further
disclosure under the same reference:

1. Whether the Council (as local planning authority) considered issuing a
Building Preservation Notice under section 58 of the Town and Country
Planning Act 1971 (or any equivalent provision) in respect of Great House
Farm at any time between July and December 1988.

2. If it was considered, who decided against it and on what grounds.

3. If it was not considered, why not, given that the building was under
active bailiff enforcement, partial demolition of outbuildings had already
occurred, and Cadw had publicly stated on 3 December 1988 that listing was
under active consideration.

A Building Preservation Notice would have provided interim protection at
the critical moment. Its absence is material to the internal review of the
original response and to the wider handling of the case.

Yours faithfully,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergenant)
Royal Signals Cyber and Electronic Warfare Professional and Life Member
Williams/ Buckler Family Estate

thread_title: Formal Governance and Integrity Notification (Chief Executive / Monitoring Officer / s151)
subject: Formal Governance and Integrity Notification — Great House Farm / Ty Mawr, Llandough
note: Gmail returned delivery-failure notices the same day for finance@, monitoringofficer@ and s151@valeofglamorgan.gov.uk ("Recipient address rejected: Access denied"). No reply from the Council appears in this thread.
body:
Sir/Madam,

I write to give formal notice of documentary evidence which, if correctly
understood, raises a potentially material question concerning the
historical identity, ownership and/or title to land formerly known as *Great
House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough*, subsequently developed for residential
purposes including *Church View Close*.

This correspondence is intended as a *governance and integrity notification*.
It is not an FOI or EIR request, nor am I asking the Council at this stage
to accept my allegations or conclusions as established fact.
1. The land and subsequent development

The land concerned is the former Great House Farm / Ty Mawr site at
Llandough.

The site was subsequently developed for residential use. Planning and
associated administrative decisions were therefore made in circumstances in
which ownership of the relevant land appears to have been treated as
sufficiently established for those purposes.

I am notifying the Council because documentary evidence now assembled
appears to raise a material question as to whether the historical title
position was in fact conclusively established, and whether that question
was adequately identified, examined and recorded within the Council's
administrative and planning records.
2. Potential title-chain discrepancy

The documentary record presently available to me indicates a historical
dispute concerning the land involving my grandmother and the
Williams/Buckler family on one side and BP-related entities on the other.

My understanding of the available records is that:

- proceedings in 1974 did not result in a final judicial determination
conclusively establishing the underlying title in the manner subsequently
assumed;
- a further hearing listed for *31 October 1974* did not proceed
substantively;
- the land was subsequently registered in the name of BP-related
entities around *1982*;
- my grandmother died in *1983*, without, on the evidence presently
available to me, a final judicial determination of the underlying ownership
dispute or compensation resolving the family's claim;
- the subsequent *1987 Court of Appeal proceedings, BP Properties Ltd v
Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2*, did not, in my assessment, constitute a
comprehensive adjudication of every underlying historical title question
now arising from the documentary record.

I emphasise that I am *not asking the Council to determine the civil title
itself*. Rather, I am asking whether the Council has properly established
what was actually determined by the courts, what remained disputed, what
documentary basis was relied upon for treating title as settled, and
whether that distinction was properly reflected in its own records and
decision-making.

That distinction is important.
3. Documentary evidence

I have assembled documentary material concerning the historical title
chain, court proceedings, registration history, conveyances and associated
records, together with a chronological record of notifications and
responses.

The core documentary evidence can be supplied to the Council immediately.

Some of the underlying material and references have also been raised in
previous correspondence with the Council and other public bodies. I
therefore request that this notification be considered alongside the
relevant material already held on Council files, rather than treated as an
isolated new allegation.
4. Authorities previously notified

The matter has previously been raised with, among others:

- the Planning Department — from 31 January 2026 and subsequently;
- the Council's FOI / Information Governance function, including case
*00210772*;
- Councillor George Carroll — through multiple contacts between February
and July 2026;
- Corporate Complaints / the Monitoring Officer — including
correspondence dated 27 July 2026 and the determination dated 12 August
2026;
- Cadw and the Royal Commission on the Ancient and Historical Monuments
of Wales (RCAHMW);
- other public bodies involved in the continuing documentary and
evidential trail.

I am concerned that the substantive governance question identified above
has not yet been independently addressed.
5. Matters requiring independent examination

In particular, I request that the Council establish:

1. *Whether the historical title dispute was ever conclusively determined
by a competent court*, distinguishing between orders concerning
possession, proceedings concerning particular issues, and an actual final
determination of the underlying title.

2. *What documentary evidence the Council historically relied upon when
treating ownership of the relevant land as established* for planning,
development, conveyancing or other administrative purposes.

3. *Whether the Council's planning and administrative records contain any
recognition of the historical dispute*, including any consideration of
competing title claims or unresolved matters affecting the identity or
ownership of the land.

4. *Whether any independent review of these issues has previously been
undertaken*, and if so, by whom, on what terms, and with what
conclusions.

5. *Whether any current Council officer involved in reviewing this
notification has previously participated materially in the decisions,
complaints, correspondence or investigations now under examination*,
and, if so, what arrangements will be made to ensure genuine independence.

6. *Whether the Council considers that any governance, record-keeping,
planning or public-confidence issue remains outstanding*, irrespective
of the ultimate determination of civil title.

6. Why independent examination is warranted

The fact that the land has subsequently been developed does not, by itself,
resolve the historical documentary question.

If the evidence demonstrates that a material title issue was overlooked,
misunderstood or inadequately recorded, that may have implications
extending beyond the original ownership dispute, including the accuracy and
integrity of public records and the basis upon which subsequent
administrative decisions were made.

Conversely, if the Council considers that the historical record
conclusively resolves the matter, I ask that it identify *the specific
documentary and judicial basis for that conclusion*.

That is why I am requesting an independent examination rather than asking
individual officers who have previously dealt with the matter simply to
reaffirm earlier positions.
7. Formal request

I therefore formally request that the Council:

*a.* acknowledge this notification and identify the officer or function
responsible for independently reviewing it;

*b.* confirm how that review will be kept independent of officers who have
previously dealt substantively with the matter;

*c.* identify the principal Council records and documentary evidence that
will be considered;

*d.* determine whether the historical title issue described above has
previously been properly examined and recorded;

*e.* identify any material governance or administrative issue that remains
outstanding; and

*f.* provide a written response setting out the process to be followed and
the anticipated timescale.

For the avoidance of doubt, I am *not asking the Council to accept that
fraud, unlawful dispossession or defective title has been established*. I
am notifying the Council that documentary evidence appears to raise a
potentially material question concerning the historical identity and/or
title to land upon which subsequent development took place, and I am asking
the Council to establish whether that question has ever been properly
examined.

If the Council considers that determination of the underlying civil title
falls outside its functions, I would nevertheless ask it to address the
separate governance question: *whether its own historical records and
decision-making properly identified and dealt with the title issue on the
evidence available to it.*

This is a *formal governance and integrity notification*, not an FOI or EIR
request.

I would be grateful for written acknowledgement and confirmation of the
process and timescale for an independent determination.

Yours sincerely,

*Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)*
Royal Signals — Cyber and Electronic Warfare Professional
Life Member

thread_title: Complaint about Cllr George Carroll (Llandough) — Monitoring Officer determination
from: Victoria Davidson, Monitoring Officer/Head of Legal and Democratic Services (VDavidson@valeofglamorgan.gov.uk)
subject: RE: Complaint – Failure to Respond / Failure to Deal Properly with Case – Cllr George Carroll (Llandough) – Great House Farm / Church View Close
body:
Dear Mr Buckler,
Thank you for your email.
I note your request for further clarification regarding my decision in my capacity as Monitoring Officer.
The assessment I undertook was limited to considering whether the information provided disclosed evidence which, if established, could indicate a failure by the member to comply with the statutory Member’s Code of Conduct. As Monitoring Officer, I do not have formal investigatory powers equivalent to those of the Public Services Ombudsman for Wales and I am not required to undertake an investigation or obtain representations from a member before deciding whether there is sufficient basis for a referral to be made. My role at this stage is to consider whether the information presented discloses evidence of conduct that appears capable of amounting to a breach of the Code.
In reaching my view, I considered the information provided within your complaint, including the chronology you supplied regarding correspondence sent to Councillor Carroll between February and July 2026. The substance of the complaint was that you had not received substantive responses to a number of emails sent over that period.
For completeness, I considered whether the conduct alleged could potentially engage any of the principal obligations contained within the Member's Code of Conduct. These include requirements that members show respect and consideration for others, do not engage in bullying, harassment or discriminatory behaviour, do not bring their office or authority into disrepute, do not improperly use their position to confer an advantage or disadvantage on any person, and do not misuse Council resources or confidential information.
Whilst I appreciate that the absence of a response to correspondence may be frustrating, the information provided did not disclose evidence of disrespectful behaviour, bullying, harassment, misuse of position, misuse of Council resources, disclosure of confidential information, conduct bringing the office of member or the authority into disrepute, or any other behaviour which appeared capable of amounting to a breach of the Code. In reaching that view, I considered the nature of the conduct alleged, namely a failure to respond to correspondence, and whether that conduct engaged any provision of the Code.
It is important to note that the Member’s Code of Conduct does not impose a general obligation on elected members to respond to all correspondence received from members of the public, nor does it prescribe timescales within which responses must be provided. The Code is concerned with standards of conduct rather than the quality, adequacy or timeliness of constituency casework. Consequently, a decision not to respond, or not to respond in the manner sought by a correspondent, does not of itself constitute evidence of a breach of the Code.
Given that the information provided did not disclose evidence which appeared capable of amounting to a breach of the Code, I did not consider it necessary or proportionate to seek comments from Councillor Carroll before reaching that conclusion. My decision was therefore based upon the information contained within your complaint and whether that information, taken at its highest, indicated a potential breach of the Code warranting further action.
For completeness, any person is entitled to submit a complaint directly to the Public Services Ombudsman for Wales if they believe a member has failed to comply with the Member’s Code of Conduct. The Ombudsman is independent of the Council and is responsible for determining whether a complaint should be investigated and, if so, whether any further action is appropriate.
I trust this clarifies the basis of my decision. Having reviewed the information provided, my position remains that I have not identified evidence which would justify further action by me in my capacity as Monitoring Officer.
Yours sincerely,

Victoria Davidson

thread_title: Complaint about Cllr George Carroll (Llandough) — Monitoring Officer determination
subject: Re: Complaint – Failure to Respond / Failure to Deal Properly with Case – Cllr George Carroll (Llandough) – Great House Farm / Church View Close
body:
Ms Davidson,

Thank you for your further response. Very much appreciate your time in this
matter.

I have considered it carefully. I now need to make one fundamental point
clear. This is not any animosity or prejudice but a matter of upmost
importance to my family, many of whome are women and too frightened to
speak out. I must do my ahsolute best and part here and take the following
position on this matter.

I do not accept the characterisation of my complaint as being simply that a
councillor failed to answer a number of emails.

That formulation removes the very circumstances which made the conduct
complained of potentially relevant to the standards expected of an elected
member.

Councillor Carroll initially responded to me and asked how he could help. I
then provided the information and evidence requested. What followed was not
an isolated unanswered email, but a documented pattern of non-engagement
over approximately five months, notwithstanding repeated approaches
concerning matters affecting his own ward, including planning, development,
historical records and a serious concern that the title upon which current
development is proceeding may itself require examination.

I am not asking the Monitoring Officer to determine the ownership of Great
House Farm by correspondence. Nor am I asking the Council to accept my
allegations as established fact.

I am asking whether the conduct of an elected member, in the circumstances
actually presented, was properly assessed against the full range of
standards applicable to that member.
1. The Code cannot be reduced to an obligation to answer emails

I accept the proposition that the Members' Code does not create a general
rule requiring a councillor to answer every email received from a member of
the public within a prescribed period.

That is not the proposition I have advanced.

The question is whether a sustained course of conduct can engage provisions
of the Code concerning respect and consideration, conduct capable of
bringing the member's office or authority into disrepute, misuse of
position, and the broader principles governing the conduct of elected
representatives.

The Council's current Constitution places the Members' Code within Section
19 and separately identifies the principles governing members' conduct.

The Public Services Ombudsman for Wales itself describes the Code as
imposing enforceable minimum standards on councillors and identifies,
amongst other matters, conduct which negatively affects an authority's
reputation, unfair use of position, bullying, and failures to treat people
equally as matters which can potentially constitute breaches.

I therefore ask you to identify precisely which provisions you considered
and, more importantly, why the particular factual circumstances I supplied
were considered incapable of engaging any of them.

A conclusion that "failure to respond is not itself a breach" does not
answer that question.
2. The actual chronology matters

Please record the chronology accurately.

This was not:

five emails were sent and a councillor did not reply.

It was:

   - I approached my elected ward councillor concerning matters affecting
   his ward;
   - Councillor Carroll responded and asked how he could help;
   - I then supplied substantive information and evidence;
   - further correspondence followed on 16 February, 4 May, 7 June, 25 June
   and 13 July 2026;
   - the correspondence concerned, amongst other things, the historical
   planning and development of Great House Farm / Church View Close, access to
   relevant public records, and an apparent defect or inconsistency in the
   historical title chain;
   - despite the initial invitation to explain how he could assist, there
   was subsequently no substantive engagement with the matters raised.

That is the conduct I asked you to assess.

I therefore ask you to confirm whether you considered the actual underlying
emails and attachments, rather than merely the summary chronology.
3. Was Councillor Carroll's account obtained?

You have now confirmed that you did not consider it necessary to seek
comments from Councillor Carroll.

I appreciate that you do not have to conduct a full investigation at this
stage.

Nevertheless, that makes the precise nature of your decision particularly
important.

You have reached a conclusion that the information provided did not
disclose evidence capable of amounting to a breach, whilst apparently not
obtaining the explanation of the person whose conduct was complained of.

That does not necessarily make the decision unlawful. But it does mean that
I am entitled to understand precisely what factual inference you drew from
the material before you.

In particular, if there was a reason why Councillor Carroll did not respond
after initially offering to help, I do not know what that reason was.

If the reason was that he considered the matter outside his role, please
say so.

If the reason was that he considered the correspondence excessive,
vexatious or otherwise inappropriate, please say so.

If the reason was connected with material I had published or discussed on
social media, please say so.

If there was another reason, please identify it.

I am not alleging any particular explanation. I am asking that the factual
basis of the conduct not simply be assumed.
4. Social media and equal treatment

I also wish to place one specific issue on record.

I understand that the Code does not simply regulate everything a member or
member of the public says on social media. The Ombudsman itself has
separate guidance concerning social media and the Code.

Accordingly, if social-media material has influenced Councillor Carroll's
decision to disengage from me, I would ask that this be disclosed rather
than silently becoming the background justification for his conduct.

It would be an obvious inconsistency if material said or published by a
constituent outside the relevant Code framework were treated as a reason
for refusing to engage with that constituent, while the resulting conduct
of the elected member were then assessed in isolation as merely "a failure
to respond".

Again, I am not asserting that this occurred. I am asking that it not be
assumed away.
5. This is also a question of democratic accountability

There is a much wider issue here which I do not believe has been addressed.

I am raising a documented public-interest concern concerning land within
the Council's area, historical planning and enforcement records, the
demolition and subsequent development of Great House Farm / Church View
Close, and an apparent problem in the title history of land now associated
with substantial residential development.

I am not asking the Council to decide my private ownership claim.

I am asking that the concern be capable of being placed before the
democratic institutions of the Council and scrutinised by the appropriate
people.

The Council itself expressly operates mechanisms for public questions at
Full Council, and its published meeting material demonstrates that
questions from the public are part of its democratic process. The Council
also states that its meetings are conducted to support and promote
democratic engagement and public interest.

Your response says that no further action will be taken by you. It does
not, however, tell me what democratic route remains available for me to
place the underlying public-interest concern before elected members.

I therefore ask you to identify that route.

Specifically, please confirm how I may:

   1.

   submit a public question to Full Council concerning the Council's
   records and handling of this matter;
   2.

   submit a petition or e-petition;
   3.

   seek consideration by the appropriate Scrutiny Committee;
   4.

   raise the adequacy of the Council's handling of the matter with the
   Governance and Audit Committee or other appropriate constitutional body; and
   5.

   request inspection of relevant historical background papers associated
   with the planning and demolition history of the site.

The answer cannot simply be that the Monitoring Officer has decided not to
take further action. That determines one particular route. It does not
extinguish democratic accountability.
6. The public-record issue needs to be separated from the ownership dispute

I also want to avoid any further misunderstanding concerning the planning
records.

I have repeatedly encountered historical material which is not presently
accessible to me through the Council's online planning system.

I am not presently asserting that this proves deliberate concealment.

There may be perfectly legitimate explanations: age of the records,
digitisation, migration between systems, retention arrangements, technical
problems, or the fact that historical material was never placed online.

But the important point is that the Council's own planning-register
arrangements acknowledge that the online register is not necessarily a
complete database of everything held by the Council.

That makes the appropriate question one of transparency:

*What records does the Council hold, what records does it no longer hold,
where are the surviving records, and how can they be inspected?*

That is a straightforward public-record question.

It should not depend upon the Council first accepting my interpretation of
the title history.

I therefore intend to pursue the records question separately and formally,
including under the applicable information-access legislation where
appropriate.
7. The historical planning record is itself relevant

The historical demolition of Great House Farm is not an invented issue
arising solely from my family account.

The historic environment record identifies Great House Farm as a
historically significant site and records its sudden and complete
demolition in December 1988 amid considerable local controversy.

Whatever conclusion is ultimately reached concerning ownership, title or
the historical allegations, the existence of a significant historical
record means that it is reasonable to ask what planning, enforcement,
demolition, committee and officer records survive and what decisions were
made.

I am therefore not asking the Council to rewrite history in accordance with
my family's interpretation.

I am asking the Council to disclose its own documentary history.
8. Monitoring Officer responsibilities

I also ask you to clarify the extent to which you have considered the
Council's own potential obligations as an authority, as distinct from your
assessment of Councillor Carroll's individual conduct.

Section 5 of the Local Government and Housing Act 1989 places a statutory
reporting function upon a Monitoring Officer where it appears that a
proposal, decision or omission by the authority, its committees,
sub-committees, officers or other specified authority actors gives rise to
the statutory circumstances identified in that provision.

I am not asserting that section 5 automatically requires you to issue a
report merely because I have asked you to do so.

I am asking a narrower and more reasonable question:

*Have you considered whether any separate omission or decision by the
Council itself — particularly concerning access to public records,
democratic engagement or the handling of this matter — engages your
statutory Monitoring Officer responsibilities?*

If you have considered that question and concluded that section 5 is not
engaged, please say so and give the reason.

If you have not considered it, please confirm that.
9. The Ombudsman

Your response expressly directs me to the Public Services Ombudsman for
Wales.

I will therefore consider making a direct Code of Conduct complaint
supported by the underlying correspondence rather than relying upon the
Council's characterisation of the matter.

That is particularly appropriate because the Ombudsman states that its
initial assessment considers whether evidence suggests that a Code breach
may have occurred and, separately, whether investigation would be
sufficiently serious and in the public interest. The Ombudsman specifically
identifies maintaining public confidence in local councillors as one factor
relevant to that assessment.

I will therefore allow the Ombudsman to make its own assessment of the
evidence.

I will provide it with the actual chronology, the original correspondence,
the initial response from Councillor Carroll asking how he could assist,
the subsequent correspondence, and your decision.
10. One final point about the characterisation of my conduct

I have been persistent because I consider the underlying matter important.

Persistence should not be confused with misconduct.

The Ombudsman itself expressly states that it does not regard behaviour as
unacceptable merely because a complainant is forceful or determined, while
also making clear that correspondence should remain polite and courteous.

I accept the latter completely.

I am therefore going to continue to pursue these matters firmly, but
through the proper channels and on the evidence.

What I will not accept is the repeated administrative reframing of a
substantive public-interest concern as nothing more than an unhappy
constituent sending too many emails.
Accordingly, I ask you to confirm:

   1.

   The exact provisions of the Members' Code of Conduct which you
   considered.
   2.

   Whether you considered the five original emails and their attachments in
   full.
   3.

   Whether you considered Councillor Carroll's initial response asking how
   he could assist.
   4.

   Whether Councillor Carroll was asked for an explanation. If not, please
   confirm that.
   5.

   Whether you are aware of any reason why he subsequently ceased
   substantive engagement.
   6.

   Whether social-media activity formed any part of the reason for his
   non-engagement.
   7.

   Whether you have considered any potential omission or decision by the
   Council itself under your statutory Monitoring Officer responsibilities.
   8.

   What democratic mechanism you say is available for me to place the
   underlying public-interest concern before elected members.
   9.

   How I can obtain or inspect the surviving planning, enforcement,
   demolition, committee and officer records relating to Great House Farm /
   Church View Close which are not available through the online planning
   system.
   10.

   Whether any relevant records are known to have been destroyed, disposed
   of, transferred, archived elsewhere or otherwise become unavailable, and,
   if so, under what records-management arrangements.
   11.

   Whether the historical demolition and subsequent development were
   considered by a Council committee and, if so, where the relevant agendas,
   reports, minutes and background papers can be inspected.

I am deliberately keeping these questions precise because I want a proper
evidential record rather than another exchange in which the substance of
the issue is lost in administrative categorisation.

I am also not asking you to endorse my conclusions concerning title.

The democratic question is much simpler:

*Where a constituent places before his elected representative a documented
concern that land within the ward may be affected by a defective or
unresolved title history, and where the historical public records needed to
examine that concern are not readily accessible, what mechanism exists for
that concern to be transparently examined rather than simply closed
administratively?*

That question remains unanswered.

I would therefore be grateful for a substantive response to the points
above.

Yours sincerely,

*Sion Hywel Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)*
*Royal Signals Cyber & Electronic Warfare Professional and Life Member*

thread_title: FOI 2026-024 — visor and lance from beneath the dining-room floor
subject: FOI - 2026-024 - Great House Farm, Llandough
body:
Dear Mr Buckler,

Thank you for your request for information received on 27 July 2026 concerning records relating to a reported discovery at Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough, including a soldier, horse remains and items described as a visor and lance.

Amgueddfa Cymru has undertaken searches of its collections management systems, accession records and associated documentation.

We have not identified any records relating to the acquisition, accession, donation, transfer or deposit of a medieval visor, lance, helmet or other item of armour associated with Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough. We have also not identified records relating to the specific discovery described in your request, including records of associated human or animal remains, reburial records, excavation reports, watching briefs or discovery reports.

Accordingly, under section 1(1)(a) of the Freedom of Information Act 2000, our response is that Amgueddfa Cymru does not hold the requested information.

For completeness, our searches identified records relating to other archaeological finds from Church Farm, Llandough and to other archaeological discoveries recorded at Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough. These records do not relate to, nor are they otherwise associated with, the discovery described in your request. We have therefore not considered them to fall within the scope of this request.

If you are dissatisfied with this response, you may request an internal review by writing to the FOI Requests mailbox within 40 working days of the date of this letter.

Cofion cynnes,

FOI Team
Amgueddfa Cymru

thread_title: FOI 2026-024 — visor and lance from beneath the dining-room floor
subject: Re: FOI - 2026-024 - Great House Farm, Llandough — internal review request
body:
Dear FOI Team,

Thank you for your response.

I am requesting an internal review of the handling of my request. I do not consider the response sufficient because it appears that the searches were conducted too narrowly around the later description of a "medieval visor, lance, helmet or other item of armour", rather than around the underlying historical discovery at Great House Farm itself.

The issue I am investigating is a reported nineteenth-century discovery at Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough. My understanding from contemporary or near-contemporary newspaper and historical accounts is that the discovery was described as involving the remains of a Roman soldier, with associated remains and objects. The dating and description of the individual objects as "medieval" may therefore itself be inaccurate, or may represent a later conflation or retelling of the original discovery.

Your response is particularly significant because it states:

"Our searches identified records relating to ... other archaeological discoveries recorded at Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough. These records do not relate to, nor are they otherwise associated with, the discovery described in your request. We have therefore not considered them to fall within the scope of this request."

I respectfully challenge that approach.

The central question is precisely whether the discovery described in later historical accounts can be identified, corroborated, corrected or explained through the Museum's records concerning archaeological discoveries at Great House Farm. If the Museum has identified records relating to other discoveries at the same historically significant site, it is not sufficient simply to conclude internally that they are unrelated without disclosing what those discoveries are, when they were recorded, and the basis upon which that conclusion was reached.

I therefore request that the internal review reconsider the scope of my request and undertake searches using, at minimum, the following terms and concepts: Great House Farm; Ty Mawr; Llandough; Llandough, Cardiff; Roman soldier; Roman burial; Roman grave; Roman remains; human remains; skeleton; horse remains; equine remains; soldier and horse; cavalry burial; military burial; grave goods; Roman military equipment; visor; helmet; lance; spear; armour; archaeological discovery; nineteenth-century discovery; 1870 and adjacent years.

Please also search for relevant records under alternative historical place-name indexing, donor names, findspot descriptions, parish names and catalogue terminology where the precise modern name "Great House Farm" may not have been used.

Most importantly, I ask that you disclose sufficient information about the "other archaeological discoveries" which your searches identified at Great House Farm to enable me to understand and assess the Museum's conclusion that they are unrelated. This should include, so far as held:

1. A description or title of each relevant discovery or record.
2. The approximate date of the discovery or record.
3. The nature of the material or remains involved.
4. Any accession number, catalogue number or archival reference.
5. The recorded provenance or findspot.
6. Any dating attributed to the discovery.
7. The basis upon which Amgueddfa Cymru concluded that each record was unrelated to the nineteenth-century discovery described in my request.

I am not asking the Museum to create new archaeological opinions or undertake speculative research. I am asking for recorded information which has already been identified during the searches and which directly concerns archaeological discoveries at the specific site named in my request.

If the Museum maintains that any of those records fall outside the original scope, then please treat this email additionally as a refined request for the recorded information identified above.

I would also ask the reviewer to consider whether the original response gave insufficient weight to the possibility that the historical account may have inaccurately dated or described the find. A search which excludes Roman, nineteenth-century, burial and equine terminology risks missing the very records capable of establishing what was actually discovered beneath Great House Farm.

Given that your searches have already identified records concerning archaeological discoveries at Great House Farm itself, I would be grateful for a full reconsideration and disclosure of the recorded information requested above.

Yours faithfully,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)
Royal Signals Cyber and Electronic Warfare Professional and Life Member

thread_title: FOI 2026-024 — visor and lance from beneath the dining-room floor
subject: RE: FOI - 2026-024 - Great House Farm, Llandough — internal review accepted; new request FOI 2026-032 registered
body:
Dear Mr Buckler

Thank you for your email requesting an internal review of our response to FOI 2026-024.

Internal Review
We have accepted your request for an internal review of FOI 2026-024.

The purpose of an internal review is to consider whether Amgueddfa Cymru handled the original request appropriately, including whether:

- the request was interpreted correctly;
- reasonable and proportionate searches were undertaken;
- relevant information held by the Museum was identified and considered; and
- the response complied with the requirements of the Freedom of Information Act 2000.

The internal review process is not ordinarily intended to redefine or broaden the scope of the original request, nor to conduct new searches solely on the basis of additional search terms or lines of enquiry proposed after the original response has been issued.
Nevertheless, the reviewer will consider the points raised in your correspondence when assessing whether the original request was interpreted appropriately and whether the searches undertaken were reasonable in the circumstances.

We aim to provide the outcome of the internal review within 20 working days of receipt of your request. If, exceptionally, we are unable to conclude the review within that period, we will write to you again explaining the position.

Additional Information Request
Your email also requests information concerning other archaeological discoveries recorded at Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough, including details of those discoveries and the records identified during our searches. We consider this element of your correspondence to be a new request for recorded information, distinct from FOI 2026-024.

We have therefore registered this as a separate Freedom of Information request, ref FOI 2026-32.

Under section 10 of the Freedom of Information Act 2000, we will respond to that request within 20 working days of receipt. Based on the date your correspondence was received, we aim to respond to the new request by 23 September 2026.

The internal review and the new request will be considered separately and may result in separate responses.

Cofion cynnes,

FOI Team
Amgueddfa Cymru

thread_title: Cadw — 'CADW failures' forensic review and Chief Inspector reply (August 2026)
from: Dr Andy Wigley, Chief Inspector, Cadw
subject: RE: CADW failures – Revised Report (10 August 2026)
body:
Dear Mr Buckler

Thank you for your latest correspondence dated 10th August in relation to your initial freedom of Information request (ATISN 27021) submitted in June 2026, which has been escalated to me for response.

As stated by my colleagues, I can confirm that all records we hold have been released to you. We do not hold any further records relating to the content or disposal of the historic records you have requested.

To confirm, colleagues in the records office have clarified the historic retention position to the best of their knowledge. Given that the issue relates to an historic record retention policy, and that no records regarding this are available, it is not possible to say exactly what CADW’s retention arrangements were over 38 years ago. However, based on their knowledge of the systems in place at the time, current colleagues have advised that it is likely that records of unsuccessful listings were only retained for a short period, usually about 3 years. This has since changed and current retention policy in relation to unsuccessful listings is to retain the files indefinitely, reviewed every 5 years.

In relation to your question ‘Did Cadw’s 1988 assessment of Great House Farm fully account for the independent professional evidence then available- particularly the H.J. Thomas RCAHMW survey of 1974- and if not why not?’. As stated, all of the records we hold have been released to you under the FOI and are now a public record. As the release consists of only two photographs we are unable to determine whether or not the 1974 survey was taken into account at the time.

In relation to question A, please see our previous emails of 2nd, 3rd, 10th and 29th July, together with the above explanation of the historic and current retention policies.

In relation to question B, content of the HER is managed by Heneb. Please contact www.heneb.org.uk<http://www.heneb.org.uk/> in relation to adding information to the HER.

In relation to question C, please refer to the FOI response provided on the 11th June 2026 which is a matter of public record and confirms Cadw’s position.

In relation to question D, noted above.

In relation to question E, Cadw are unable to require or facilitate the installation of a heritage marker at the site.

Yours sincerely,

Andy Wigley
