thread_title: Cadw — 'CADW failures' forensic review and Chief Inspector reply (August 2026)
subject: Re: CADW failures – Revised Report (10 August 2026)
body:
Dear Dr Wigley,

Thank you for your response and for the further clarification concerning the surviving Cadw records and the historic retention arrangements.

Having considered your response alongside the evidence set out in my report of 10 August, I think it is important to distinguish between two quite separate propositions:

   1. *Cadw has released all records concerning the 1988 assessment which it can now locate*; and
   2. *the surviving records establish the evidential and administrative basis upon which the December 1988 decision was made.*

Your response appears to establish the first, but not the second.

That distinction is important because the surviving evidence is exceptionally limited: two photographs. The absence of the underlying assessment papers means that a number of historically significant questions cannot now be answered from Cadw's records.

I am therefore asking for clarification of the position rather than asking Cadw to recreate records which no longer exist.
1. What the surviving record establishes

Could Cadw please confirm whether the following is an accurate description of the present evidential position:

*Cadw's surviving records do not establish the evidential or administrative basis of the December 1988 decision not to list Great House Farm. In particular, the surviving records do not establish what evidence was considered by the inspector or decision-maker, whether the H.J. Thomas RCAHMW survey of 26 April 1974 was considered, whether the relevant SMR/GGAT archaeological material was considered, what inspection findings were recorded in December 1988, or whether any internal recommendation or consultation took place.*

If that is correct, I would be grateful if Cadw would confirm it expressly.

I am not suggesting that the absence of records proves that those matters did not occur. Equally, however, the absence of records means that Cadw cannot now establish that they did occur.

That is the central evidential limitation created by the loss of the 1988 working papers.
2. The 1974 H.J. Thomas RCAHMW survey

Your response says:

"we are unable to determine whether or not the 1974 survey was taken into account at the time."

That is a particularly important clarification.

The RCAHMW survey was not a document subsequently created in response to the dispute. It was a professional survey undertaken on 26 April 1974 and recorded architectural features including the late-17th-century construction, Type A sub-medieval cross-passage plan, substantial timber framing and the barrel-vaulted cellar.

I therefore ask Cadw to confirm simply:

*Cadw cannot now establish from its surviving records whether the inspector or decision-maker responsible for the December 1988 assessment had considered the H.J. Thomas survey before concluding that Great House Farm was "not of sufficient architectural merit".*

If that is Cadw's position, I will record it as such.
3. The archaeological evidence

The same issue appears to arise in relation to the archaeological assessment.

My report identifies evidence predating December 1988 concerning Roman, Iron Age and medieval activity at the site, including the recorded SMR material and the 1978–80 archaeological investigations.

I appreciate that the later 1994 excavation cannot simply be projected backwards and treated as evidence which Cadw necessarily possessed in 1988.

The relevant question is narrower:

*Can Cadw now establish, from any surviving record, what archaeological information was actually considered when the December 1988 conclusion was reached that the site was "not of sufficient archaeological interest"?*

If it cannot, please confirm that this cannot now be established.

This would avoid conflating the later archaeological discoveries with the separate question of what information was available to Cadw in 1988.
4. The July "YYY" coding

There remains an important unresolved point concerning the July 1988 photographs.

Cadw has previously explained that the "YYY" coding indicated that the building did not meet the listing criteria. The photographs were taken on 29 July 1988.

The contemporary press report of 3 December 1988, however, records Cadw as saying that it was then "considering" asking the Secretary of State to protect Great House Farm as a listed building and that an inspector would visit that weekend.

I appreciate that the records necessary to resolve this may no longer exist.

Nevertheless, could Cadw confirm whether it can establish:

   - what "YYY" specifically represented within the July 1988 process;
   - whether it was a final assessment or provisional coding;
   - whether it was applied by the July inspector;
   - whether the July assessment was subsequently reviewed in December; and
   - whether the December inspector had access to the July photographs or any associated assessment.

If none of these matters can now be established, I would be grateful for that to be confirmed rather than inferred.
5. Identity of the December decision-maker

One further factual gap remains.

Can Cadw establish the identity of:

   - the inspector who undertook the December 1988 inspection; and
   - the person who made or authorised the decision communicated on 5 December 1988 that Great House Farm was not of sufficient architectural merit and archaeological interest?

If the relevant individual(s) cannot now be identified from surviving records, please confirm that.

This is not a request for personal information beyond what would ordinarily form part of the historical administrative record. It is simply an attempt to establish whether the decision itself can still be attributed to an identifiable office-holder.
6. The retention explanation

I also wish to clarify an important qualification in your latest response.

You state that current colleagues have advised that, based on their knowledge of the systems then in place, unsuccessful listing files were *"likely"* to have been retained for approximately three years.

I understand that this is necessarily a reconstruction of historic practice because the relevant records no longer exist.

Could you therefore confirm whether Cadw has located:

   - a 1980s retention schedule;
   - a disposal or destruction policy applicable to the relevant records;
   - a disposal schedule;
   - a destruction certificate or log;
   - a transfer/accession record to RCAHMW or another repository; or
   - any other contemporaneous record showing what happened to the Great House Farm material.

If none has been located, I would be grateful if Cadw could state expressly that *the approximately three-year retention period is an account of the general historic practice as presently understood by current staff, and not documentary evidence establishing that the Great House Farm records were actually destroyed after three years.*

That is an important distinction for the historical record.
7. What I am seeking from Cadw

I am not asking Cadw to speculate about matters for which the documentary evidence has disappeared.

Indeed, the purpose of my report was deliberately to separate:

*what is established; what is a reasonable inference; and what can no longer be verified because the records do not survive.*

Your latest response is helpful in establishing the third category.

I would therefore be grateful if Cadw could confirm, insofar as its records permit, the following concise position:

*The surviving Cadw records relating to the December 1988 Great House Farm assessment consist of two photographs. Cadw cannot now establish from surviving records the detailed evidential or administrative basis of the decision, including whether the 1974 H.J. Thomas RCAHMW survey or relevant archaeological records were considered. Cadw has not located records establishing the disposal or transfer of the missing assessment material, and the approximately three-year retention period represents the best present understanding of historic practice rather than documentary evidence concerning the disposal of this particular file.*

If that accurately reflects Cadw's position, I would regard that clarification as extremely useful.
8. Historical record and next steps

I will separately approach Heneb concerning the Historic Environment Record, as you have advised, and will pursue the question of any appropriate heritage interpretation or marker with the relevant local authority.

I also appreciate your clarification that Cadw cannot require or facilitate installation of a marker.

My purpose in continuing this correspondence is therefore narrower than seeking to reopen the FOI request. I am seeking to ensure that the historical record does not inadvertently suggest that the absence of surviving records means that the basis of the 1988 decision has been established.

On the evidence presently available, the more accurate position appears to be that *the decision is documented, but its underlying evidential and administrative reasoning is no longer recoverable from Cadw's surviving records.*

That is a significant historical finding in its own right.

Thank you again for your assistance. I would be grateful for confirmation of the above points, particularly the status of the 1974 survey, the July "YYY" coding, the identity of the December decision-maker, and the evidential basis (if any) for the disposal of the missing records.

Yours sincerely,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)

thread_title: Cadw — 'CADW failures' forensic review and Chief Inspector reply (August 2026)
subject: Re: CADW failures – Revised Report (10 August 2026)
body:
Dr Wigley,

One further point has arisen from my continuing examination of the archival material which I would like to place on the record before you respond to my previous correspondence.

I was recently directed to material held at Glamorgan Archives to *Glamorgan-Gwent Archaeological Trust (GGAT) planning papers concerning Great House Farm*. If I recall by the longstanding Llandough Council Clerk, who retired the day he finally replied to my FOI's. The references state that the property had previously been described as a *“county treasure”* and that this was recorded in GGAT documentation in connection with the development process.

I am presently tracing the underlying GGAT document so that I can establish its precise file reference, author and date before relying upon the wording as a primary citation. I therefore do *not* ask Cadw to accept the “county treasure” description as an established fact at this stage.

The significance of the material is instead that it identifies another potentially important body of *professional archaeological documentation concerning Great House Farm which appears to pre-date, or be contemporaneous with, the demolition and development process*.

This is relevant to the question I raised in my previous email:

*Can Cadw establish from its surviving records what pre-existing archaeological information concerning Great House Farm was actually considered in reaching the December 1988 conclusion that the site was “not of sufficient archaeological interest”?*

I appreciate that Cadw may now be unable to answer that question. If so, that inability should be distinguished from evidence that the information was not available or was not considered.

I also wish to make one clarification concerning the additional Llandough material I mentioned previously.

I am *not* seeking to bring the architectural or listing status of St Dochdwy’s Church within the scope of my Great House Farm enquiry. The church is relevant only insofar as the archaeological evidence concerning the wider Llandough site may assist in understanding the archaeological context in which Great House Farm was assessed.

The focus remains exclusively on *Great House Farm and the December 1988 spot-listing decision concerning that building*.

The evidential position I am attempting to establish is therefore increasingly precise:

   1. What professional architectural and archaeological evidence concerning Great House Farm existed before December 1988?
   2. What of that evidence can Cadw establish was considered by the 1988 inspector or decision-maker?
   3. Where Cadw cannot establish this because the assessment records no longer survive, can that evidential limitation be expressly acknowledged?

I will continue separately with Glamorgan Archives/Heneb to identify the underlying GGAT “county treasure” reference and will provide the precise citation once established.

Please treat this email as a further supplementary note to my existing submission rather than as a new FOI request.

Yours sincerely,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)

thread_title: Joint letter to Stephen Doughty MP and Cllr George Carroll
subject: Great House Farm, Llandough
note: No reply from Cllr Carroll appears in the mailbox.
body:
Good Sirs,

I'm writing to you both as elected representatives because, frankly, the
institutional dysfunction I am uncovering is becoming quite extraordinary.

My family — including the last remaining members of my dispossessed Welsh
family in South Wales — have spent 38 years living with the consequences of
what happened to our home and land. They have been frightened into silence,
while the institutions responsible for safeguarding justice, heritage and
public accountability appear, time and again, to have preferred discretion,
obfuscation and exquisitely worded emails to the rather unfashionable
concept of actually answering the questions.

I have now spent considerable time reconstructing what happened. The deeper
I dig, the more the story appears to unravel.

We were not merely separated from a house. We were separated from ancestral
land, family history and heritage. And now the woodland on that land is
being cleared for a development of 133 homes.

One might reasonably ask: *whose history is being developed over, and whose
history is being erased?*

Whatever one's political position, the fact remains that possession being
awarded through historical court proceedings does not magically make every
underlying question of title, evidence, procedure or institutional conduct
disappear. A court order is not an archaeological dig, a title
investigation, or a certificate of immaculate institutional behaviour.

I attach a summary of my grievances concerning CADW, particularly its
historic involvement in this matter. I also attach a mock court application
which I have been developing alongside AI-assisted legal research, not as a
substitute for legal advice, but as a means of stress-testing the evidence
and identifying the questions that require proper legal determination.

I hope you will read them carefully.
This is considerably larger than one parcel of land

The parcel my family occupied — Church View Close — may ultimately prove to
be only one piece of a much larger story.

The same apparent pattern of irregularity that I am investigating in
relation to our parcel appears potentially relevant to:

- the parcel we leased immediately to the east, now proposed for the
133-home development;
- the playing fields subsequently acquired by the council;
- the 33 acres associated with the limeworks; and
- potentially the underlying question of whether the Marquess of Bute
possessed the freehold interest that has subsequently been assumed.

That last question is obviously not something I intend to settle by
rhetorical flourish. It is precisely the sort of question that should be
settled by *documents, title records and evidence*.

One relevant public-record reference is here:

https://www.whatdotheyknow.com/request/2020_01590_hyb

That is the point of my investigation.

I am not asking anybody to accept my conclusions simply because I have
reached them.

*I am asking institutions to produce the evidence.*
What happened to my family cannot simply be filed away

What happened to my family and our home in the 1980s was, in its human
consequences, devastating. From my perspective, it amounted to an assault
on our family itself. And decades of it. At least mid 40's by Western
Ground Rents and onwards.

For decades there has been no meaningful after-support, no meaningful
attempt at reconciliation, no reparative process and, above all, no
satisfactory account of what actually happened.

Instead, the historical record appears fragmented, inaccessible and in
places remarkably difficult to obtain.

CADW is only one of numerous agencies about which my representatives are
now compiling material.

The emerging picture includes questions concerning procedural fairness,
court proceedings, evidential failures, institutional decision-making,
heritage protection and the apparent absence of effective oversight.

The more documents I obtain, the more questions arise.

And I am increasingly uncomfortable with the proposition that *the
descendants of the people affected should have to conduct the investigation
themselves simply to discover what the institutions already ought to know.*

It is particularly distressing that I am having to investigate matters
surrounding my own father's and grandmother's lives and deaths in this way.
I am asking for accountability, not theatre

I appreciate that public bodies have procedures.

I appreciate that officials have workloads.

I appreciate that nobody likes receiving an inconvenient historical file
with several decades' worth of questions attached to it.

But carefully crafted sentences, selective disclosure, unexplained
omissions and silence are not substitutes for accountability.

I have repeatedly encountered what appears to be a culture of concealment,
stealth and institutional defensiveness. Sometimes I receive an answer.
Sometimes I receive an answer to a question I did not ask. Sometimes I
receive an exquisitely polished paragraph which manages, with almost
breathtaking elegance, to avoid answering the actual question.

It is rather like asking for the keys to the filing cabinet and being
handed a brochure about the importance of filing cabinets.

That may be administratively impressive.

It is not an answer.
I am asking you to intervene

I do not expect either of you to determine the merits of my family's
historical or legal claims yourselves.

I am asking you to ensure that the matter receives *proper independent
scrutiny*.

Specifically, I am asking you to assist in ensuring that:

1. relevant surviving records are identified and preserved;
2. agencies holding potentially material records provide substantive
answers rather than procedural evasions;
3. the historical involvement of CADW and other public bodies is
properly examined;
4. the underlying title, conveyancing and land-history evidence is
obtained wherever it survives;
5. any allegations of procedural unfairness or institutional failure are
referred to the appropriate independent bodies where necessary; and
6. my family is finally given a meaningful opportunity to establish,
through evidence, what actually happened.

I have no interest in mythology.

I want the documents.

I want the chronology.

I want the title deeds.

I want the correspondence.

I want the decisions.

I want to know who knew what, when they knew it, what they did with that
information, and why.

If the evidence ultimately disproves some of my suspicions, so be it.

*But the evidence must first be allowed to speak.*
And yes, I am angry

I make no apology for that.

I served this country. I spent years working in public service. I have
worked for the Vale Council. I have served in the military and operated in
circumstances considerably more dangerous than sending an email to a public
authority.

I am therefore perfectly capable of distinguishing between legitimate
administration and institutional stonewalling.

I am no longer asking to be placated.

I am asking for cooperation in recovering whatever evidence remains and
allowing it to be examined properly.

The local community members who have contacted me have long memories. Many
remain convinced that something about this episode was profoundly wrong. I
intend to establish exactly what happened — not through rumour, grievance
or inherited mythology, but through the surviving documentary record.

And if the record contradicts me, I will accept that.

But if the record supports my family, then somebody is eventually going to
have to explain why it took a descendant *38 years, hundreds of enquiries
and an obscene amount of archival digging* to uncover it.

That is not an acceptable model of public accountability.
So, gentlemen — enough of the situationship.

Whatever happened to:

*“We don't negotiate with terrorists”?*

Is there peace?

*No.*

Is there peace?

*No.*

Is there peace?

*No.*

There is, however, apparently an absolutely fabulous quantity of
bureaucracy.

What there has not yet been is accountability.

I therefore ask you, gentlemen, to address this matter with the seriousness
it deserves and to assist my family in obtaining the answers that have been
denied to us for far too long.

I am not asking for special treatment.

I am asking for the truth.

And if the institutions involved have nothing to hide, then surely they
should have nothing to fear from producing the documents.

Regards,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)

thread_title: Cadw — Forensic Critique v5 and Chief Inspector's closing reply (29 August – 4 September 2026)
to: Andy.Wigley@gov.wales (cc cadwplanning@gov.wales, Amy.Longford@gov.wales, Michael.Weatherhead@gov.wales) (bcc cadw@gov.wales, cadw@tfw.wales, cadw@wales.gsi.gov.uk)
subject: Great House Farm, Llandough
note: Blind copies sent to cadw@gov.wales and cadw@wales.gsi.gov.uk were rejected on delivery. The copy to cadw@tfw.wales was delivered.
body:
Sirs/Ma'am,

Further to my last two emails this week, and in response to yours, which is appreciated, please see the attached documents.

My latest version file on yourselves; CADW. And a mock application to a mock AI chancery court; a simulation I'm running in a karpathy autoresearch loop as a long horizon agent to refine the arguments my family made for the last century before being silenced. And spending the last 4 decades like hostage prisoners of war.

While CADW may ultimately have played what could appear to be a relatively small part in the wider circumstances surrounding my family's dispossession of our home and land, I want that part to be fully understood, accurately recorded and, where necessary, properly scrutinised. Any possible institutional failure you might have identified isn't the ice berge here, I assure you. Not even the tip of it.

I am not approaching this simply to apportion blame, although I am both horrified and furious reading into all this. I am trying to establish, as honestly and completely as I can, what happened, what was known at the time, what was recorded, what decisions were made, and whether proper care was exercised when it mattered.

Thank you in advance for your cooperation. This may ultimately develop into a formal complaint, and if it does, CADW will of course be given a fair opportunity to respond to the concerns we identify. At this stage, however, I am trying to understand the full scope of what happened before reaching those conclusions.

As my research continues, I may also be in a position to provide CADW with records concerning your own involvement which may not presently be readily apparent from your current records or understanding of the matter. I hope that, if that happens, they will be received in the same spirit in which I am providing them: to establish the historical truth.

In the much wider context of my family's grievances concerning BP and the local authorities, and the eventual destruction of what had been described as a "county treasure", CADW may prove to be only a small part of the overall story. Nevertheless, I have also attached a draft Chancery Court application so that you can see the wider context of our grievance and understand where CADW's involvement sits within it.

I believe that context is important.

For 38 years, my family has lived with the consequences of what happened in
1988. We were portrayed publicly as little more than "squatters being evicted", and that description has stayed with us and shamed us ever since. The reality was considerably more complicated and, for my family, profoundly distressing. It was, in fact, the first time we had been off our land — land which we may even still own — since the 16th century, having acquired the estate in 1667.

It remains a theory, but it is possible that an alternate, untold story is yet to be told, including that Llandough was once called Cedwyn Estate, and that the 1,000-year freehold for it, with 640 years left on that agreement, passed from Sir Herbert of Swansea to the Vaughan family and onto us, not Bute.

Given that we occupied the manorial house for so many centuries, it is entirely plausible that we are the rightful holders of the freehold — and that the heirlooms Bute purchased from the last heirs of the Vaughan family did not actually include Cedwyn Estate. He nevertheless acted as though he did, dividing the land parcels. Developing his houses and the town etc. And I note things like the 1824 David Stewart survey in which our estate, being reduced to a home on the parcel it occupied, was recorded as Great House alias "Cedfin". Elsewhere Ked fin. And other variations.

The same method used in 1974 with BP's licence letters was also used in 1955 (rendering our owner/occupier status merely permissive), and this may have occurred on multiple other land parcels prior to this — potentially in clandestine collaborations with the British State, given that 33 acres were carved out for the limeworks in the WWI effort, and War Ag occupied the land adjacent to ours in WWII. The council also absorbed our "playing fields" and so forth: a sort of eminent domain without our family receiving proper reparations (except once, in 1878). Llandough may have been the last of Wales to be colonised.

I can tell you as a soldier. In Nicosia the indigenous Greeks and many Turks too, would approach the green line with old records of their land holding the UN occupied, even 4 decades later, and the UN would have to surrender those lands back to the indigenous. I draw a lot of parallels between this, our case and Wales' dream of devolution/ decolonisation. This case also might show we've been in a land market bubble and so a land market crash is coming. Our case isn't isolated or unique.

I was a child in that house. My mother was pregnant, and the three of us were still young children. The people who removed us by force — following BP and the UK Government (synonymous at the time) after awarding themselves victory in their courts, (Magistrates as oppose to Chancery or before the Bench as a matter of equity, as should have happened on the merits of this case) — caused my mother's shoulder to become dislocated when she attempted to serve them with a High Court injunction ordering the occupiers not to destroy our home or remove our belongings. Despite that injunction, the house was ultimately destroyed and our possessions removed, including all our furniture, which came from Cardiff Castle, £30,000 of goods, a stone Roman-villa-type pillar, and so forth.

The ITV coverage at the time showed some of what happened, including the injury to my mother, but not that she was pregnant and that three young children were inside. ITV, it seems, never aired that footage, and instead of responding to my FOI request, they quietly published it to a YouTube archive last year — apparently hoping that I, or my AI agents, or anyone else, would not notice this suppression. I also hold other ITV footage which they have not admitted to or disclosed, showing my younger baby sister held to watch the looting of our home.

The MP is hesitant to respond, the Llandough councillor will not respond, and the longstanding Llandough clerk retired after initially trying, and failing, to dismiss me. I am ashamed of my nation. I served in war too, and left my military career with honours; I am bona fide, having also completed 22 years in Oath in 2024, the last 2 under the employ of the Vale of Glamorgan Council in adult care. The Land Registry also tried everything to steer me away from identifying their mistake in allowing BP to register our land in their name, without our ownership claim being lodged, in 1983. The fact that my nan — who had already spent 40 years challenging her ownership claim by 1983 — died within the two weeks she would have had to challenge BP's registration of our land in their name, is another matter requiring investigation.

Much like my late father's sudden death at age 41, between BP's application and approval of housing development, his ECHR claim was rejected, and his appeal of the 1987 ruling was dismissed — on the grounds that BP's companies were treated as one and the same. Yet in the ruling itself, BP's companies were considered separately, meaning our challenge to one would not have affected the other. Outrageous. The same judge also went out of his way to say my nan "conceived the notion she owned" and said the unajudicated ownership dispute, set aside to award BP possession of our land, was final. Very suspect and nobody raised questions or challenged except our family i.e. 'Buckler vs United Kingdom' at the ECHR in 1988/89. Who also ruled in lieu of BP rights over ours as the owners. In 1974 the ownership hearing was ajourned. Ownership to this day has never been properly adjudicated.

For us, this was not simply a "squatters being evicted" case, as was falsely reported in the news. It was the loss of our family home since 1667, and the forceful and prolonged seperation and severing of our connection to that land, which our family had maintained for generations and owned, and still appear to own in spite of who awarded themselves possession of it or occupy it — and perhaps not just the parcel we were on, but half the town of Llandough, by birthright. With 6 centuries left on that freehold from the Knight in 1500, to a military commander and leader like myself. The true title chain. All the while the occupiers operate from defective title. It's possible getting to me may prove more difficult than how my dad before me or nan before him were gotten to, as I am a military warfare professional of almost 3 decades now.

It is otherwise difficult to explain what all we went through does to a family, particularly when the public account of what happened does not reflect the reality experienced by those of us who were inside the house at the time. My younger sister had nightmares when I brought this up with her. It's subsequently cruel to see her having to visit archieves for a 4th time, to try to see again what we are there to see.

I therefore hope that CADW will understand why I am asking you to approach this matter with some care and humanity, as well as with the proper historical and professional scrutiny that it deserves. The non response from the Llandough councillor, classification of the 133 house plans on the council planning portal, delay from MP responding, is also an outrage. And clear bias towards the houses being developed on our stolen occupied land, by the holders of the defective title. No wonder my surviving family, of mainly women, aren't speaking up or out. It just horrifies me how they have had to live like such hostages under such terrorists. After a literal act of terrorism against us.

I was involved in the effort in Iraq to break two SAS soldiers out of an Iraq prison under police guard, days before their execution. Me and a lot of the squadrons of soldiers I have around me to this day. I see my family in a similar light there, under the tyranny of this. And I am not standing for it. I'm only 41, I'm in full mental and physical health. I may have a lot of years left in my life which I'm able to dedicate to this.

I have also passed this matter to my Cardiff based BBC producer friend, who also confirmed they'll be looking into this too. And Gareth Wyn Jones and others will a platform. This is a matter of public and national interest. It should not be drawn into clandestine warfare, with silence and violence, albeit that is my domain. Because there's already been plenty of it by the looks of it. I want this to remain in the open. Emails, open letters, courts and Senedd public enquiry etc.

Application of Property Law, did in this case, result in an inhumane outcome in my estimation. It may need to be petitioned to be rectified.

I am not asking CADW to accept my conclusions simply because I have reached them. I am asking you to look at the evidence, to consider what your own records show, and to be willing to acknowledge anything that may have been overlooked, misunderstood, or inadequately dealt with at the time.

If mistakes were made, I would much rather see them acknowledged and properly understood than defended simply because they are now part of an institutional record.

I trust you will now appreciate the importance, significance and magnitude of this matter for my family. I will continue to provide the material I uncover, and I sincerely hope that CADW will continue to give it the proper care and attention it deserves.

Regards,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)

Royal Signals Cyber/Electronic Warfare Professional and Life Member

subject: Great House Farm, Llandough
body:
Information Governance Team,

I refer again to the internal review of Case Ref 00210772 (Great House Farm
/ Ty Mawr, Llandough), requested on 7 July 2026.

On 5 August 2026 you stated that further enquiries were ongoing and that
you would write further by 14 August 2026.

On 14 August 2026 I chased and required the completed internal review
decision by close of business on 24 August 2026.
No substantive response or decision has been received.

This is a further formal chase. The delay is now substantial and continues
to breach the requirement under the Environmental Information Regulations
2004 that internal reviews be completed promptly.

Please provide the completed internal review decision within 5 working days
of this email (i.e. by close of business on Friday 4 September 2026).

If a full response is not received by that date I will need to escalate the
matter to the Information Commissioner’s Office for non-compliance with the
statutory timescales under the EIR.

In addition to the outstanding review, and under the same reference, please
confirm the following:

Whether the Council (as local planning authority) considered issuing a
Building Preservation Notice under section 58 of the Town and Country
Planning Act 1971 (or any equivalent provision), or a demolition stop order
/ equivalent interim protection, in respect of Great House Farm at any time
between July and December 1988.

If considered, who decided against it and on what grounds.

If not considered, why not, given that the building was under active
bailiff enforcement, partial demolition of outbuildings had already
occurred, and Cadw had publicly stated on 3 December 1988 that listing was
under active consideration.

Whether the 1984 Council meetings that raised the “county treasure”
significance of the house were considered in any relevant planning process,
including any BP application and any consideration of a demolition stop
order or Building Preservation Notice.

Whether the 1974 inspection by historians that noted the architectural
significance of the house was considered in any relevant planning process,
including any BP application and any consideration of a demolition stop
order or Building Preservation Notice.

Whether the 1974 planning application by BP for 13 houses is held and
available for disclosure.

Why the current planning permission for the 133 houses is not downloadable
on the planning portal, and whether the full documentation can be provided.

Whether any report or allegation of fraud / concerns raised by my late
father (William “Billy” Buckler) was received and documented by the
Council. If so, please provide the relevant records or confirm their
destruction / non-retention and the date of any such action.

Please also supply a copy of the Council’s current complaints procedure (or
a direct link to it).

Regards,

Sion Buckler (Ret’d Sergeant)
Royal Signals Cyber/ Electronic Warfare Professional and Life Member

thread_title: Cllr Christopher Franks — “Good God” (August–September 2026)
subject: Re: Good God
body:
Chris,

Thank you for your prompt response and for making your position clear. It
is appreciated.

It's not a Netflix documentry yet, but here's my scrapbook prelude:
https://youtube.com/shorts/SNUY-XFAjyE?is=__JoJpbo3m6yVXVp

I also attach what my AI agents have drafted, including a draft court
application that has been stress-tested in a Chancery Court simulation.
These documents set out our family’s position and arguments in detail.

I will not treat any further non-response as an offence. Your reply alone
means a great deal after the past year of trying to raise these concerns
with local authorities. Simply having my concerns acknowledged is
significant, given the difficulty I have encountered obtaining even basic
FOI answers. My aim remains straightforward: to understand what happened to
our family in the 1980s, and why.

I'm working on plans to rebuild a replica of our 800-year-old former
"county treasure" (former court house) home in Patagonia, which our county
allowed to be stolen and demolished in lieu of the 20 characterless houses.
Our ownership claim to it has still never been legally extinguished. BP and
the UK Government, synonymous at the time, merely awarded themselves
possession in their own courts (magistrate, not Equity, Bench/Chancery, so
not judged on the merits of the case). This was done in a slew of highly
questionable and suspicious circumstances: procedural unfairness, an
evident land registry mistake based on perjury and concealment, theft, etc.

Great House Farm II, here at the Welsh Settlement in Argentina, is where
Welsh history and herritage and people are celebrated, not erazed, replaced
and ethnically cleansed like in Wales, under Brit'ish occupancy and rule.
Here in Puerto Madryn, the full story of the erazure and ongoing supression
of our Christian stronghold and sacred/ holy Cedwyn Estate in Llandough,
can be told in this open house/ museum here:
https://youtube.com/shorts/-c0UvjM-lwA?is=wvITZl9F2YT8QbuF

With the 133 houses next to the 20 on our stolen occupied land, you will
have successfully created, the Brit'ish pinnacle of invention of a
concentration work camp. But I'm telling you, from when I was guard
commander of Akrotiri (with powers of arrest), when I'd take my soldiers on
tour to Nikosia, the UN occupying had to return parcels of land back to
indigenous Greeks or Turks who demanded and got, their ancestral lands
back.

My security group's research so far (50+ soldiers I served with, including
in war) tells me that the definition of "whole farm" in the 1955 court
order did not include our land parcel. The definition had changed from the
1916 agricultural tenancy (two plots) to one plot, i.e., excluding ours,
following a 1928 enactment of an 1877 agreement. The 1955 court’s comment
excluding our parcel by reference to my grandmother Mary Williams’s
"condition and resistance," while omitting any mention of her ownership
claim, looks like an earlier attempt (pre-dating BP’s 1974 reattempt) to
disingenuously and dishonourably convert our occupancy to a merely
permissive one and to create what is, in substance, a defective title. BP
did not have clean hands when entering court with this, which would have
mattered if it were tried in the court it should have been. Having paid
nothing since 1928, even without our paper title, we would have qualified
for adverse possession of the parcel by around 1940. The subsequent
multi-generational lawfare appears fundamentally flawed.

The fraud, concealment and suspected government involvement I believe
engage exceptions to the limitation period and justify the case being
reopened. Given the public-interest elements—our home’s associations with
Marconi, Peerless Jim’s first fight there, the large medieval burial site,
the monastery and Roman villa, and the fact that furniture looted during
the eviction originated from Cardiff Castle—I consider a Senedd public
inquiry warranted.

My family remain too fearful to speak openly. The conveniently timed deaths
of our father and grandmother, and the public reporting of us as
"squatters" being evicted (the first time we had been off our land or out
of our home since the 16th century), form part of that context.

Last week South Wales Police already started accepting reports of
casualties like Mamgu, who in fact died of what was a biological weapon.
How much more burying your heads in the sand do you want to get back there?
I'm a military warfare professional, so I pride myself on being difficult
to catch and kill, and on getting to my enemies before they get to me. War
veteran commanders and leaders with full mental and physical health, like
myself, remain on the outskirts of society and upwind for a reason. What
happened to my family is ongoing; be vigilant of it. Learn from it. It was
a manufactured Problem > Reaction > Solution. It was and remains a racket.
Our case is the case to shine light on it because it's so well documented
in the courts and press.

The effort already to drag all this back into the shadows, into more
clandestine/silent and violent warfare, defeats the object here. South
Wales Police want to discuss by phone, not email, after already lying by
saying they hold no records on this. CADW initially lied, albeit they're
cooperating a bit more now. The long-standing council clerk for Llandough
initially declined to engage, before directing me to records on the day his
retirement was announced.

I appreciate you may not have intended “injustice” as a finding of legal
liability, and I do not treat it as such. Having considered what I put
before you, however, you have expressed that you are sure an injustice
occurred. This is the first response I have received from an elected
representative that expressly acknowledges, after consideration of the
material, that an injustice appears to have taken place.

Could you clarify which aspects of the circumstances you were referring to?

I am not asking you to determine legal title. I am asking you to
distinguish between the underlying injustice you recognise and those
particular aspects you consider to lie outside the Council’s remit.

If, for example, you regard the core property dispute as outside the
Council’s jurisdiction, but consider that the Council’s own handling of
planning, heritage, records, FOI requests or constituent concerns remains
within its proper role, I would be grateful if you could identify that
distinction. That would help me understand precisely what you meant and
what, if anything, can properly be addressed through Council channels.

Regards,

Sion

thread_title: Re-Opening of BP vs Buckler 1987 — request for CPS consideration (s.6(2) POA 1985)
subject: Re-Opening of BP vs Buckler 1987
attachments: CADW_Forensic_Critique_Great_House_Farm_v5.0.0 (1).pdf; Particulars_of_Claim_Great_House_Farm (1).pdf; Unearthing_Cedfin_v0.4 (2).pdf; 14464_88 Decision of the Commission (4).PDF
body:
Sir/Madam,

I write to formally place before the Crown Prosecution Service evidence concerning suspected historical fraud and related criminal conduct arising from the dispossession and subsequent treatment of the former Great House Farm, Llandough, Vale of Glamorgan.

I am currently investigating the matter and preparing proceedings concerning the underlying proprietary dispute. I am also considering the institution of a private prosecution in respect of any criminal offences disclosed by the evidence.

I specifically invite the CPS to consider, at this stage, whether this is a case in which the Director of Public Prosecutions should exercise the power under section 6(2) of the Prosecution of Offences Act 1985 to take over the conduct of a private prosecution, should proceedings be instituted.

The principal concern is not simply the disputed ownership of land. The historical evidence appears to disclose a possible pattern in which the family's established occupation and proprietary position were progressively characterised as merely permissive.

Of particular significance is the apparent treatment of the occupation in the 1955 proceedings, followed by the more explicit attempt in 1974 to establish a rent-free licence arrangement concerning the property. I am investigating whether these were independent legal positions or whether they formed part of a longer and coordinated course of conduct intended to create or manufacture a documentary/legal basis for treating an established proprietary occupation as permissive, thereby facilitating the acquisition or retention of the land.

The subsequent involvement of BP Properties Ltd and BP Pension Trust, the registration of title WA231076 in 1982, and the litigation culminating in the 1987 Court of Appeal proceedings are material to that investigation.

I do not ask the CPS to determine the civil title dispute. The question I ask is whether the documentary sequence discloses evidence capable of supporting criminal offences involving fraud, conspiracy, false or misleading representations, concealment of material information, or other offences arising from the alleged acquisition or preservation of property rights.

I am particularly concerned that conduct occurring at different stages may only become intelligible when examined as a single historical sequence rather than as isolated civil proceedings. The apparent attempt to establish permissive occupation in 1955, the subsequent licence proposal in 1974, the later registration of title, and the representations made in the litigation may therefore warrant consideration together.

I recognise that the CPS will need sufficient evidence to apply the Full Code Test and that the existence of a civil dispute does not itself establish criminal conduct. I am not presenting the allegation as proved. I am presenting the documentary evidence and asking the prosecuting authority to determine whether it warrants criminal investigation and/or prosecution.

The CPS's published guidance confirms that a private prosecutor may ask the CPS to take over a private prosecution and that, when specifically requested to intervene, the CPS must make a decision whether or not to take it over. The guidance further recognises that the CPS may take over and continue a private prosecution where the Full Code Test is satisfied and there is a particular need for the CPS to conduct the prosecution, including in serious or complex cases or cases involving substantial disclosure issues.

I therefore expressly request that the CPS:

1. Consider whether it would be prepared to take over a private prosecution under section 6(2) of the Prosecution of Offences Act 1985 if proceedings are instituted;
2. Confirm whether the matter should instead be referred to an investigative authority for investigation before the CPS considers taking over proceedings;
3. Identify the appropriate CPS division or office to which the evidence should be submitted; and
4. If the CPS is not prepared to consider taking over such proceedings, expressly confirm that position and the reason for it.

I am able to provide an indexed evidential bundle containing the relevant 1955 and 1974 material, historical conveyances and plans, Land Registry documentation concerning WA231076, relevant court records and a chronology identifying the specific documentary inconsistencies and matters which I consider require investigation.

I would prefer the CPS to have the opportunity to consider the matter at this stage rather than for a private prosecution to be commenced without first giving the public prosecuting authority an opportunity to determine whether it considers the case sufficiently serious, complex or otherwise appropriate for public prosecution.

Please therefore treat this correspondence as a formal request for consideration of CPS involvement and potential exercise of the DPP's section 6(2) power, and confirm the appropriate procedure for submitting the evidence for that purpose.

There's 133 houses approved for development on land that I believe to be concealed sacred even holy ancient welsh woodland. And my land as surviving, unestiguished claim and heir and successor of that claim has been a position our family have maintain unto our suspicious and conveniently timed deaths (my father while planning was approved for 20 houses, my nan before him in the 2 weeks she will have had to challenge BP registering and merging our land as theirs at the land registry in 1983). The current possessor holds defective title, in my humble estimation. And I hold interest in the land, which is being ignored along with my concerns, by local authories who have vested interest in the development of the houses. The councillor for Llandough and MP both will not reply. The council clerk retired. This is being dragged into the shadows and I suspect clandestine warfare, silence and violence. Whereas I am trying to keep the matter open, transparent and in the public eye as it is a matter of public interest being a site of historic and archeological signficants I.e. monestry, roman villa, county treasure home, medieval burials etc.

My investigation is ongoing. But I do see a multi generational racket was used for a land grab. And I am a military warfare professional, not just the son of William Buckler.

Yours faithfully,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)

thread_title: FOI 2026-036 — schedule of all Great House Farm / Church Farm records and 1875–1915 registers
subject: Great House Farm, Llandough, Cardiff
body:
FOI Team,

This is a new request under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. It is not a repeat of FOI 2026-024 and it is not a comment on the internal review of that request.

In your letter of 25 August 2026 (FOI 2026-024) you stated:

  “For completeness, our searches identified records relating to other archaeological finds from Church Farm, Llandough and to other archaeological discoveries recorded at Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough. These records do not relate to, nor are they otherwise associated with, the discovery described in your request. We have therefore not considered them to fall within the scope of this request.”

I now request those records.

Please provide:

1. A schedule of every object, archive file, accession, loan, enquiry or correspondence record that Amgueddfa Cymru holds which is indexed, provenanced or otherwise recorded as from Great House Farm / Ty Mawr / Llandough Farm, Llandough (Penarth / Vale of Glamorgan). For each entry: accession or archive number, object or file title, date of acquisition or creation, donor or excavator if recorded, and a one-line description.

2. The same schedule for Church Farm, Llandough, but only so far as the records were retrieved in the 2026-024 search and can be identified without a new full trawl.

3. Any accession, register entry, day-book, donations book or correspondence in the collections of Amgueddfa Cymru or of its predecessor Cardiff Museum / Welsh Museum of Natural History / National Museum of Wales, dated 1875–1915, recording ironwork, armour, a visor, a lance, a helmet, “armour from Llandough”, or a find from Great House / Llandough Farm.

   Published sources which state that such ironwork is in the National Museum, and which therefore make a search of predecessor registers reasonable, are:

   • GGAT, Land at Great House Farm, Llandough: An Archaeological Assessment, August 1990 (planning file 89/01396/OUT and 92/00671/RES): “it is likely that some medieval ironwork which is held by the National Museum of Wales was discovered under the rear wing c 1880 (RCAHMW 1988).”

   • Holbrook & Thomas, Medieval Archaeology 49 (2005), p. 70 n. 142: “medieval ironwork was discovered under the rear wing of Great House Farm
c. 1880. It is now in the collections of the National Museums & Galleries of Wales.”

   I note that the National Museum of Wales was not founded until 1907. If a find of c.1880 entered a public collection in Cardiff it would have done so through the earlier municipal museum. Please search those predecessor accession registers, not only the post-1907 NMW database.

4. Any object record for Llandough ironwork that is not labelled “visor” or “lance” but is or was associated with the farmhouse floor or rear wing / dairy (the room identified on H. J. Thomas’s 1974 RCAHMW plan).

Please treat this as a request for recorded information only.

Regards,

Sion Buckler
[redacted]

thread_title: Cardiff Castle furniture / movable property (became FOI 2026-020)
subject: Internal Review: FOI 2026-020 - Great House Farm, Llandough | Cardiff Castle Furniture
body:
Dear Mr Buckler

Thank you for your request for an internal review of FOI 2026-020 concerning furniture, furnishings, antiques, fixtures, heirlooms and other movable property originating from Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough.

The reviewer has considered your original request, the responses provided by the Museum, the additional enquiries undertaken following your request for clarification on 3rd August 2026, and the concerns raised in your email requesting an internal review.

We are satisfied that the request was interpreted correctly and that reasonable and proportionate searches were undertaken to identify information falling within the scope of the request. Following the original response, the Museum undertook additional enquiries across relevant collections records and archived electronic records in order to satisfy itself that no information had been overlooked.

We are satisfied that the searches undertaken were appropriate to the nature and scope of the request and that no further searches are required in order to determine whether Amgueddfa Cymru holds information within scope. The review therefore upholds the original decision that Amgueddfa Cymru does not hold recorded information concerning furniture, furnishings, antiques, fixtures, heirlooms or other movable property originating from Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough falling within categories 1 to 9 of your request.

Response to the points raised

1. Information identified concerning Great House Farm
During the additional enquiries, a small number of records referring generally to Great House Farm, Llandough were identified. These records do not relate to furniture, furnishings, antiques, fixtures, heirlooms or other movable property originating from Great House Farm and do not fall within categories 1 to 9 of your original request. The reviewer is therefore satisfied that they fall outside the scope of the request.

2. Scope of the archived electronic search

We are satisfied that archived electronic records reasonably capable of containing information within scope were considered as part of the searches undertaken. Any data stored within a system or database pre-dating the existing Collections Management Systems, would have been migrated into the incumbent solution, and therefore included in the search.

3. Correspondence and administrative records
The review considered whether correspondence or administrative records relating to the requested items were held.

The Museum's collections records include accession documentation and associated collection records relating to objects acquired by the Museum. Searches of those records did not identify any furniture, furnishings, antiques, fixtures, heirlooms or other movable property originating from Great House Farm. As no such objects were identified as having been acquired by the Museum, no associated acquisition, provenance, ownership, loan, disposal or related correspondence concerning such objects was identified.

The review did not identify evidence that the Museum holds correspondence concerning the identification, ownership, recovery or location of Great House Farm furniture or household effects.

4. Search terms
We are satisfied that appropriate search terms and variants were used across the relevant collections management systems, collection records and associated documentation. These included relevant location names, property names, family names and associated variants reasonably capable of identifying records within scope.

The review is satisfied that the search methodology was reasonable and proportionate in the circumstances.

5. Transfer, disposal and destruction
The statement that the Museum is not aware of relevant records having been transferred or destroyed reflects the outcome of the searches undertaken and the knowledge of relevant collections staff. The review did not identify any records showing that information within the scope of your request had been transferred to another institution or destroyed.

For clarity, the Museum's position is that no relevant records were identified.

6. Records concerning external institutions
We note that your request sought records concerning communications with Cardiff Council, Cardiff Castle, the Bute Estate and other bodies regarding objects originating from Great House Farm. Searches were not limited solely to object catalogue records. Relevant collection documentation and associated records were also considered.

No records were identified concerning furniture, furnishings, antiques, fixtures, heirlooms, or other movable property originating from Great House Farm, including correspondence with the organisations referred to in your request.

7. Advice and assistance
The Museum does not hold information identifying a specific department, collection, archive or record series within Cardiff Council or Cardiff Castle that is likely to contain the information you seek. The advice previously provided reflected our general view that those organisations would be more likely than Amgueddfa Cymru to hold records relating to the ownership, management or disposal of property associated with Great House Farm.

Conclusion
Having considered all of the information available, we are satisfied that Amgueddfa Cymru undertook reasonable and proportionate searches and that, on the balance of probabilities, the Museum does not hold recorded information falling within the scope of your request. The original decision is therefore upheld.

If you remain dissatisfied, you have the right to complain to the Information Commissioner's Office.

Cofion cynnes,

FOI Team
foi.requests @museumwales.ac.uk
amgueddfa.cymru | museum.wales

Rhif elusen | Charity number 525774

thread_title: Cardiff Castle furniture / movable property (became FOI 2026-020)
subject: Re: Internal Review: FOI 2026-020 - Great House Farm, Llandough | Cardiff Castle Furniture
note: This email also makes a new request (limbs A and B) for the records identified in the FOI 2026-020 searches.
body:
Dear FOI Team,

Thank you for the internal review outcome dated 8 September 2026.

I note that the review upholds the original decision. I do not, however, consider that the review has answered the substantive questions raised in my request for internal review.

I am therefore putting the position on record, while also making a separate new request for recorded information which your review confirms already exists.

1. Records identified during the additional searches

On 14 August 2026, Amgueddfa Cymru stated that the additional enquiries had identified:

"some information relating generally to Great House Farm and the surrounding area".

The internal review now describes these as:

"a small number of records referring generally to Great House Farm, Llandough".

The wording has therefore changed slightly, but the material fact has not: the Museum confirms that records referring to Great House Farm were identified.

My internal-review request specifically asked for those records to be identified and, where not exempt, provided.

The review does not do so.

Simply stating that the records are considered to fall outside categories 1 to 9 does not identify what they are, where they are held, when they were created, or their reference numbers.

2. Archived electronic systems

My request of 14 August specifically asked:

- which archived systems were searched;
- the approximate date ranges covered;
- whether historical email or correspondence archives were searched;
- whether legacy collections-management databases were searched; and
- whether any archived systems were unavailable, incomplete or incapable of being searched.

The review answers none of these questions individually.

Instead, it states:

"archived electronic records reasonably capable of containing information within scope were considered"

and:

"Any data stored within a system or database pre-dating the existing Collections Management Systems, would have been migrated into the incumbent solution, and therefore included in the search."

The first statement describes a conclusion, rather than identifying the systems actually searched.

The second is an assumption about migration completeness. "Would have been migrated" is not a search result and does not establish that the relevant historical data was in fact migrated, completely migrated, retained, searchable and included in the particular search undertaken.

3. Correspondence independent of accessioned objects

This is the most significant issue.

The original request expressly sought correspondence and administrative records concerning, among other things:

- identification;
- recovery;
- ownership;
- location;
- the Buckler and Williams families;
- Cardiff Council;
- Cardiff Castle;
- the Bute Estate;
- museums; and
- other public authorities.

Those categories were deliberately not restricted to objects which had subsequently been accessioned by the Museum.

The review states:

"As no such objects were identified as having been acquired by the Museum, no associated acquisition, provenance, ownership, loan, disposal or related correspondence concerning such objects was identified."

That reasoning addresses correspondence attached to an identified accessioned object. It does not establish that correspondence was searched for independently of an accession record.

For example, an enquiry concerning an item, a communication about possible provenance, a request to identify an object, a discussion concerning temporary custody, a disposal enquiry, a communication with another institution, or correspondence about the contents of a property could exist without the item ever becoming an accessioned Museum object.

Accordingly, the fact that no accessioned object was identified does not itself establish that no such correspondence existed or was held.

The subsequent statement:

"The review did not identify evidence that the Museum holds correspondence concerning the identification, ownership, recovery or location of Great House Farm furniture or household effects."

still does not establish whether the relevant correspondence repositories were actually searched.

4. Search terms

My internal-review request set out specific terms and variants and asked the Museum to confirm whether those terms had been used.

The review now states only:

"appropriate search terms and variants were used"

and refers generally to:

"location names, property names, family names and associated variants".

That does not confirm whether the specific terms identified in my request were searched.

In particular, the review does not say whether searches included combinations or variants involving:

"Bute Estate", "Bute", "Cardiff Castle", "Cardiff Council", "household effects", "contents", "dispersal", "recovery", "transfer", "demolition", "provenance", "ownership"

and the other terms specifically identified in my 14 August correspondence.

The distinction matters because a search for a property name or family name is not necessarily equivalent to a search for correspondence concerning the dispersal, recovery, transfer or ownership of its contents.

5. Transfer, disposal and destruction

My request also asked what evidential basis existed for the earlier statement that the Museum was not aware of relevant records having been transferred to another institution or destroyed.

The review now says:

"The statement that the Museum is not aware of relevant records having been transferred or destroyed reflects the outcome of the searches undertaken and the knowledge of relevant collections staff."

This combines two different things: documentary searches and institutional recollection.

It does not tell me whether the Museum searched:

- transfer or accession-out records;
- disposal records;
- retention and destruction records;
- archival transfer documentation; or
- other records capable of establishing whether material had previously been transferred or destroyed.

There is an important distinction between:

"no record of transfer or destruction was identified in the records searched"

and:

"there is no evidence that any transfer or destruction occurred".

The review does not make that distinction sufficiently clear.

6. Searches concerning external institutions

The original request expressly contemplated records concerning Cardiff Council, Cardiff Castle, the Bute Estate and other external bodies.

The review states:

"Searches were not limited solely to object catalogue records."

That is helpful, but it still does not identify what non-catalogue repositories were searched.

For example, it does not identify whether searches were made of curator correspondence, departmental files, donor correspondence, acquisition/disposal correspondence, provenance files, loan files, institutional correspondence indexes, or other historical administrative records in which communications with external institutions might have been recorded.

Again, the issue is not whether the Museum considers the search reasonable. It is whether the relevant classes of records were actually searched.

7. The significance of the "balance of probabilities" conclusion

I note the review's conclusion that, "on the balance of probabilities", the Museum does not hold recorded information within the scope of the request.

I do not dispute that a negative FOI determination may ultimately be reached on that basis.

However, the balance-of-probabilities conclusion necessarily depends upon the quality, scope and rigour of the searches on which it is based. The ICO's guidance states that, where a requester disputes whether relevant information has been located, the authority should be able to provide a reasoned and detailed account of how it determined that further information was not held, including the areas searched, staff consulted and, for electronic searches, the keywords, accounts and time parameters used.

My concern remains that the review repeatedly substitutes statements such as "we are satisfied", "appropriate", "reasonably capable" and "on the balance of probabilities" for the underlying factual information about what was actually searched.

I therefore consider the review outcome insufficiently informative on the specific search methodology raised in my review request.

I reserve my right to refer the handling of FOI 2026-020 and the internal review to the Information Commissioner's Office.

Separate new FOI request

Separately from the above, I am now making a new request under the Freedom of Information Act 2000.

This new request is deliberately limited to recorded information which your own correspondence confirms was identified or generated in connection with the searches already undertaken.

Please provide:

A. Records identified

The "small number of records referring generally to Great House Farm, Llandough" identified during the additional enquiries referred to in your email of 14 August 2026 and the internal review outcome of 8 September 2026.

For each record, please provide, where recorded:

- title or description;
- date;
- collection, series or department;
- system or repository;
- reference, accession or record number; and
- a copy of the record, subject to any applicable exemption.

If any part of a record is exempt, please identify the exemption relied upon and provide the remainder where reasonably practicable.

Limb A is confined to the records your 14 August and 8 September letters say were identified in the FOI 2026-020 additional enquiries. It is not a new collection-wide search. If any of those records are also in scope of FOI 2026-032 or FOI 2026-036, please schedule them once and cross-refer. Please do not refuse this request as a duplicate.

B. Existing search records

Any recorded information already held concerning the searches undertaken for FOI 2026-020 or its internal review, including any existing:

- search notes;
- search logs;
- search checklists;
- system lists;
- search-term lists;
- IT tickets or instructions;
- archived-system enquiries;
- staff search records; or
- other contemporaneous records documenting the searches undertaken.

I am asking only for recorded information already held. I am not asking the Museum to create a new narrative or retrospective report.

If no such search records are held, please state that expressly.

Please register this as a new FOI request and provide it with its own reference number. It is not a further internal review of FOI 2026-020, nor is it a request to reopen or amend FOI 2026-032 or FOI 2026-036.

I would therefore be grateful if this request could be processed separately and not treated as a clarification or continuation of those matters.

Regards,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)
Royal Signals Cyber and Electronic Warfare Professional and Life Member

thread_title: Escalation to the Leader — ward member silence and the commemorative tree (Monitoring Officer reply)
subject: Escalation — Llandough ward member silence: Great House Farm / Church View Close and removal of commemorative tree
body:
Councillor Burnett,

I write to you as Leader of the Vale of Glamorgan Council because the
elected member for Llandough, Councillor George D. D. Carroll, has not
answered a sequence of written enquiries spanning more than six months. I
am going above him for that reason alone. I am not asking you to adjudicate
the historic title dispute. I am asking that a constituent with a
documented family interest in the ward receive a reply that the ward member
has declined to give.

I understand that elected members do not have a line manager in the
employment sense. Councillor Carroll is Leader of the Conservative Group.
You are the political head of the authority. After the ward member and the
Monitoring Officer, you are the proper next addressee.

Why I am writing to you rather than waiting further

1. Councillor Carroll has not sent a single substantive reply to me at
gdcarroll@valeofglamorgan.gov.uk.
2. On 27 July 2026 I filed a formal complaint about that silence (copied to
him, Democratic Services and the Monitoring Officer).
3. On 12 August 2026 Victoria Davidson, Monitoring Officer, wrote that the
matter fell outside the Corporate Concerns and Complaints Policy and that
she had not identified a Code of Conduct breach. That determination did not
require him to respond. It left the original questions unanswered.
4. I followed up with the Monitoring Officer on 12 August, 21 August and 24
August 2026. The position did not change.
5. I copied Councillor Carroll again on 28 August 2026 (joint letter with
Stephen Doughty MP). Still no reply from him.

The questions he has not answered include a simple, current, ward-level
one: who removed the tree my great-grandfather planted to mark the family’s
claim, as recorded in the Collection of Wales / archival image. That is a
local enquiry a ward member can signpost to Parks, Highways, Planning or
the landowner. It is not a request that he retry BP Properties Ltd v
Buckler.

From his public output, Councillor Carroll appears to concentrate on
blocked drains, potholes and similar highway defects. Those matters matter.
The correspondence I sent him is of a different character: heritage,
planning and enforcement records, the 1988 demolition of Great House Farm
(Ty Mawr), now Church View Close, and the removal of a commemorative tree.
I accept that may be outside the type of casework he usually handles. That
is why a short, honest reply — even if only to say the questions sit with
named officers, and to pass the tree query to the correct department —
would have been sufficient. Silence is not.

Recorded approaches to Councillor Carroll (gdcarroll@valeofglamorgan.gov.uk)

All sent. No substantive reply on any of them.

- 16 February 2026 — “Title Fraud and Procedural Concealment – Church View
Close, Llandough (formerly Great House Farm / Ty Mawr)”. Planning and
record-keeping gaps; 1988 demolition.
- 4 May 2026 — follow-up on BP v Buckler 1987; ITV footage; request for
attention as Llandough councillor.
- 3 May 2026 — joined the public “George Carroll for Llandough” Facebook
group (approved). Not a substitute for a council-email reply.
- 9 May 2026 — a wider formal notice also addressed to
gcarroll@valeofglamorgan.gov.uk. That address bounced. Subsequent mail used
the correct gdcarroll@ address.
- 7 June 2026 — “Church View Close, Llandough”. 1988 events from public
records, family testimony and media.
- 25 June 2026 — “Great House Farm, Llandough”. Asked whether he had
reviewed the earlier concerns and whether any discussion was possible.
- 13 July 2026 — “Great House Farm / Church View Close”. Full timeline
restated. Ten-working-day request. Explicit question: who removed the tree
my great-grandfather planted to commemorate the ownership claim, as shown
in the Collection of Wales archive image.
- 27 July 2026 — formal complaint to complaints@valeofglamorgan.gov.uk,
copied to Councillor Carroll, Democratic Services and the Monitoring
Officer.
- 28 August 2026 — further letter to Councillor Carroll and Stephen Doughty
MP on the same site.

What I am asking you to do

1. Note that the ward member has not answered, and that the complaint
process produced no requirement that he do so.

2. Ask Councillor Carroll, or the relevant Director, to provide a short
written reply on the tree: which department or landowner authorised or
carried out its removal, on what date, and under what power or works order
— or to confirm that the Council holds no such record.

3. Identify the correct officer contact for heritage, trees and historic
planning records at Church View Close / former Great House Farm, so I am
not left circling a silent ward inbox.

4. Confirm whether the Council will treat a documented family connection to
a demolished historic farmstead in the ward as a legitimate basis for a
reply, even where the correspondent is not presently resident in Llandough.

The thesis of my concern is that the lawfare/ warfare that systematically
attempted to make our occupancy permissive as early as the 40's (with my
grandmothers statement of title being stolen, a failed attempt to get us
into a tenancy afterwards, and ambiguity in a 1955 order for another parcel
we leased and defaulted on, which later meant it was able to be
misinterpreted to make it appear our parcel of land (now Church View Close)
was part of theirs, like it was in 1916 - 1928) is a racket. The ownership
dispute was a problem created. The reaction followed and the solution was
to focus on possession. And so in 1987 BP were awarded possession with what
was a defective title chain.

I do not expect you to reopen 1987 litigation. I do expect the authority,
once the ward member has been given months and a formal complaint, to
answer a factual question about a tree on land in that ward. Because that
tree was part of a long list of evidence supporting our ownership claim.

I can supply the original emails and the 27 July complaint in full if
Democratic Services does not already have them. See attached the
aforementioned tree planting ceremy image. I also enclose a draft chancery
court allocation so you can understand the legal arguments.

Due to a lot of suspicious and conveniently timed deaths in our family,
surrounding this case, like my grandmother dying in the 2 weeks she will
have had to challenge BP quietly registering our land parcel in their names
in 1983, without declaring our ownership claim, which was never
exstinguished as the first 1974 court case was ajourned. Or my fathers
death after his appeal of the 1987 ruling was dismissed on grounds of
"heads BP win, tails we lose". Followed by ECHR rejection citing BP own the
land, despite BP only seeking possession and never seeking or gaining
ownership.

I have a trove of evidence and I am collecting more and investigating and
in talks with CPS and Fraud Police and MoJ and Land Registry. The initial
thing I would like from you is the record of the removal of the tree we
planted. The picture attached depicts its location. I'd like to know who
