thread_title: FOI 2026-024 — visor and lance from beneath the dining-room floor
subject: FOI Internal Review - 2026-024 - Great House Farm, Llandough
body:
Dear Mr Buckler

Thank you for your request for an internal review of Amgueddfa Cymru's response to your Freedom of Information request concerning a reported archaeological discovery at Great House Farm, Llandough.

I have now completed my review of the handling of your request, including the searches undertaken and the concerns raised in your request for review.

Having reviewed the original request, the searches conducted and the response provided, I am satisfied that the request was handled appropriately and that reasonable and proportionate searches were undertaken in those locations where information falling within the scope of the request would reasonably be expected to be held.

In your request for review, you suggest that additional searches should have been undertaken using a wider range of terms and concepts, including references to Roman burials, military burials, cavalry burials, human remains, horse remains and other archaeological terminology. I have carefully considered this point. However, when assessing whether information is held for the purposes of the Freedom of Information Act 2000, the relevant issue is not whether every conceivable search term has been used, but whether the authority has undertaken searches that are reasonable and proportionate in the circumstances and reasonably likely to identify relevant information if held.

Your request concerned a specific reported discovery at a named location. Accordingly, the location identified in the request was used as the primary search criterion. Searches were undertaken across Amgueddfa Cymru's information holdings where records relating to acquisitions, accessions, archaeological finds, provenance information and associated correspondence would reasonably be expected to be held. This included collections management systems, accession records, archived documentation, shared electronic records and other organisational record repositories.

Records identified through those searches were reviewed by collections staff and the FOI team to determine whether they related to the reported discovery described in your request. As the search methodology was location-based rather than focused on a particular object type, archaeological period or interpretation, it was reasonably likely of identifying relevant records regardless of whether associated material had been recorded as Roman, medieval or otherwise. I have therefore considered your suggestion that later historical accounts may have inaccurately described the nature, date or attribution of the reported discovery. I am satisfied that this possibility would not have affected the outcome of the searches undertaken.

I have also considered whether broader keyword searches would have been appropriate. Given the scale and diversity of Amgueddfa Cymru's collections and records, generic terms such as "horse", "burial" or "skeleton" would retrieve large volumes of records relating to many different sites and periods and would not provide a reliable or proportionate means of locating records relating to a specific reported discovery at a named location. I am satisfied that the location-based search strategy adopted was the most appropriate and proportionate approach.

The searches undertaken did not identify any records relating to:
* the acquisition, accession, donation, transfer or deposit of a visor, lance, helmet, armour or related objects associated with the discovery described in your request;
* associated human or animal remains connected with that discovery;
* reburial records relating to that discovery; or
* excavation reports, discovery reports or watching-brief records relating to the discovery described in your request.

Having reviewed both the scope of the original request and the searches undertaken, I am satisfied on the balance of probabilities that, if information relating to the reported discovery were held by Amgueddfa Cymru, those searches would have been likely to identify it.

You also raised concerns regarding the reference in the original response to other archaeological records identified during the course of the searches. Those records were reviewed and were not considered to relate to, or otherwise be associated with, the reported discovery described in your request. However, I can confirm that this aspect has been subject to further consideration and a separate response will be issued in relation to those records.

I therefore uphold the original conclusion that Amgueddfa Cymru does not hold recorded information falling within the scope of your request.

This concludes Amgueddfa Cymru's internal review process. If you remain dissatisfied, you may complain to the Information Commissioner's Office under section 50 of the Freedom of Information Act 2000.

Cofion cynnes,

FOI Team
foi.requests @museumwales.ac.uk
amgueddfa.cymru | museum.wales

Rhif elusen | Charity number 525774

thread_title: FOI 2026-032 — other archaeological discoveries at Great House Farm and Church Farm
subject: FOI - 2026-032 - Great House Farm, Llandough
attachments: FOI 2026-032 - 1924.jpeg; FOI 2026-032 - burial data.pdf; FOI 2026-032 - Filling the gaps.pdf; FOI 2026-032 - Llandough excavation.pdf; FOI 2026-032 - PAS finds.pdf; FOI 2026-032 - Roman Villa LLandough.pdf; FOI 2026-032 - Timeline Doc by Sion Bucklet.pdf; Llandough 82-44H details.xlsx; Llandough 95-56H details.xlsx; FOI - 2026-032 - explanatory doc.docx; Llandough 95-56H list.xls; Llandough 82.44H list.xls
note: FOI 2026-032 was registered by the Museum from the family's internal-review email of 26 August 2026 (transcribed under FOI 2026-024 above).
body:
Dear Mr Buckler

Thank you for your request for information, registered as FOI 2026-032.

As explained in our previous correspondence, this request has been considered separately from the internal review relating to FOI 2026-024.

We have identified a number of records relating to archaeological discoveries recorded at Great House Farm and Church Farm, both at Llandough. These records were identified during searches undertaken in connection with the earlier request but were not considered to fall within the scope of that request, which concerned a specific reported discovery.

We have now reviewed those records for the purposes of your new request.

Attached are copies of the relevant records. Certain information has been redacted from the disclosed records under section 40(2) of the Freedom of Information Act 2000, where it comprises the personal data of third parties. Disclosure of that information would contravene the data protection principles set out in UK data protection legislation.

To assist interpretation, we have also included a brief descriptor for each record, together with any available reference or catalogue information held within the Museum's records.

Further to these documents, we have also identified some publicly available records which I have referenced below.

An Early-medieval Monastic Cemetery at Llandough, Glamorgan: Excavations in 1994: Medieval Archaeology: Vol 49 , No 1 - Get Access<https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/epdf/10.1179/007660905x54044?needAccess=true>

Highlight 5: Llandough early medieval cemetery, Glamorgan (1994) - Cotswold Archaeology<https://cotswoldarchaeology.co.uk/highlight-5-llandough-early-medieval-cemetery-glamorgan-1994/>

Please note that the provision of these records should not be taken as indicating any association between them and the discovery you have described in FOI 2026-024. The records are being disclosed in response to your separate request for information relating to other archaeological discoveries recorded at the site.

If you are dissatisfied with the handling of this request, you may request an internal review within 40 working days of this response.

Cofion cynnes,

FOI Team
foi.requests @museumwales.ac.uk
amgueddfa.cymru | museum.wales

thread_title: Cadw — Formal complaint of 17 September 2026, re-service and supplement
subject: Supplement to complaint re-served 20 September 2026 — Great House Farm (Tŷ Mawr), Llandough
body:
Dr Wigley,

This is a supplement to the complaint re-served on 20 September, not a chaser. I do not expect a reply before the stage-one response. It adds seven matters under the existing headings at section 7, and one addition to the outcomes at section 9, set out at the end.

The public interest is engaged alongside my family's. Great House Farm stood beside the Grade I church at Llandough, was recorded by the Royal Commission in 1974, sat within a known archaeological site, and was described in the post-demolition planning record as a "county treasure". I do not ask Cadw to treat the 1994 discoveries as knowledge it had in 1988. They show what was lost; the pre-1988 record is the measure of Cadw's process.

On my family's account and the contemporary press report, protection was being sought in the first days of December 1988 and the house was demolished almost immediately afterwards. I do not ask Cadw to determine responsibility for the demolition. The grievance is narrower: protection was sought at the critical moment, and Cadw cannot now show what it considered.

1. The adopted development plan (matter A)

The planning officer's report on application 89/01396/OUT records that the supporting information to Policy H.2 of the East Vale Local Plan "states that buildings on the site should be retained, however were unfortunately demolished a little while ago." I do not say this bound Cadw or required listing. I ask:
(a) was Cadw aware of it in December 1988;
(b) did the planning authority draw it to Cadw's attention; and (c) if neither can be established, will Cadw say so expressly.

2. The search undertaken on 21 May (matters D and F)

Mr Weatherhead wrote that he had asked a colleague to search other paper files, "including the Welsh Office files", and would write again with the result, while fairly warning that some files had quite likely been destroyed. I have not received that letter. Please confirm whether the search was carried out, which series were searched, what was found, and whether Cadw regards the ATISN 27021 response of 11 June as its report of that search.

3. The meaning of "YYY" (matter J)

Cadw has given two accounts of the marking — that the buildings were "marginally below the bar for listing" (21 May) and that the building did not meet the criteria (10 July) — and one inference, that it did not meet the criteria "as it was not included on the list" (29 July). I ask for one settled meaning, the documentary source for it, and, if there is none, a statement to that effect.

4. The retention period (matter J)

Your email of 27 August said that no records of the historic retention arrangements are available, and that the three-year period is what current colleagues advised from their knowledge of the systems then in place. I ask only that the complaint response confirm expressly that this is an account of general practice, not evidence that the Great House Farm file was in fact destroyed after three years.

5. Professional archaeological knowledge of this site before December 1988 (matter C)

On 22 September 2026 Amgueddfa Cymru disclosed to me, under FOI 2026-032, its collections records for two accessions from this site. The first, 82.44H, is the material from the Glamorgan-Gwent Archaeological Trust's excavation of 1979 on land formerly part of Great House Farm, carried out in advance of housing development. The museum's records give the findspot as ST 168 733, the donor as Wales & West Housing Association Ltd, and the published report as Owen-John 1988. The accession runs to several hundred entries and includes Roman coins, samian, glass, a bone scabbard slide and querns, together with medieval pottery and ironwork.

This is not archaeology discovered after the event. By the time Cadw considered this building, the site had been professionally excavated, the finds had been accessioned by the national museum under a 1982 accession number, and the excavation report had been published. I therefore ask, as an addition to matter C:
(a) whether Cadw held, or had access to, the 1979 excavation record or its published report when it considered the buildings in 1988; (b) whether that material was drawn to its attention by GGAT, the planning authority or the Royal Commission; and (c) if neither can now be established, that Cadw say so in terms.

I do not say this material required the building to be listed. I say that the conclusion recorded in December 1988, that the site was not of sufficient archaeological interest, was reached against a professional record that already existed and is still held by the national museum today.

6. The National Museum attribution (matter H)

The GGAT assessment of August 1990, which Cadw supplied to me on 21 May, states that "it is likely that some medieval ironwork which is held by the National Museum of Wales was discovered under the rear wing c 1880 (RCAHMW 1988)."

The museum's disclosure allows that sentence to be tested, and the position is more precise than either of us has previously put it. The museum does hold medieval ironwork from this site — knife blades, arrowheads, a buckle and a pair of compasses within accession 82.44H — but as excavated material from 1979, not as an 1880 discovery beneath the rear wing. Its searches found no accession, donation or deposit answering the c.1880 provenance at all. The museum's own explanation, given in its disclosure, is that objects recorded as found at Church Farm, Llandough in 1858 and donated in 1963 under accession 63.24 "could well be the basis for such a local story/tradition".

I therefore no longer ask Cadw to accept that the attribution is uncorroborated in the round. I ask, more narrowly, whether Cadw holds anything supporting the c.1880 rear-wing provenance beyond the GGAT sentence it forwarded, and whether it will ask that the derived record note the museum's findings rather than continue to carry the 1880 attribution unqualified.

7. Correcting the record (matter H)

You directed me to Heneb as manager of the HER, which was reasonable. The only substantive reply I have had from Heneb is its statement of 22 May that it is not subject to FOI as a limited company; a schedule I sent on 19 September remains outstanding.

The museum's disclosure now gives a firm anchor for what the record should show. Accession 95.56H comprises the material from the Cotswold Archaeological Trust excavation of 1994, donated by Ideal Homes Wales Ltd, and its locality is recorded in the museum's own collections database as "Great House Farm Llandough" at ST 1681 7331 — the grid reference carried by the historic environment record for this site. That accession runs to several hundred sets of early medieval human remains from this ground.

As the statutory duty to keep historic environment records rests with the Welsh Ministers, I ask:
(a) which body is responsible for correcting an inaccurate or incomplete historic environment record; (b) what Cadw's own role is where the record is managed by Heneb; and (c) what Cadw will do if the entry for this site (GGAT02038s) is not corrected to reflect the 1979 and 1994 excavations and the accessions arising from them.

Correction to my letter of 20 September

I said cadw@gov.wales had rejected my correspondence on three occasions. Having checked properly, it rejected messages on at least eight occasions between January and September 2026: 23 January; 9 May (twice); 17 May; 10 August; 11 August; 29 August; and 17 September. Separate failures on 29 August and 17 September came from the retired address cadw@wales.gsi.gov.uk. I correct this because I have asked Cadw to distinguish what is established from what is inferred, and the same standard applies to me.

Addition to the outcomes at section 9

6. A written acknowledgement that the 21 May undertaking was not reported on, and that Cadw's accounts of the 1988 assessment have varied.
7. A single statement of what can and cannot now be established about the 1988 decisions, which my family can rely on and cite.
8. That Cadw write to Heneb and the Royal Commission asking that their records for this site reflect that statement and the museum's accession records.
9. Consideration, under the Welsh Government complaints policy, of redress for the time and trouble my family has spent since May pursuing questions that Cadw's own records could not answer.

I am content to supply the museum's disclosure to Cadw if that would assist, and my offer of 20 September stands: any 1988 Cadw correspondence recovered from the Royal Commission or Heneb will be sent to you. I remain grateful for the courtesy you and your colleagues have shown me.

Yours sincerely,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)
Royal Signals Cyber/Electronic Warfare Professional and Life Member

thread_title: Sept 2026 request — March 1983 GGAT warehouse fire and archive custody
subject: FOI "Llandough Roman villa & medieval house finds were destroyed in a 1983 fire"
note: No Heneb reply to this request is in the mailbox as of 13 October 2026.
body:
Dear Heneb: The Trust for Welsh Archaeology,

I am writing to request access to recorded information concerning the March 1983 fire at the former Glamorgan-Gwent Archaeological Trust (GGAT) warehouse in Swansea, particularly the reported destruction of archaeological finds, excavation records and photographic material from Llandough, together with records concerning the subsequent custody, preservation, transfer and integrity of archaeological records relating to Great House Farm (Tŷ Mawr), Llandough.

I recognise that Heneb is an independent private company limited by guarantee and registered charity rather than a body ordinarily subject to the Freedom of Information Act 2000.

However, Heneb now maintains the statutory Historic Environment Records for Wales on behalf of the Welsh Ministers. Sections 194 and 195 of the Historic Environment (Wales) Act 2023 require the Welsh Ministers to maintain publicly accessible Historic Environment Records, including information concerning archaeological investigations and their findings.

I therefore ask that this request be considered under any applicable statutory information-access regime, including the Environmental Information Regulations 2004 insofar as Heneb considers that it falls within their scope.

If Heneb considers that the EIR do not apply to any or all of the information requested, please state that expressly and identify the legal basis for that position. I would nevertheless be grateful if Heneb would consider the request voluntarily as an information-access request, particularly where the information forms part of, or supports, the statutory Historic Environment Record or associated archaeological archive maintained on behalf of the Welsh Ministers.

I have copied Cadw and the Royal Commission on the Ancient and Historical Monuments of Wales because the request concerns the statutory HER system and records said to have been transferred or accessioned into the National Monuments Record of Wales.

The request is for existing recorded information only. I am not asking Heneb to create a new report or undertake fresh archaeological interpretation.

Purpose and evidential context

This request arises from a wider forensic examination of the surviving documentary record concerning Great House Farm (Tŷ Mawr), Llandough.

Two companion forensic critiques, dated 21 September 2026, have been prepared concerning respectively Cadw and GGAT/Heneb. They are not presented as proof of dishonesty, bad faith, corruption or deliberate destruction. Rather, they identify a series of documentary gaps, inconsistent records and questions which cannot properly be resolved without access to the underlying primary records.

In particular, the GGAT critique identifies questions concerning the Trust's historical roles as archaeological adviser, contractor, investigator, curator and record-holder, and concerning the provenance and subsequent custody of the 1990 Great House Farm assessment and associated material.

The purpose of this request is therefore to establish, from the records themselves, what material existed, what was lost, what survived, where it was held, when it was transferred, and whether the present HER and archive accurately represent the historical record.

The two distinct archaeological areas at Llandough

For the avoidance of doubt, I ask that the following be treated as separate investigations.

1. Llandough Farm / Roman villa area south of St Dochdwy's church

GGAT undertook excavation in this area in 1978–79, with the HER identifying event GGATE001109 as "Llandough Farm". The associated site record concerns an Iron Age/Roman villa complex with later early-medieval burial activity.

2. Great House Farm (Tŷ Mawr) area north of St Dochdwy's church

GGAT undertook an archaeological assessment/evaluation of Great House Farm in 1990, followed by the substantially larger Cotswold Archaeological Trust excavation in 1994.

These should not be conflated in the records or in any response to this request.

Part A — March 1983 warehouse fire

I have identified contemporaneous newspaper reports concerning the March 1983 fire at the GGAT Swansea warehouse.

Those reports state that substantial quantities of archaeological material were destroyed and specifically identify finds from Llandough among the losses. They also report the destruction of a photographic studio/darkroom and a substantial quantity of photographic material.

I therefore request:

1. Any surviving inventory, catalogue, accession register, storage list, box list, find list, archive schedule or other contemporaneous record identifying archaeological material held at the Swansea warehouse immediately before the fire.

2. Any surviving inventory, assessment or other record identifying material from the 1978–79 Llandough Farm excavation which was destroyed, lost, damaged or rendered unrecoverable in the fire.

3. Any records identifying Llandough photographic material lost in the fire, including, where recorded:

- original negatives;
- contact sheets;
- prints;
- transparencies/slides;
- photographic registers or catalogues;
- site photography logs; and
- duplicate or working copies.

4. Any post-fire salvage, recovery, reconciliation or damage-assessment records concerning archaeological material or photographic material recovered from the warehouse.

5. Any insurance claim, loss schedule, valuation, stock reconciliation, internal audit, board/minute record, memorandum or other contemporaneous document assessing the scale or nature of the archaeological and photographic losses.

6. Any correspondence concerning the fire or its archaeological losses with Cadw/Welsh Historic Monuments, the Welsh Office/Welsh Government, Amgueddfa Cymru/National Museum Wales, RCAHMW, local authorities, funding bodies, insurers, fire authorities or other archaeological organisations.

7. Any GGAT annual report, internal report, memorandum or other record discussing the fire, the losses, salvage, replacement of records, reconstruction of catalogues or subsequent archive-management arrangements.

Part B — What survived from the 1978–79 Llandough excavation

8. Any surviving GGAT records showing what material from the Llandough Farm excavation survived the 1983 fire, including finds, site records, plans, drawings, photographs, notebooks, context records, catalogues, reports and publication material.

9. Any surviving records showing where surviving Llandough material was subsequently stored, transferred, deposited or otherwise held.

10. Any transfer, accession or deposit records identifying material from the Llandough excavation now held by Heneb, Amgueddfa Cymru/National Museum Wales, RCAHMW, the Archaeology Data Service or another repository.

11. If Heneb no longer holds material formerly held by GGAT from this excavation, please provide any recorded information showing when and how that material ceased to be held by GGAT or its successor organisations.

Part C — Great House Farm (Tŷ Mawr): the 1990 GGAT assessment

12. Any records showing the complete archival history and custody of the GGAT 1990 archaeological assessment of Great House Farm, including the report associated with HER record GGAT02038s.

13. Please provide any surviving records showing:

- the date on which the assessment was completed;
- the date on which it was received or entered into GGAT records;
- its original file or archive reference;
- where the original and working copies were held;
- any subsequent movement between GGAT offices, stores or repositories;
- any transfer or deposit to RCAHMW/the National Monuments Record of Wales;
- the date and reference of any such accession; and
- the identity and present location of associated archive material.

I understand that the 1990 assessment was accessioned into the National Monuments Record of Wales on 20 March 2019.

Please confirm whether that date is correct and provide the underlying accession, transfer, deposit or cataloguing record.

14. If the assessment was not accessioned into the National Monuments Record until 2019, please provide any recorded information showing where the assessment and associated archive material were held between completion of the assessment and that accession.

15. Please provide any surviving pre-1990 or 1990 GGAT material relating to Great House Farm/Tŷ Mawr, including correspondence, field notes, photographs, plans, drawings, draft reports, site notebooks, assessment notes and archaeological planning correspondence.

16. Please specifically provide any surviving material corresponding to, or identified as, Appendix B and Appendix E of the 1990 GGAT assessment, together with any records showing whether either appendix has been lost, separated from the principal report, transferred elsewhere, superseded, or otherwise disposed of.

17. Any records concerning the preparation, internal review, approval, issue and circulation of the 1990 assessment and its appendices.

18. Any records concerning the commissioning, procurement, quotation, specification, fee, contract, invoice or other administrative arrangements under which GGAT undertook the 1990 Great House Farm assessment.

19. Any records showing what information supplied by GGAT about Great House Farm was entered into, amended within, cross-referenced within, or omitted from the then South Glamorgan/West Glamorgan Sites and Monuments Record.

20. Any audit trail, change history, correction record or equivalent metadata showing subsequent amendments to the relevant HER records and references for Great House Farm/Tŷ Mawr.

Part D — Relationship between the 1990 assessment and the 1994 excavation

21. Any records showing what information or archive material from the 1990 GGAT assessment was supplied to, transferred to, or made available to Cotswold Archaeological Trust in connection with the 1994 excavation.

22. Any correspondence between GGAT and Cotswold Archaeological Trust concerning the archaeological potential, results, interpretation, extent or recording of the Great House Farm site.

23. Any records showing whether the 1990 GGAT trench plan, archaeological potential map, appendices or conclusions were used to determine the location, extent or methodology of the 1994 excavation.

24. Any records identifying any material change between GGAT's 1990 assessment and the findings of the 1994 excavation, including any contemporary acknowledgment within GGAT's records that the 1994 findings differed materially from the conclusions or zoning of the 1990 assessment.

Part E — The 1994 Cotswold Archaeological Trust excavation archive

25. Any records held by Heneb concerning the surviving archive of the 1994 Great House Farm excavation, including information on where the archive was deposited or transferred.

26. Any records showing the date, destination and scope of any transfer or deposit of the 1994 excavation archive, including:

- finds;
- human-remains records;
- context sheets;
- plans and drawings;
- photographs;
- catalogues;
- databases; and
- specialist reports.

27. The published excavation record states that 1,026 inhumation burials were examined, whereas the current Heneb HER record states 858 inhumations.

Please provide any records held by Heneb which explain the difference between these figures, including whether they represent different stages of excavation, different archaeological categories, different counting methodologies, or subsequent correction or revision of the HER.

28. Any records showing whether material from the 1994 excavation remains with Heneb/GGAT, Cotswold Archaeology, Amgueddfa Cymru/National Museum Wales, RCAHMW, the Archaeology Data Service or another repository.

29. I understand that archive material relating to the 1994 excavation was deposited in or around 2014. Please confirm whether this is correct and, if so, provide the relevant accession/deposit information and identify the repository concerned.

Part F — Archive management following the 1983 fire

30. Any records concerning the archive-management arrangements implemented by GGAT following the 1983 fire for the preservation, cataloguing, duplication, storage and eventual deposition of excavation archives, photographs and associated records.

31. Any records showing whether records affected by the fire were reconstructed, recreated, copied, replaced or otherwise restored, and which archaeological projects were affected by any such work.

32. Any records concerning subsequent reviews of the completeness of excavation archives affected by the fire.

33. Any retention schedules, disposal schedules, archive policies, accession procedures or records-management guidance used by GGAT during the relevant period which governed the retention or disposal of archaeological project records and photographs.

Part G — Present completeness and custody of the archaeological record

34. Any surviving GGAT/Heneb records identifying missing, lost, destroyed, separated or otherwise unaccounted-for archive components relating to either the Llandough Farm excavation or Great House Farm/Tŷ Mawr.

35. Any records showing whether the 1978–79 Llandough excavation archive, the 1990 Great House Farm assessment and the 1994 Great House Farm excavation archive were ever cross-referenced, reconciled or treated as related archaeological records.

36. Any records identifying discrepancies between the historical GGAT records, the present Heneb HER, the National Monuments Record of Wales and the published archaeological reports concerning these sites.

Part H — Heneb's statutory HER role and custody of information

37. Please identify the legal and administrative basis on which Heneb maintains the relevant Historic Environment Record on behalf of the Welsh Ministers, including any agreement, contract, service specification, grant agreement, memorandum of understanding or other instrument governing that arrangement.

38. Does Heneb consider that information forming part of the statutory Historic Environment Record is held:

a. by Heneb in its own capacity;

b. by Heneb on behalf of the Welsh Ministers; or

c. on some other legal or administrative basis?

Please explain.

39. Where historical GGAT material now held by Heneb forms evidence supporting a statutory HER record, please identify whether the underlying source archive is regarded as part of the HER itself, associated reference material, or a separate archaeological archive.

40. If any of the information requested above is held by Heneb solely on behalf of the Welsh Ministers, please identify the relevant Welsh Government/Cadw body responsible for access to that information and the applicable access regime.

Searches and records no longer held

I appreciate that some historical records may no longer survive.

Where information requested above is no longer held, please state that clearly and, where recorded information exists concerning its destruction, disposal, transfer, loss or separation, please provide that information.

For each material category where the original record is no longer held, please provide any surviving record showing:

- when it ceased to be held;
- why it ceased to be held;
- whether it was destroyed, lost, transferred or otherwise disposed of;
- whether any replacement, copy or reconstruction was made; and
- the repository or organisation to which it was transferred, where applicable.

If Heneb's searches establish that a record formerly known to exist cannot now be located, please identify the relevant search terms, archive locations or record systems searched and the outcome of those searches, insofar as such information is itself recorded.

Where records have been transferred to another body, please identify that body together with any accession, archive or reference number known to Heneb.

Scope and cost

If Heneb considers that this request is too broad or that responding to it would exceed any applicable statutory cost limit, please identify the specific questions or categories causing the difficulty and advise how I can narrow the request while retaining the central questions concerning:

1. the scale and nature of the archaeological and photographic losses in the March 1983 warehouse fire;
2. what material from the 1978–79 Llandough excavation survived;
3. the complete custody history of the 1990 Great House Farm assessment and its appendices;
4. the relationship between that assessment and the 1994 excavation;
5. the whereabouts and completeness of the 1994 excavation archive; and
6. the present accuracy and provenance of the relevant HER records.

If some information is already publicly available or is held by another body, please identify the relevant repository and, where possible, provide the relevant archive, accession or catalogue reference rather than simply directing me to the organisation generally.

This request is made in the public interest and is intended to establish the documentary record. It should not be read as an allegation that any individual or institution acted dishonestly, in bad faith, corruptly, or deliberately destroyed or concealed evidence.

I would be grateful for confirmation of receipt and for the request to be dealt with under the appropriate applicable information-access regime.

Regards,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)

Royal Signals Cyber/ Electronic Warfare Professional and Life Member

thread_title: Independent Complaints Reviewer — referral ICR/090/26
subject: Great House Farm, Llandough
body:
Dear Sirs,

I am seeking an independent review of HM Land Registry's handling of my complaint concerning the historic registration of land belonging to the Williams/Buckler family at Great House Farm / Tŷ Mawr, Llandough, Cardiff, and the subsequent registered title history, including WA231076, WA240304 and the later woodland title WA735527.

HM Land Registry has now replied to my MP and has maintained, in essence, that it does not accept that a mistake was made.

My concern is not simply that HM Land Registry reached a conclusion with which I disagree. It is that the conclusion appears to leave fundamental documentary questions unanswered and relies heavily upon historical proceedings which did not determine the underlying documentary root of the family's ownership claim.

I have spent approximately twenty years researching this matter and have assembled a substantial body of documentary, archival, court, Land Registry and family evidence. I am not asking ICR to determine ownership itself. I am asking it to review whether HM Land Registry properly investigated and answered the complaint put before it, whether it addressed the evidence I supplied, and whether the reasons given for its conclusion adequately explain how the disputed registration was accepted and subsequently maintained.
1. The underlying family ownership claim

The family's position is that our historic Parcel A was a distinct parcel of land around the farmhouse and woodland and that our underlying freehold interest was never lawfully extinguished.

My grandmother, Mary Williams, consistently asserted ownership of the family parcel. The documentary history presently available to me raises a substantial question as to whether Parcel A was ever conveyed to Western Ground Rents in the manner subsequently assumed.

There is an important distinction between:

   - the family-occupied Parcel A surrounding the farmhouse; and
   - the eastern agricultural Parcel B which was the subject of the later agricultural tenancy arrangements.

The 1939 revised agricultural tenancy documentation which I have located appears to concern Parcel B and its associated land. The accompanying plan does not appear to include the family-occupied Parcel A.

This raises a basic documentary question:

What instrument actually conveyed Parcel A to Western Ground Rents, if it was ever conveyed to them at all?

I have not yet obtained a document which satisfactorily answers that question.
2. The 1928 / 1938 / 1939 documentary sequence

The present reconstruction begins with the 1877 arrangements involving the Marquess of Bute and Daniel Thomas & Son and the subsequent quarrying arrangements.

My understanding from the evidence presently assembled is that the relevant quarrying arrangements were completed by 1928 and that the family thereafter continued in occupation of Parcel A as its own land.

The later 1938 conveyancing from the Bute estate to Western Ground Rents therefore requires close examination as to precisely what land was conveyed.

This is particularly important because the 1939 revised agricultural tenancy record naming Western Ground Rents as landlord appears, from its plan, to concern Parcel B rather than Parcel A.

That record was brought to my attention by the clerk for Llandough Town, who directed me to the archive material shortly before his retirement earlier this year.

If Parcel A was not conveyed to Western Ground Rents in 1938, and was not included in the 1939 agricultural tenancy, the subsequent legal narrative by which the family's occupation came to be treated as permissive requires considerably more examination than HM Land Registry's present response appears to have given it.
3. The successive attempts to characterise the family occupation as permissive

The historical evidence reveals a sequence of events which I believe needs to be examined as a whole rather than in isolation.

These include:

*1949* — an attempted tenancy arrangement concerning Parcel B which appears to have sought to include my grandmother in the tenancy and thereby connect her occupation of Parcel A with the agricultural tenancy of Parcel B;

*1951* — the disappearance of important family papers, including the family's title documentation, which my grandmother reported as stolen;

*1955* — possession proceedings in which the language concerning the “whole farm” requires comparison with the actual definition of the agricultural holding and its separate parcels. The order also expressly excluded the “house and garden” and referred to my grandmother's “condition and resistance”;

*1959* — an offer of a tenancy of the farmhouse and garden, which my grandmother rejected while continuing to assert an ownership claim;

*1962* — a possession order concerning the farmhouse and garden, the legal effect and subsequent enforcement history of which require examination;

*1965* — a further attempt to place “Mrs Williams” into a weekly tenancy, again rejected;

*1974* — an ownership action was adjourned; leave to enforce the 1962 possession order was obtained but the warrant was not pursued; and BP subsequently relied upon the two letters of 31 October 1974 as establishing a licence relationship.

The family interpretation is that these were not independent, isolated events but a succession of attempts to convert or present an allegedly proprietary occupation as permissive.

I appreciate that this is an interpretation requiring documentary testing. That is precisely why I believe HM Land Registry should have engaged with the underlying documents rather than treating the later registered position and the 1987 Court of Appeal judgment as effectively resolving the matter.
4. The 1987 judgment does not answer the documentary provenance question

A particularly important part of my complaint concerns the way HM Land Registry has relied upon *BP Properties Ltd v Buckler* [1987] EWCA Civ 2.

I do not dispute that this was an important Court of Appeal decision.

However, the case concerned the adverse-possession and possession issues concerning the farmhouse and garden. The Court considered the registered/paper-title position relied upon by BP, the previous possession proceedings and the legal effect of the 1974 letters upon the character of Mrs Buckler's occupation.

The judgment itself records that Mary Williams had asserted that she had a title to Great House Farm through her grandfather and believed that documents existed establishing that title, but that such documents were not produced.

The point is therefore not that the Court of Appeal “never touched title”. It plainly considered BP's registered/paper-title position.

The point is narrower and, in my view, fundamental:

The 1987 judgment is not itself the conveyance, plan, root deed or other documentary instrument establishing how the woodland and the family's historic Parcel A entered BP's registered title.

Nor did it adjudicate the validity of Forest of Cardiff's separate 1994 acquisition of the woodland.

I am concerned that HM Land Registry's present response treats the 1987 judgment as though it answers a documentary provenance question which it did not determine.
5. The 1969 conveyance and 1971 abstract

HM Land Registry has also told me that BP supplied a title chain extending back to 1969.

That raises another substantial documentary issue.

There were only thirteen years between the 1969 conveyance and BP's first registration in 1982.

The 1969 conveyance from Western Ground Rents to BP Pension Trust therefore requires examination as to exactly what proprietary interest was being conveyed.

I understand the later title documentation to recite the 1969 conveyance as a root document, while the 1971 abstract refers to the 1962 possession order and an OS plan.

If the underlying title to Parcel A was never conveyed to Western Ground Rents, the critical question is how an asserted interest arising from possession proceedings could subsequently be treated as though it were documentary title to the parcel itself.

The 1971 abstract is therefore particularly important.

HM Land Registry's own correspondence has recorded that such an abstract was lodged. The 30 July 2026 schedule of surviving first-registration documents does not identify the 31 December 1969 conveyance itself, nor does it resolve the evidential gap concerning the 1971 abstract.

I am continuing to pursue those underlying records.
6. The 1982–83 registrations

My principal concern is that BP may have registered not the family's actual historic Parcel A, supported by a lawful root title, but a later constructed or “synthetic” parcel derived from the succession of possession, tenancy and licence documents which had been used to characterise the family occupation as permissive.

I use “synthetic parcel” as a description of the issue I am investigating, not as a statement that this is already legally established.

The essential question is:

What precise land did BP apply to register in 1982–83, what documentary instrument entitled BP to register that land, and did that land correspond to the land actually conveyed to BP's predecessors?

The later amalgamation of the BP titles is also significant because what may have originated as separate parcels or interests appears subsequently to have been brought together within the registered estate.

It is necessary to establish whether that process merely recorded an existing lawful title or whether it caused an underlying proprietary boundary to disappear within a later registered estate.
7. HM Land Registry's response

HM Land Registry has now maintained that it was correct to register the land and has relied, in part, upon the 1987 judgment.

I respectfully submit that this does not answer the complaint.

An administrative conclusion that a registration was “correct” cannot itself reconstruct a missing conveyance, establish the precise boundary of land conveyed decades earlier, or demonstrate that a later registered proprietor had documentary title to a distinct parcel where the underlying conveyancing remains disputed.

Nor does the existence of the 1987 judgment establish the documentary provenance of WA735527 or the validity of the separate 1994 transfer to Forest of Cardiff.

I am particularly concerned that HM Land Registry appears to regard its reliance upon the 1987 judgment as effectively validating the 1982–83 registration, when the registration itself pre-dated the judgment.

The chronology matters.

The registration came first.

The litigation came afterwards.

I therefore cannot see how a later judgment concerning possession and adverse possession can, without further analysis, resolve whether the earlier registration accurately represented the documentary title existing at the date of registration.
8. Notification and my grandmother's death

Another issue which requires consideration is notification.

To my knowledge, the family was not notified that BP had applied to register the relevant land in 1982.

My grandmother died on 14 March 1983, shortly after the first registration and within the period in which the registration would have been capable of being challenged had she known of it.

She had spent decades rejecting attempts to characterise her occupation as permissive and consistently maintaining an ownership claim.

The fact that she died shortly after the registration is not itself proof of wrongdoing. It is, however, a material chronological fact when considering whether she had a meaningful opportunity to challenge the registration and whether HM Land Registry appropriately considered the notification history.

I ask the ICR to consider whether HM Land Registry has adequately addressed:

   - what notice was given of the 1982 application;
   - to whom it was given;
   - what information was supplied to the persons potentially affected;
   - whether any competing ownership claim was disclosed by the applicant;
   - and what records exist showing how HM Land Registry assessed those matters.

9. Possible fraud, concealment and institutional involvement

Through my research I have also identified matters which I consider may warrant investigation for possible fraud, deliberate concealment, misrepresentation, mistake and institutional involvement.

I want to be precise about this.

I am not asking the ICR to find that fraud occurred.

I am asking the ICR to consider whether HM Land Registry adequately investigated evidence raising those questions, particularly where the evidence concerns missing historic documents, the distinction between Parcel A and Parcel B, the provenance of the 1969 title, the 1971 abstract, the 1982–83 registrations and the subsequent amalgamation of titles.

I have deliberately distinguished established documentary facts from matters which remain hypotheses requiring investigation.

There are also serious questions concerning the destruction or absence of historical records and the later treatment of the land. Those matters are being pursued through separate archival and documentary channels.
10. The human and public-interest dimension

This is not merely an abstract registration dispute.

My grandmother was a disabled widow and amputee who maintained an ownership claim to the family land through decades of litigation and repeated attempts to characterise her occupation as permissive.

The family was ultimately removed from the property in 1988. The historic farmhouse, which had been our family home and which we believe had significant architectural and historic importance, was subsequently demolished.

I was a child when we were removed.

Family possessions and historic material were lost or dispersed, while the land was subsequently developed and altered.

The family's connection with the site is recorded as extending back to the seventeenth century, and I was born at Great House Farm.

There are also wider heritage and archaeological questions concerning the site and its subsequent development, which I am investigating separately.

I mention these matters because they explain why I have continued the investigation for approximately twenty years and why the accuracy of the underlying land record matters so profoundly to my family.

My professional background is in military cyber and electronic warfare, and much of my research has involved reconstructing fragmented documentary histories and identifying discrepancies between records. I have approached this as an evidential investigation rather than simply as a family grievance.
11. Why I am approaching the ICR

I therefore ask the ICR to review HM Land Registry's handling of my complaint and, in particular, whether it:

   1.

   adequately investigated the distinction between historic Parcel A and Parcel B;
   2.

   adequately considered the 1938 conveyance and 1939 revised tenancy plan;
   3.

   adequately addressed the documentary provenance of the 1969 conveyance and the 1971 abstract;
   4.

   adequately examined the precise land comprised in the 1982–83 registration applications;
   5.

   relied upon the 1987 *BP v Buckler* judgment for a proposition which the judgment itself did not determine;
   6.

   adequately considered the chronology whereby the 1982–83 registration preceded the 1987 judgment;
   7.

   adequately investigated the notification given to persons asserting ownership of the land;
   8.

   adequately addressed the missing or unavailable historic documents and the evidential gaps I have identified;
   9.

   adequately considered the evidence I supplied rather than simply reaffirming the existing registered position; and
   10.

   provided reasons sufficient to explain why, notwithstanding those unresolved documentary questions, HM Land Registry considers that no mistake or registration error occurred.

I am not asking the ICR to adjudicate the family's ultimate title claim.

I am asking for an independent examination of whether HM Land Registry's investigation and reasoning were adequate, proportionate and properly responsive to the evidence and issues actually raised.
12. Documents and evidence

I can provide the relevant correspondence with HM Land Registry, the response to my MP, registration material, historical conveyancing, court records, archival plans, family evidence and other documents relied upon in my complaint.

I also maintain a detailed chronology of the matter, including:

1916 — agricultural tenancy;

1928 — completion of the relevant quarrying arrangements;

1938 — Bute / Western Ground Rents conveyancing;

1939 — revised agricultural tenancy and plan;

1949 — tenancy attempt;

1951 — missing/stolen title documentation issue;

1955 — possession proceedings;

1959 — farmhouse and garden tenancy offer;

1962 — possession order;

1965 — further tenancy attempt;

1969 — Western Ground Rents → BP Pension Trust conveyance;

1971 — abstract and plan material;

1974 — ownership proceedings, possession enforcement history and licence letters;

1975 — BP Pension Trust → BP Properties transfer;

1982 — first registration;

1983 — subsequent registration and title dealings;

1987 — *BP Properties Ltd v Buckler* Court of Appeal judgment;

1988 — final removal from the farmhouse and demolition; and

1994 — subsequent acquisition of the woodland by Forest of Cardiff.

The chronology is significant because it demonstrates why I do not consider the 1987 judgment, standing alone, capable of answering the earlier registration question.
13. What I am asking for

I respectfully ask the ICR to accept this as a request for independent review of HM Land Registry's handling of the complaint.

In particular, I ask that the reviewer consider whether HM Land Registry has actually answered the documentary questions raised, rather than merely reaffirming the registered position.

I would also ask that the underlying Land Registry records relevant to the 1982–83 registration, notification, supporting title documents, plans, the 1969 conveyance and the 1971 abstract be considered where they remain available.

I am not seeking a finding against individual Land Registry staff.

I am seeking an independent assessment of whether the institution's handling of this matter has been adequate and whether the reasons given for refusing to recognise a possible mistake are properly supported by the underlying record.

The issue remains live because the disputed land is now being dealt with through subsequent titles and, in the case of the woodland, is presently subject to a proposed disposal by Forest of Cardiff.

I therefore respectfully ask the ICR to consider this matter on the basis of the documentary chronology and evidence rather than treating the existence of the current register as dispositive of the historical question.

I am willing to provide a structured evidence bundle and chronology to assist the review.

Yours faithfully,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)
Royal Signals Cyber/Electronic Warfare Professional and Life Member

body:
Sirs/ Ma'ams,

I need to correct a date I have used in earlier correspondence about Great House Farm / Tŷ Mawr, Llandough, titles WA231076 and WA240304.

I had treated 1983 as the year the two titles were merged. That was wrong. HM Land Registry’s own letter of 23 March 2026 (Lisa Griffiths, ref N610CGV) separates the two acts.
1982–83 was first registration of two live titles, not a merger. 30 November 1982: application to first-register WA231076. The Court of Appeal later treated BP Properties Ltd as registered proprietors of “the farm” from November 1982.
23 February 1983: application to first-register a second title, WA240304. 26 March 1983: Mary Williams died. On the family’s case, notice of those applications did not reach us until after her death, while the family was in mourning. She had no window in which to object. The family was not in a position to use any window that arrived after that.
Those two titles remained separate through first instance.
24 July 1986: Hollis J. Both titles were still live. The judgment language treats Great House Farm as one holding. It had not been one holding on the register. On the family’s case it had not been one holding since the 1877 split: Parcel A (house, buildings, garden/yard and about 10 acres, the Thomas/Williams line) and Parcel B (the eastern fields retained by Bute and later WGR/BP).
2 February 1987: application to amalgamate the two titles. WA240304 was then closed and registration continued under WA231076. That is the merge. It was made after the 1986 ruling and before the Court of Appeal gave judgment on 31 July 1987.
So 1983 is silent first registration of a second title while Mary was still in Parcel A, or had only just died. 1987 is the administrative merger, carried out while the appeal was still open.
This was not a dispute about a single land parcel that BP already owned. Mary was on Parcel A, which the family says she owned, with occupation on that house parcel running in the family from at least 1667. BP, and WGR before it from 1949, were the neighbouring interest on Parcel B. From 1949 onwards the family’s case is that those neighbours ran a decades-long series of tenancy offers, “whole farm” wording, possession orders and the 1974 letters to make her occupation of her own parcel look permissive, and to make both parcels look like one estate they had acquired. They never produced a conveyance of Parcel A. What they had was an unfounded claim that her occupancy was permissive.
Please treat any earlier letter from me that said the titles merged in 1983 as corrected by this email. The dates that matter are:
1982/83 — first registration of two titles, without the occupier being heard;
24 July 1986 — first-instance judgment describing one farm while two titles still stood;
2 February 1987 — amalgamation, before the appeal ended;
31 July 1987 — Court of Appeal.
Yours faithfully,

Sion Buckler
Refs where relevant: N610CGV; 260919-6726246; titles WA231076 and WA240304. Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)

body:
Thank you for contacting HM Land Registry. This is an automated response to confirm that we have received your correspondence. We aim to formally provide an acknowledgement within three working days. If you have any special requirements that mean you would like us to communicate with you in a specific way, please let us know and we will make adjustments if we can.

If you are contacting us in respect of any matters relating to property registration or have a general customer enquiry – Our team are unable to respond to any general registration enquiries or provide updates on any property applications. Please redirect your customer enquiry to our Customer Support colleagues, using any of the methods below:

  * Online contact form: HM Land Registry Contact Us form<https://customerhelp.landregistry.gov.uk/guide-page-external/?stepid=2b31bc48-eb96-eb11-b1ac-002248413956>
  * Website - www.gov.uk/guidance/contact-hm-land-registry<http://www.gov.uk/guidance/contact-hm-land-registry>
  * Telephone
  * English language 0300 006 0411
  * Welsh language 0300 006 0422

Telephone lines are open between 08:00 and 17:00 Monday to Thursday. This does not include Bank Holidays.

  * Post

HM Land Registry Citizen Centre
PO Box 74
Gloucester
GL14 9BB

There is no direct contact e-mail address for Customer Support. Please use the online contact form and any responses will be issued via e-mail.

If you have made a request under the Freedom of Information Act or Environmental Information Regulations – the statutory timescale for response is 20 working days following receipt of your request.

If you have made a request in relation to your data rights, for example, a subject access request for personal data – the statutory timescale for response is one calendar month following receipt of your request.

Please note that where personal data is held on our register, it is exempt from the right of subject access under UK GDPR.

Where any personal data is held on record for a registered title, the exemption provided at Schedule 2, Part 1, Paragraph 5(1) of the Data Protection Act 2018 would be engaged.

This states:

“5(1) The listed GDPR provisions do not apply to personal data consisting of information that the controller is obliged by an enactment to make available to the public, to the extent that the application of those provisions would prevent the controller from complying with that obligation.”

Please see the section below titled 'Register information and your data protection rights' for further explanation.

If you have only copied your correspondence to us - we will not respond.

Yours sincerely

Information Rights Team
HM Land Registry

Accessing information held by HMLR on our register of title

To assist you in accessing information held by HMLR, please be aware most of the information held within our registers is open to public inspection and accessible via statutory routes of access. This means that we may be unable to provide access to this information via a Freedom of Information Act 2000 (FOIA) request.

Statutory Routes of Access to information held on Public Registers

The Land Registration Act 2002 is the principal legislation governing land registration in England and Wales. It sets out provisions for keeping a register of title to land and property, and in accordance with Section 66 & 67 of the Land Registration Act, it is a requirement that the Chief Land Registrar makes this information (including any documents held on the register of title) available for public inspection.

How to access information held on our Registers

The information you have requested is available to access under our statutory protocol under section 66 & 67 of the Land Registration Act 2002.

Search for Land and Property

Please visit our website for further information about our registers:

www.gov.uk/get-information-about-property-and-land<http://www.gov.uk/get-information-about-property-and-land>

Official Copies

For information about how to apply for official copies of documents held in relation to registered titles, and information about the types of documents available, please refer to practice guide 11:

www.gov.uk/government/publications/inspection-and-application-for-official-copies/practice-guide-11-inspection-and-application-for-official-copies<http://www.gov.uk/government/publications/inspection-and-application-for-official-copies/practice-guide-11-inspection-and-application-for-official-copies>

Index of proprietors’ names

Under rule 11 of the Land Registration Rules 2003 the registrar is required to keep an index of proprietors’ names which shows for each individual register the proprietor of the registered estate and the proprietor of any registered charge together with the title number. When you search the index of proprietors’ names, you will receive a list of titles that are owned by, or mortgaged to, the name that you have searched against.

For further information about this please refer to practice guide 74:

www.gov.uk/government/publications/searches-of-the-index-of-proprietors-names/practice-guide-74-searches-of-the-index-of-proprietors-names<http://www.gov.uk/government/publications/searches-of-the-index-of-proprietors-names/practice-guide-74-searches-of-the-index-of-proprietors-names>

Section 21 FOIA exemption: Information accessible to the applicant by other means

Where information held on the register of title is available for inspection through these statutory routes of access it is exempt from disclosure under section 21(2)(b) of FOIA.

Section 21 states:

“21 Information accessible to applicant by other means.

(1) Information which is reasonably accessible to the applicant otherwise than under section 1 is exempt information.

(2) For the purposes of subsection (1)—

(a) information may be reasonably accessible to the applicant even though it is accessible only on payment, and

(b) information is to be taken to be reasonably accessible to the applicant if it is information which the public authority or any other person is obliged by or under any enactment to communicate (otherwise than by making the information available for inspection) to members of the public on request, whether free of charge or on payment.”

Therefore, we are unable to provide information held on our register through FOIA, as it covered by this exemption.

Advice and assistance

Under Section 16 of FOIA and in accordance with the Section 45 FOIA code of practice, we have a duty to provide you with reasonable advice and assistance.

Please note that the ICO has previously reviewed HM Land Registry’s use of the section 21 exemption. Relevant decision notices can be accessed here<https://icosearch.ico.org.uk/s/search.html?collection=ico-meta&profile=decisions&query&query=&f.By+authority%7CpublicAuthority=HM%20Land%20Registry&f.By+section%7CsectionOfLegislation=FOI%2021> including IC-173302-N4J1<https://ico.org.uk/media/action-weve-taken/decision-notices/2022/4022883/ic-173302-n4j1.pdf>, FS50685812<https://ico.org.uk/media/action-weve-taken/decision-notices/2017/2172810/fs50685812.pdf> and FER0454056<https://ico.org.uk/media/action-weve-taken/decision-notices/2012/780474/fer_0454056.pdf>.

The ICO has agreed that this position is long established, and the Commissioner is satisfied that section 21 would be engaged for this type of request.

For assistance on how to obtain official copies of documents you can contact our Customer Support Centre by telephone between 8am and 5pm, Monday to Thursday on 0300 006 0411 or online through our Contact Us<https://customerhelp.landregistry.gov.uk/guide-page-external/?stepid=2b31bc48-eb96-eb11-b1ac-002248413956> form.

Our Customer Support colleagues are trained to handle queries which relate to information that is held on the register of title.

Information about how to apply to inspect or obtain official copies is contained with practice guide 11:

www.gov.uk/government/publications/inspection-and-application-for-official-copies/practice-guide-11-inspection-and-application-for-official-copies<http://www.gov.uk/government/publications/inspection-and-application-for-official-copies/practice-guide-11-inspection-and-application-for-official-copies>

If you need any support completing the application form for official copies or to determine which documents to order, you may contact our Customer Support colleagues:

www.gov.uk/guidance/contact-hm-land-registry<http://www.gov.uk/guidance/contact-hm-land-registry>

You may also refer to our Publication Scheme which includes information about how to access information that is held on the register of title under the heading ‘Request information’:

www.gov.uk/government/organisations/land-registry/about/publication-scheme#request-information<http://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/land-registry/about/publication-scheme#request-information>

Please refer to HMLR’s Transaction Data webpage which contains information in respect of commonly used abbreviations:

www.gov.uk/guidance/hm-land-registry-transaction-data#abbreviations-used-in-transaction-data<http://www.gov.uk/guidance/hm-land-registry-transaction-data#abbreviations-used-in-transaction-data>

If you need any independent advice about individual’s rights under information legislation you can contact the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO). The ICO is the UK’s independent authority set up to uphold information rights in the public interest, promoting openness by public bodies and data privacy for individuals.

The contact details for the ICO are detailed below. There is useful information on the ICO website which explains the rights of individuals:

www.ico.org.uk/for-the-public<http://www.ico.org.uk/for-the-public>

Please refer to the top tips:

www.ico.org.uk/for-the-public/official-information<http://www.ico.org.uk/for-the-public/official-information/>

Register information and your data protection rights

Data protection law permits HM Land Registry to use personal data for our official purposes.

The lawful basis for HM Land Registry processing personal data under the United Kingdom (UK) General Data Protection Regulation (UK GDPR) is that it is necessary to enable us to perform our public task of the registration of land and property (Article 6(1)(e) of UK GDPR). This is defined in the Land Registration Act 2002.

Paragraph 5 of Schedule 2 Part 1 of the Data Protection Act 2018 provides the following exemption from the specified UK GDPR provisions:

“The listed UK GDPR provisions do not apply to personal data consisting of information that the controller is obliged by an enactment to make available to the public, to the extent that the application of those provisions would prevent the controller from complying with that obligation.”

The Land Registration Act 2002 is the principal legislation governing land registration in England and Wales. It sets out provisions for the keeping of a register of title to land and requirements for its administration by HM Land Registry under a Chief Land Registrar.

The Chief Land Registrar is required by the Land Registration Act 2002 and to make register information (including any documents held on the register of title) available to the public, therefore the following data protection provisions do not apply:

  * the requirement to provide ‘privacy notices’ to individuals
  * the requirement to provide personal data in response to subject access requests
  * the requirement to rectification
  * the requirement to comply with requests to erasure (right to be ‘forgotten’)
  * most of the principles of UK GDPR

Please visit our website for further information about our registers:

www.gov.uk/get-information-about-property-and-land<https://www.gov.uk/get-information-about-property-and-land>

For further information in relation to your rights and how HMLR processes personal data please refer to our Personal Information Charter:

www.gov.uk/government/organisations/land-registry/about/personal-information-charter<http://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/land-registry/about/personal-information-charter>

HM Land Registry’s purpose is to protect your land ownership and provide services and data that underpin an efficient and informed property market. Our vision is: “A world-leading property market as part of a thriving economy and a sustainable future”.

We check all mail and attachments for known viruses. However, you are advised that you open any attachments at your own risk. If you have received this email and it was not intended for you, please let us know, then delete it.

We welcome correspondence in English and Welsh.

To see how HM Land Registry treats your personal information, read our Personal information charter: www.gov.uk/government/organisations/land-registry/about/personal-information-charter.

2 February 1987: application to amalgamate the two titles. WA240304 was then closed and registration continued under WA231076. That is the merge. It was made after the 1986 ruling and before the Court of Appeal gave judgment on 31 July 1987.
So 1983 is silent first registration of a second title while Mary was still in Parcel A, or had only just died. 1987 is the administrative merger, carried out while the appeal was still open.
This was not a dispute about a single land parcel that BP already owned. Mary was on Parcel A, which the family says she owned, with occupation on that house parcel running in the family from at least 1667. BP, and WGR before it from 1949, were the neighbouring interest on Parcel B. From 1949 onwards the family’s case is that those neighbours ran a decades-long series of tenancy offers, “whole farm” wording, possession orders and the 1974 letters to make her occupation of her own parcel look permissive, and to make both parcels look like one estate they had acquired. They never produced a conveyance of Parcel A. What they had was an unfounded claim that her occupancy was permissive.
Please treat any earlier letter from me that said the titles merged in 1983 as corrected by this email. The dates that matter are:
1982/83 — first registration of two titles, without the occupier being heard;
24 July 1986 — first-instance judgment describing one farm while two titles still stood;
2 February 1987 — amalgamation, before the appeal ended;
31 July 1987 — Court of Appeal.
Yours faithfully,

Sion Buckler
Refs where relevant: N610CGV; 260919-6726246; titles WA231076 and WA240304.
Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)
greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com
